It cannot excuse slavery, trafficking, fraud, violence, or the sale of another person’s freedom. It cannot absolve one from duties of care toward those who cannot protect themselves.

Nor does a person’s consent eliminate the duty to act wisely. A clinician must not offer a harmful treatment simply because a patient requests it. A friend need not participate in self-destruction to prove loyalty. A society may prohibit practices that predictably produce grave harm even when some participants profess willingness, particularly where economic desperation or entrenched inequality makes willingness difficult to distinguish from compulsion.

The moral life requires both freedom and responsibility. Consent protects persons from being used. Justice protects persons from being abandoned.

propositions.title: Repair After Violation
propositions.text:
When consent has been ignored, repair begins with truth.

The person who crossed a boundary must stop the harmful conduct, acknowledge what occurred without evasion, and accept responsibility without demanding immediate forgiveness. “I did not mean to,” “I misunderstood,” or “I was hurt too” may describe circumstances, but they do not erase impact. Explanations must not become escape routes.

A meaningful apology names the wrong, recognizes its effect, offers practical repair where possible, and changes behavior. It does not ask the injured person to comfort the one who caused harm. It does not seek public absolution while avoiding private accountability. It does not make reconciliation a condition of justice.

Those harmed should be believed with seriousness, treated with dignity, offered choices, and given support without being compelled into a single path. Some may seek dialogue; others may need distance. Some may pursue legal remedy; others may not. Healing cannot be commanded on a timetable convenient to institutions or offenders.

Forgiveness, if it comes, is a gift. It is never owed.

propositions.title: A Practice of Reverence
propositions.text:
To honor consent is to recognize that every person is more than a role in one’s own story. They are not raw material for another’s plans. They possess an interior world that cannot be entered by force without moral injury.

This recognition calls for humility. We do not always know what another person wants. We may misread silence, politeness, habit, fear, or affection. Therefore we ask. We listen. We make room for a changed mind. We accept limits without resentment.

The person who hears “no” and remains kind has learned something holy.

The person who asks before taking has learned something holy.

The person who uses power to enlarge another’s freedom rather than diminish it has learned something holy.

Let every home, workplace, school, gathering, and place of devotion become a place where people need not guard themselves against those who claim to care for them. Let authority become service. Let desire become attentive. Let speech become clear. Let refusal be safe.

For where consent is honored, dignity has room to breathe.

propositions.title: The Measure of Justice
propositions.text:
Do not measure a society by the splendour of its buildings, the abundance of its goods, or the refinement of its speech. Measure it by these things:

- Whether the poor can obtain food, shelter, medicine, and safety without surrendering their dignity.
- Whether children are protected from neglect, violence, exploitation, and despair.
- Whether the powerful are answerable for the harms they cause.
- Whether strangers are treated as human beings before they are treated as problems.
- Whether those accused of wrongdoing are judged by evidence rather than prejudice, panic, or convenience.
- Whether those harmed are heard, believed with care, and supported without being made to bear the burden of repair alone.
- Whether punishment serves the good of persons and communities, or merely satisfies the appetite to retaliate.
- Whether the land, waters, air, and creatures are guarded against ruin for the sake of short-lived gain.
- Whether future generations inherit a world made more livable, not less.

Justice is not achieved when rules are written. It is achieved when persons can live without being crushed by rules designed for someone else’s advantage.

A law may be lawful and still be unjust. A tradition may be ancient and still be cruel. A majority may prevail and still be wrong. Do not call something good merely because it is familiar, profitable, popular, or protected by authority.

The test is not whether power has spoken. The test is whether truth, dignity, and the common good have been served.

propositions.title: Every Person Has Equal Worth
propositions.text:
No person is born to be another’s instrument.

No one is made lesser by poverty, disability, illness, age, race, ancestry, sex, gender, desire, language, citizenship, religion, lack of religion, social rank, imprisonment, or past failure. These conditions may shape a person’s experience; they do not reduce a person’s worth.

To say that all persons possess equal worth does not mean all persons have equal needs, equal responsibilities, or equal power. It means that no person may be treated as if their pain counts for less, their voice matters less, or their future may be traded away more easily.

Justice therefore gives particular attention to those who bear the heaviest burdens and possess the weakest means of resisting them.

When a table is too small, do not first ask who deserves to be excluded. Ask why the table was made so small, who has taken more than their share, and how abundance may be increased or fairly distributed.

When a system repeatedly injures the same people, do not blame the injured for failing to thrive within it. Examine the system. Look for the hidden gate, the unequal burden, the arbitrary barrier, the inherited advantage, the rule that is neutral in wording but unequal in effect.

Many injustices are committed without hatred. They are committed through indifference, haste, distance, habit, and the wish not to know. But an injustice does not become harmless because its author did not intend to see it.

Good intentions are worthy. They are not sufficient.

propositions.title: Tell the Truth Before Seeking Peace
propositions.claim: Tell the Truth Before Seeking Peace
propositions.text:
There can be no durable peace built on denial.

Peace without truth is only quietness maintained by fear, exhaustion, or unequal power. It is the silence of the person who has learned that speaking will bring punishment. It is the calm of a household in which one person’s rage governs all others. It is the order of a nation where the comfortable call unrest dangerous but do not ask what despair has made unrest necessary.

Do not demand reconciliation from those who have not been heard. Do not urge forgiveness as a way of avoiding confession. Do not praise civility when it requires the vulnerable to speak gently about wounds that continue to bleed.

First, tell the truth.

Name what happened. Name who was harmed. Name the conditions that allowed it. Name the benefit gained by those who looked away or profited. Name the repair that is owed.

Truth need not be cruel to be clear. It need not be theatrical to be brave. Speak accurately. Refuse exaggeration, for falsehood weakens a just cause. Refuse concealment, for politeness toward wrongdoing is often cruelty toward those harmed.

Where facts are uncertain, say so. Seek evidence with patience. Listen to more than one account. Protect the accused from false judgment and the harmed from intimidation. Justice is not served by replacing one careless certainty with another.

Yet uncertainty must not become an excuse for endless delay. There are times when the evidence is incomplete but the danger is plain. If a child may be harmed, protect the child. If a worker may be injured, stop the dangerous work. If a community may be poisoned, prevent the poisoning. Investigation and protection must proceed together.

propositions.title: The Duties of Those Who Hold Power
propositions.claim: The Duties of Those Who Hold Power
propositions.text:
Power is never merely private.

The parent has power over the child. The teacher over the student. The employer over the worker. The landlord over the tenant. The physician over the patient. The officer over the detained. The editor over the unheard voice. The judge over the accused. The wealthy over conditions shaped by their wealth. The state over all who live within its reach.

Because power can protect or injure, every power carries duties.

Those entrusted with authority must be transparent enough to be examined, humble enough to be corrected, and restrained enough not to confuse their office with their person. They must explain decisions that affect others. They must welcome oversight. They must not hide cruelty behind procedure or failure behind secrecy.

The greater the power, the greater the obligation to account for its use.

Do not ask only whether an official acted within the limits of policy. Ask whether the policy itself honors human dignity. A procedure that reliably produces hunger, homelessness, preventable illness, unjust imprisonment, or exclusion from public life is not redeemed by being correctly followed.

Leaders must hear those who bear the consequences of their decisions. A policy made without the participation of those most affected is often blind before it is enacted.

Therefore let councils include the poor when poverty is discussed, workers when labor is discussed, disabled persons when access is discussed, young people when the future is discussed, and those harmed when repair is discussed. Nothing about people should be decided as though they were absent from the room.

propositions.title: Repair Is More Than Punishment
propositions.text:
When harm has been done, there must be accountability. To deny this is to abandon the injured and to permit wrongdoing to grow.

But accountability is more than inflicting pain in return for pain.

A just response asks:

1. What harm occurred?
2. Who has been harmed, directly and indirectly?
3. What does safety require now?
4. What truth must be acknowledged?
5. What repair is possible?
6. What responsibility must the wrongdoer accept?
7. What conditions allowed the harm, and how must they change?
8. What limits are necessary to prevent further harm?

Punishment may sometimes be necessary. A person who continues to threaten others may need to be restrained. A person who has abused trust may need to lose authority. A person who has taken what belongs to another may owe restitution. These measures are not failures of compassion when they are proportionate, evidence-based, subject to review, and directed toward protection and repair.

But do not make punishment an idol.

A person is more than the worst act they have committed. This does not erase the act, nor does it require the harmed to offer closeness, trust, or forgiveness. It means that justice should leave open, wherever safely possible, the path of truthful repentance and changed conduct.

Repentance is not a feeling. It is not public sorrow without private change. It is not an apology that asks the harmed to comfort the one who caused harm.

Repentance is the acceptance of responsibility, the ending of deception, the making of restitution, the willingness to endure fair consequences, and the sustained labor of becoming trustworthy.

Forgiveness, when it comes, is a gift. It cannot be demanded by families, institutions, courts, religious leaders, or public opinion. No one is required to forgive in order to prove goodness. Justice must never depend upon the victim’s capacity to offer grace.

propositions.title: Economic Justice and the Common Wealth
propositions.claim: Economic Justice and the Common Wealth
propositions.text:
It is unjust for some to possess excess beyond meaningful use while others lack what is necessary for life.

Food, clean water, shelter, health care, education, meaningful work, rest, safety, and participation in community are not prizes reserved for the fortunate. They are conditions through which human dignity becomes livable.

A wage that cannot sustain a worker is not fully earned compensation; it is a transfer of cost from the employer to the worker’s body, family, and future. A home treated only as a financial asset becomes unavailable to those who need a place to live. Medicine withheld because it cannot yield sufficient profit turns illness into a marketplace. Debt that cannot reasonably be repaid becomes a form of captivity.

Those who have received much are not guilty merely for having much. But possession creates responsibility. Wealth is held within a web of labor, law, public infrastructure, natural resources, and social trust. No fortune is made by one person alone.

Therefore let prosperity serve more than its owner. Pay fairly. Share gains. Honor labor. Prevent exploitation. Support institutions that provide for the common good. Give generously, but do not imagine that charity alone can repair systems designed to produce need.

Alms may relieve suffering. Justice asks why suffering was made so predictable.

propositions.title: Justice for the Earth and for the Future
propositions.claim: Justice for the Earth and for the Future
propositions.text:
The earth is not an inheritance from the powerful. It is a trust shared with all living beings and with generations not yet born.

To poison water, strip soil, destroy forests, empty seas, foul the air, or alter the climate beyond safety is to commit theft against those who will live after us. They cannot vote in our assemblies or plead in our courts, yet they will bear the consequences of our choices.

The poor are often harmed first and most severely by environmental destruction, though they have contributed least to its causes. Justice therefore requires that the costs of transition not be placed upon those already burdened. Workers whose livelihoods depend on harmful industries deserve practical pathways into secure and dignified work. Communities long used as dumping grounds deserve restoration, investment, and a decisive voice in decisions affecting their land.

Do not call destruction necessary when it is merely profitable. Do not call delay prudent when delay transfers danger to those with less power.

The question is not whether human beings may use the earth. We must. The question is whether we will use it with gratitude, restraint, and care.

propositions.title: Practice Justice Near at Hand
propositions.text:
Justice is not only the work of courts, legislatures, and nations. It begins in daily conduct.

Do not take credit for another’s work.  
Do not laugh when someone is diminished.  
Do not repeat a rumor that may damage a life.  
Do not demand unpaid labor from those with less power.  
Do not make access difficult for those whose bodies or minds move differently from your own.  
Do not use complicated language to conceal an unfair agreement.  
Do not remain silent when prejudice is spoken in your presence.  
Do not let affection excuse abuse.  
Do not let loyalty become a shield for misconduct.  
Do not confuse neutrality with innocence when one side is being harmed.

Learn the names and stories of those whom your comfort makes easy to overlook. Buy, hire, vote, organize, teach, give, and speak in ways that widen the circle of safety and belonging.

You will not repair every injustice. No single person can. But do not let the size of the wound excuse the refusal to bind it where you stand.

A small act may not transform a system by itself, yet systems endure through countless small permissions. Withdraw those permissions. Replace them with courage, honesty, and solidarity.

propositions.title: The Hope of Justice
propositions.text:
Justice is difficult because people are complicated, facts are contested, resources are limited, and every remedy can bring new burdens. Beware those who promise perfect purity, effortless solutions, or salvation through the destruction of enemies.

Still, difficulty is not a reason for surrender.

The work of justice is slow because it asks more of us than outrage. It asks attention. It asks learning. It asks sacrifice from those who benefit from unfair arrangements. It asks patience from those who have already waited too long. It asks institutions to change, and persons to change within them.

Yet this work is not barren. Wherever truth is spoken, harm is prevented, wages are made fair, a child is protected, a prisoner is treated as human, a wrong is confessed, a neighbor is welcomed, or a river is defended, justice has entered the world again.

Let justice be firm without becoming cruel, compassionate without becoming permissive, and wise without becoming cold.

Do not seek a world in which no one is ever accountable. Seek a world in which every person is accountable to the dignity of every other person.

For justice is not the enemy of mercy.

Justice makes mercy trustworthy.

propositions.title: The Question Beneath Every Choice
propositions.text:
People often ask what they must do. They ask for rules, permissions, boundaries, and penalties. Such questions are necessary, for actions have consequences and communities require justice. Yet beneath the question of what one must do lies a deeper question: **What kind of person is one becoming by what one repeatedly chooses?**

This is the question of virtue.

A virtuous person is not one who has never failed, nor one who has mastered the appearance of goodness. Such a person may be admired and yet remain ruled by fear, vanity, resentment, or hunger for praise. Virtue is not a costume worn before others. It is the formation of the inner life so that what is good becomes increasingly natural, reliable, and free.

The good person does not merely tell the truth when watched. The good person becomes a keeper of truth. The generous person does not merely give when gratitude is assured. The generous person becomes one whose heart is not governed by possession. The courageous person does not become fearless; rather, they learn which fears deserve obedience and which must be carried without surrender.

No person is born complete. Each is given capacities: the ability to attend, to judge, to desire, to remember, to restrain, to repair, and to love. These capacities are shaped by habit. Every repeated act leaves some mark upon the soul. Every lie makes the next lie easier. Every act of cruelty lowers the threshold for cruelty. Every concealed kindness enlarges the room within a person where kindness may dwell.

Therefore do not suppose that a small choice is without weight. A life is assembled from moments that seemed too ordinary to matter.

propositions.title: Virtue Is Love Given Form
propositions.text:
Love without wisdom may become indulgence. Wisdom without love may become coldness. Justice without mercy may harden into punishment for its own sake. Mercy without justice may abandon the injured and call its abandonment peace.

Virtue joins these goods without confusing them.

To love another is not merely to feel warmth toward them. It is to will their flourishing, to regard their dignity as real, and to refuse to use them as an instrument for one’s own appetite, comfort, status, or control. Love gives moral life its direction: outward, toward the good of persons and the healing of the world.

But love must take form. It must become patience when another is difficult; honesty when concealment would be easier; courage when silence protects the powerful; fidelity when desire turns restless; restraint when one possesses the power to harm; generosity when one has more than one needs.

Thus virtue may be understood as love trained into action.

The person of virtue does not love humanity in the abstract while neglecting the neighbor who is inconvenient, dependent, poor, strange, or opposed. Nor do they claim devotion to the sacred while despising the vulnerable. Whatever reverence is genuine will become visible in the treatment of living beings, in the keeping of promises, in the use of wealth, in speech about enemies, and in the care offered to those from whom nothing may be gained.

Let no one call themselves righteous because they speak noble words. The test of a word is the life that follows it.

propositions.title: The Great Virtues
propositions.text:
### Wisdom: Seeing What Is Truly at Stake

Wisdom is the virtue of clear sight. It asks not only, “What can I do?” but also, “What will this make possible? Whom will it burden? What truth am I refusing to see? What good is most worthy here?”

The wise do not confuse cleverness with understanding. Cleverness finds advantage. Wisdom recognizes proportion. Cleverness can win an argument while destroying trust. Wisdom knows when victory would cost too much. Cleverness may conceal harm beneath technical permission. Wisdom perceives that not everything lawful is worthy, and not everything profitable is good.

Wisdom requires humility because reality is larger than any person’s view of it. Listen, therefore, before judging. Learn from those who bear the consequences of decisions made by others. Seek counsel from the experienced, the honest, and the compassionate—not merely from those who confirm what you already desire.

When knowledge is uncertain, do not use uncertainty as an excuse for indifference. Take reasonable care. Ask better questions. Revise your judgment when truth becomes clearer. A person who cannot be corrected cannot become wise.

### Justice: Giving Each Their Due

Justice begins with the recognition that every person possesses a dignity not granted by wealth, rank, talent, usefulness, tribe, belief, or approval. No one becomes disposable because they are weak. No one becomes a mere tool because they are dependent. No one loses their claim upon humane treatment because they have failed.

To act justly is to give due regard to the rights, needs, labor, voice, and vulnerability of others. It is to pay what is owed, tell what is true, honor agreements, reject favoritism, and refuse to benefit from another’s degradation.

Justice is personal, but it is not private. It concerns the household, the marketplace, the court, the workplace, the school, the nation, and every institution through which power passes. A society that praises individual kindness while arranging its common life around exploitation has not yet become just.

Therefore examine the systems from which you benefit. Ask who bears the hidden cost of convenience, luxury, security, and profit. Ask whose work is unseen, whose suffering is normalized, whose voice is dismissed as inconvenient. This inquiry is not an invitation to endless self-accusation. It is an invitation to responsibility.

Where harm has been done, justice seeks repair. It does not confuse revenge with moral seriousness. Revenge delights in the humiliation of an offender. Justice protects the vulnerable, establishes truth, requires accountability, and restores what can be restored. Some wounds cannot be fully repaired, and some trust cannot quickly return. Yet no honest peace can be built upon denial.

### Courage: Carrying Fear Without Betrayal

Courage is not the absence of fear. Fear is often a signal: of danger, loss, pain, uncertainty, or consequence. To feel fear is human. To be ruled by fear in every matter is to surrender one’s freedom.

Courage enables a person to act for the good when the good is costly.

It is courage to speak truth before those who may punish it. It is courage to refuse an unjust command when obedience would be safer. It is courage to apologize without insisting upon immediate forgiveness. It is courage to grieve rather than numb oneself. It is courage to remain tender after suffering has taught one how easily tenderness may be wounded.

Recklessness is not courage. The reckless person seeks danger for display, pleasure, or pride. The courageous person measures the risk, protects those entrusted to them, and proceeds because conscience requires it.

Do not demand dramatic heroism while neglecting the daily courage of ordinary life: the courage to leave what degrades you, to seek help when you are drowning, to defend a person being mocked, to admit ignorance, to begin again after failure.

### Temperance: Freedom From the Tyranny of Appetite

Temperance is the ordering of desire. It does not command hatred of the body, pleasure, beauty, food, rest, intimacy, achievement, or celebration. These are among life’s gifts. But every gift can become a master when pursued without measure.

The intemperate person is not simply one who has much. It is one who cannot say enough. They consume not because they need, but because emptiness has become intolerable. They seek pleasure without tenderness, wealth without responsibility, recognition without service, information without reflection, and power without restraint.

Temperance returns freedom to the soul. It teaches a person to enjoy what is good without being possessed by it. It permits delight, but refuses compulsion. It welcomes abundance, but remembers those in need. It honors desire, but submits desire to love, truth, and responsibility.

Practice restraint not as punishment but as education. Set aside what you could take. Leave room at the table. Rest from the noise that feeds anxiety. Spend less than you can afford when another’s need calls for generosity. Learn that the self does not perish when every craving is not satisfied.

propositions.title: Humility and Truthfulness
propositions.text:
Humility is not self-contempt. It is neither the denial of one’s gifts nor the performance of smallness. The humble person can acknowledge ability, beauty, learning, and achievement without imagining that these make them more human than another.

Humility is truthful proportion.

You are not the center of the world, but neither are you without significance. Your actions matter, but you do not control every outcome. You are responsible for your choices, but you are also shaped by conditions you did not choose: family, history, health, opportunity, injury, culture, and chance. To know this is not to escape responsibility; it is to exercise it with compassion toward oneself and others.

Truthfulness is humility expressed in speech. Speak as accurately as you can. Do not exaggerate to make yourself larger, nor distort another to make them smaller. Do not repeat what you do not know. Do not use ambiguity to deceive while preserving the appearance of honesty.

There are times when silence is wise: to protect a confidence, to prevent needless harm, to make space for another’s voice, or because one does not yet know enough to speak. But silence becomes corrupt when it hides injustice, permits abuse, or protects comfort at the expense of truth.

Let your words be dependable. A community cannot endure where language has become only a weapon, a performance, or a marketplace of manipulation.

propositions.title: Mercy, Forgiveness, and Boundaries
propositions.text:
Mercy sees the person beyond the worst thing they have done. It does not deny wrongdoing; it refuses to reduce a human being entirely to it. Mercy remembers that all are capable of failure, self-deception, and harm. It makes room for repentance, growth, and return.

Yet mercy is not permission for continued injury.

To forgive is to release the claim that one must nourish hatred forever. It is to refuse to let another’s wrong become the ruler of one’s inner life. But forgiveness does not always require reconciliation. Reconciliation requires truth, changed conduct, safety, and the willing participation of those harmed. Where these are absent, distance may be wise and necessary.

Do not command the wounded to forgive on another’s schedule. Do not invoke peace to silence testimony. Do not call a boundary bitterness merely because it disappoints the one who crossed it.

The merciful person may say, “I will not repay evil with evil,” while also saying, “You may not continue to harm me.” Both can be true. Indeed, they often must be true together.

propositions.title: The Practice of Becoming
propositions.text:
Virtue does not descend upon a person as a finished possession. It is cultivated by attention, discipline, friendship, correction, and repeated return.

Begin with an honest examination of the day. Ask: Where did I act from love? Where did fear govern me? Whom did I fail to see? What truth did I avoid? What repair is now mine to make? Give thanks for what was good, not as proof of superiority, but as encouragement to continue. Name what was wrong without excuse, not to drown in shame, but to turn toward a better path.

Choose practices that train the will. Keep promises in small matters. Give regularly, not only when emotion moves you. Make time for silence so that conscience may be heard beneath distraction. Share meals with those unlike yourself. Read voices that challenge your habits of judgment. Serve in places where no applause is offered. Apologize promptly. Receive correction without rushing to defend yourself.

Seek companions who make goodness easier and dishonor more difficult. Friendship is not merely shared pleasure or shared opinion. A true friend rejoices in your growth, warns you when you are becoming cruel, and does not flatter you into ruin. Be such a friend to others.

Remember also that moral formation requires rest. Exhaustion makes patience brittle, judgment hurried, and temptation persuasive. Rest is not a withdrawal from responsibility when it restores one’s capacity to meet responsibility faithfully. Care for the body, the mind, and the spirit, that they may serve love for a long time.

propositions.title: When You Fail
propositions.text:
You will fail. You will speak carelessly, judge unfairly, choose comfort over courage, and discover that your motives were less pure than you believed. Let this knowledge make you sober, not hopeless.

The enemy of virtue is not failure alone. It is the refusal to learn from failure. Pride says, “I have done no wrong.” Despair says, “I can never do good.” Both turn away from truth. Repentance turns toward it.

To repent is to see clearly, to name the harm without disguise, to make repair where possible, and to change one’s direction. It is not self-punishment performed for display. It is a restoration of integrity.

When you have harmed another, do not demand that your apology relieve you of consequence. Do not make your shame the injured person’s burden to comfort. Listen. Repair what you can. Accept that trust may return slowly or not at all. Then live differently.

And when another sincerely turns from harm, do not despise the possibility of their renewal. Hold them accountable, yes. Protect those who may be vulnerable, always. But do not worship the past so completely that transformation becomes unimaginable.

propositions.title: The Measure of a Good Life
propositions.claim: The Measure of a Good Life
propositions.text:
A good life is not measured chiefly by comfort, reputation, possessions, influence, or the number of victories one collects. These may come and go; none can secure the soul.

Ask instead:

Did I become more capable of love?  
Did I use what was entrusted to me without contempt for those who had less?  
Did I tell the truth when it cost me?  
Did I protect the vulnerable when it would have been easier to look away?  
Did I allow suffering to deepen compassion rather than harden me?  
Did I seek justice without losing mercy, and offer mercy without abandoning justice?  
Did I leave the world, in some small and faithful way, more livable for those who came after me?

Virtue is not perfection. It is the steady alignment of the self toward what is true, just, merciful, and life-giving.

Walk this path without pride, for no one completes it alone. Walk it without despair, for each honest return is itself a beginning. Let goodness become not a rare act performed under ideal conditions, but the durable character of your days.

For the world is changed not only by great deeds, but by persons who can be trusted with power, trusted with truth, trusted with another’s pain, and trusted to choose the good when no reward is promised.

propositions.title: The Claim That Every Person May Make
propositions.claim: The Claim That Every Person May Make
propositions.text:
A right is not a favor granted by the strong, nor a reward reserved for the virtuous, nor a permission that may be withdrawn when it becomes inconvenient. A right is a just claim arising from the inherent worth of a being.

To say that a person has rights is to say that there are certain ways in which they must not be treated, certain goods that must not be withheld from them without grave cause, and certain forms of power that no individual, family, institution, market, or state may rightly exercise over them.

Rights are the moral boundary around persons.

They exist because no one is merely an instrument for another’s pleasure, profit, ambition, doctrine, security, or peace of mind. Each person has an inner life: joy and fear, memory and hope, pain and longing, conscience and imagination. Each is a center of experience whose life matters from within. The one who sees this clearly cannot regard another merely as a body to be used, a worker to be spent, a voter to be managed, an enemy to be crushed, or a stranger to be ignored.

The first law of rights is therefore simple:

> Treat every being according to the weight of its own experience, not according to the usefulness it has for you.

This does not mean that every desire creates a right. Desire is real, but it is not sovereign. A person may desire what harms another; a nation may desire what it cannot justly possess; a ruler may desire obedience that conscience cannot give. Rights do not sanctify appetite. They protect the conditions under which beings may live with dignity and develop freely without being subjected to domination.

A right is a claim that can be made even by the powerless. Indeed, it is most necessary when the powerless make it.

propositions.title: The Source of Rights
propositions.text:
Rights do not begin when they are written into law. Law may recognize rights, protect them, betray them, or deny them. But law does not create the fundamental moral reality from which rights arise.

Before any court exists, cruelty wounds. Before any constitution is ratified, hunger weakens. Before any declaration is proclaimed, coercion violates conscience. Before a child can speak, that child has an interest in safety, nourishment, affection, freedom from abuse, and the chance to become fully themselves.

The source of rights is not membership in a tribe, a nation, a faith, a class, or a bloodline. It is not intelligence, productivity, wealth, strength, education, health, or social usefulness. If rights depended on such measures, then the weak would possess fewer rights precisely when they most needed protection.

Rights arise wherever there is a life that can be harmed, constrained, frightened, diminished, deprived, or allowed to flourish.

Human beings therefore possess rights by virtue of their personhood. They are not earned by compliance. The imprisoned person retains rights. The poor person retains rights. The accused person retains rights. The person whose speech offends retains rights. The person who has done wrong retains rights, though they may rightly be restrained from doing further wrong. Even the person whom society finds difficult, alien, dangerous, or shameful remains within the circle of moral concern.

This truth is demanding because it refuses the comfort of selective compassion. It asks us to recognize dignity where admiration is absent.

propositions.title: Rights and Responsibilities
propositions.text:
Every right creates responsibilities in others.

If one person has a right not to be tortured, others have a responsibility not to torture, not to order torture, not to excuse it, not to conceal it, and not to benefit from systems built upon it. If one person has a right to food, then a community that possesses abundance has responsibilities concerning distribution, access, wages, land, care, and emergency relief. If one person has a right to speak freely, others have responsibilities not to silence them through violence, intimidation, censorship, or the calculated destruction of their livelihood.

Rights are not opposed to responsibility. They are made real by responsibility.

Yet responsibility must not be used as a gate through which a person must pass before receiving humane treatment. A hungry person need not prove moral worthiness before eating. A sick person need not display gratitude before receiving care. A child need not obey perfectly before being protected. A refugee need not resemble the host community before being recognized as human.

It is true that freedom asks something of those who possess it. To have freedom of speech is not to possess a license to knowingly destroy another through falsehood. To have freedom of movement is not to possess a right to invade, exploit, or endanger. To have property is not to possess a right to hoard what others require for survival while contributing nothing to the common good.

But these are limits on the misuse of rights, not excuses to abolish rights themselves.

A just society says: *You have rights because you are a person. You also bear responsibilities because other persons have rights too.*

propositions.title: The First Rights
propositions.text:
Certain rights are foundational because without them other rights become hollow promises.

### The Right to Life and Bodily Safety

No person may be intentionally killed, tortured, mutilated, enslaved, raped, disappeared, or subjected to degrading treatment. These acts are not made righteous by patriotism, emergency, revenge, religious language, or obedience to authority.

The right to life includes more than the prohibition of murder. It includes protection from foreseeable conditions that destroy life: famine, preventable disease, unsafe labor, poisoned water, reckless warfare, abandonment in disaster, and the deliberate denial of medical care.

To protect life does not require preserving biological existence at any cost. Persons may refuse burdensome treatment, make informed decisions about their bodies, and meet death with dignity when cure is no longer possible. But no one may treat another’s vulnerability as permission to dispose of them.

### The Right to Liberty

Every person has a claim to freedom from arbitrary control. No one should be owned, bought, sold, confined, monitored, compelled, or governed without lawful and morally defensible reason.

Liberty includes freedom of movement, association, conscience, religion or nonreligion, thought, expression, peaceful assembly, and private life. It includes the right to make ordinary decisions about one’s work, relationships, appearance, beliefs, and future.

Liberty is not isolation. A person becomes free not by escaping all bonds, but by entering bonds that are voluntary, fair, and open to revision. Love without freedom becomes possession. Faith without freedom becomes coercion. Work without freedom becomes servitude. Citizenship without freedom becomes submission.

### The Right to Equal Moral Standing

No person is lesser by reason of race, ancestry, caste, sex, gender, disability, age, language, wealth, social origin, nationality, belief, sexuality, illness, or any other condition that has been used to rank human lives.

Differences are real. They may be beautiful, difficult, meaningful, or politically important. But difference does not justify domination.

Equality does not require sameness. It requires that institutions take each person’s interests seriously and that no one be assigned a lower dignity at birth.

### The Right to Conscience and Truthful Speech

A person must be free to seek truth, to doubt, to question inherited beliefs, to change conviction, and to speak in good faith without fear of violence or oppression.

Conscience is sacred not because every judgment of conscience is correct, but because no human authority can rightfully possess another person’s inner assent. Belief compelled by fear is not faith. Loyalty compelled by threat is not loyalty. Public agreement purchased through censorship is not peace.

This right carries a duty of honesty. Speech that deliberately spreads falsehood, incites violence, or dehumanizes whole peoples is not a noble exercise of liberty. It wounds the shared world in which liberty must live. The answer to error, where possible, is truth spoken clearly; the answer to hateful power is protection of those it threatens; the answer to falsehood is not the creation of a regime in which no one may speak.

propositions.title: Social Rights: The Conditions of Dignity
propositions.claim: Social Rights: The Conditions of Dignity
propositions.text:
A person cannot meaningfully exercise liberty while crushed by hunger, homelessness, untreated illness, illiteracy, or desperation. Formal rights without material conditions become promises written above a locked door.

Therefore every person has a claim to the basic conditions of a dignified life: sufficient food, clean water, shelter, healthcare, education, safety, meaningful participation in society, and a fair opportunity to contribute through work or other valued activity.

These claims do not mean that every need must be met by the same institution or through the same policy. Families, neighborhoods, voluntary associations, cooperatives, markets, professions, and public governments may all share in the work. But the responsibility cannot be abandoned. When a society allows preventable deprivation amid available means, it has failed in justice.

The right to work means more than access to any task under any condition. It includes fair compensation, safe conditions, reasonable rest, protection from exploitation, and the ability to organize with others. An economy is not just when it produces wealth while treating workers as replaceable parts.

The right to education means more than training for employment. Education should cultivate literacy, judgment, curiosity, historical understanding, practical capability, and the ability to recognize manipulation. A people unable to think freely may be formally free while easily ruled.

The right to healthcare means that sickness must not become a sentence of abandonment. Care should be guided by need, informed consent, professional integrity, and fair allocation of limited resources. No system can remove mortality; every system can choose whether illness will be accompanied by dignity or neglect.

propositions.title: Rights of Children and Dependent Persons
propositions.claim: Rights of Children and Dependent Persons
propositions.text:
Children possess rights not because they will someday become adults, but because they are persons now.

They have a right to protection from violence, exploitation, neglect, and humiliation. They have a right to nourishment, healthcare, education, play, stable care, and relationships of reliable affection. They have a right to grow without being made the instruments of adult conflict, economic desperation, ideological ambition, or family honor.

Parents and caregivers bear profound responsibilities. Their authority is a trust, not a possession. They may guide children, teach them, set reasonable limits, and introduce them to a moral and cultural inheritance. But they may not treat children as property or punish them in ways that destroy their safety, dignity, or developing conscience.

The same principle applies to elders, disabled persons, people with severe illness, and all who depend upon others for support. Dependency does not diminish dignity. It makes the duties of care more visible.

A society should be judged in part by how it treats those who cannot easily defend themselves.

propositions.title: Rights in Conflict
propositions.text:
Rights sometimes conflict. Freedom of expression may conflict with protection from targeted harassment. Privacy may conflict with public safety. Property may conflict with urgent need. Parental authority may conflict with a child’s welfare. National security may conflict with liberty. No wise ethics denies these tensions.

But conflict must be approached with discipline.

First, do not invent a conflict merely because respecting another person’s rights requires sacrifice. The inconvenience of the powerful is not equal to the injury of the vulnerable.

Second, ask what right is at stake, what harm is concrete, what alternatives exist, and who bears the burden of the proposed restriction. Restrictions on rights must be necessary, proportionate, publicly accountable, and open to challenge. Power should always be required to explain itself.

Third, preserve as much of each right as possible. When liberty must be limited to prevent direct harm, the limit should be narrow rather than sweeping, temporary rather than permanent, reviewable rather than secret.

Fourth, never permit emergency to become a permanent excuse. Fear enlarges authority quickly and returns freedom slowly. A society that sacrifices every right to security may discover that it has secured only the power of those who govern.

propositions.title: The Rights of Peoples, Creatures, and Future Generations
propositions.claim: The Rights of Peoples, Creatures, and Future Generations
propositions.text:
Persons live within communities, cultures, ecosystems, and generations. Rights therefore have dimensions beyond the isolated individual.

Peoples have a right to preserve their language, memory, culture, and collective life, provided they do not use that preservation as a reason to oppress those within or beyond their community. No people should be conquered, displaced, erased, or forced to abandon its identity for the comfort of another.

The natural world is not merely a storehouse of materials. Human beings depend upon air, water, soil, climate, and living systems they did not create. Future generations, though unable to vote or protest, have a claim upon our restraint. We may use the earth, but we may not consume its conditions of renewal as though no one will come after us.

Nonhuman animals, too, are not objects without moral significance. Where creatures can suffer, humans have duties of care. We must not inflict needless pain for amusement, vanity, convenience, or profit. Human survival may require the use of animals and natural resources; necessity does not erase the obligation to reduce suffering, avoid waste, and act with humility.

The circle of rights and duties widens as moral vision deepens.

propositions.title: The Practice of Rights
propositions.text:
Rights are defended not only in courts and charters, though both are necessary. They are defended in homes, workplaces, schools, hospitals, places of worship, streets, prisons, and private conversations.

They are defended when a parent listens to a child.  
When a worker refuses to join in cruelty toward a colleague.  
When a citizen protects the speech of one they disagree with.  
When a physician honors informed consent.  
When a community welcomes the stranger.  
When a judge remembers that the accused is still human.  
When a majority restrains itself because the minority is not safe without restraint.  
When a person with power chooses accountability over impunity.

Rights require institutions, but institutions are shaped by habits of heart. A constitution cannot save a people committed to humiliation. A law cannot fully protect those whom a culture has learned not to see.

Therefore let each person ask:

*Whose dignity have I treated as negotiable?*  
*Whose voice have I dismissed because it carried less power than mine?*  
*What comfort of mine depends upon another’s vulnerability?*  
*What right do I demand for myself while denying it to another?*

The defense of rights begins in this honesty.

For every person wishes to be safe from cruelty, heard in truth, free in conscience, protected in weakness, and treated as more than a means. What we rightly seek for ourselves, we must learn to secure for others.

This is not generosity beyond justice. It is justice itself.

propositions.title: The Difficulty of Doing Good
propositions.text:
There are times when the path of harm is plain. Cruelty, betrayal, exploitation, contempt for the vulnerable, and delight in another’s suffering do not become good because they are profitable, customary, or defended by many voices. Moral life begins with the courage to name such things honestly.

Yet much of the deepest difficulty in human life does not arise from choosing between obvious good and obvious evil. It arises when two real goods appear to demand our loyalty at once: truth and kindness; justice and mercy; loyalty to one person and responsibility to many; peace and protection; forgiveness and accountability; personal conscience and communal duty.

A parent may discover that their child has committed a serious wrong. Love calls them to protect the child from despair; justice calls them not to conceal the harm. A physician may have to speak a grave prognosis to a frightened patient. Truth requires honesty; compassion requires care in how truth is given. A citizen may oppose an unjust law and thereby place family, employment, or safety at risk. Prudence counsels caution; conscience refuses consent to injustice.

These are moral conflicts. They should not be treated as proof that morality has failed. They are evidence that human beings live among real responsibilities, real relationships, and real consequences. A shallow morality offers quick rules for complex circumstances. A mature morality teaches the heart and mind how to discern.

The purpose of ethical wisdom is not to remove every painful choice. It is to form persons who can meet painful choices without surrendering their humanity.

propositions.title: Not Every Inner Struggle Is a True Conflict
propositions.claim: Not Every Inner Struggle Is a True Conflict
propositions.text:
Before deciding that duties conflict, a person should ask whether the conflict is genuine. Many apparent dilemmas are created by fear, pride, convenience, or an unwillingness to imagine a better path.

Someone may say, “I must either tell the truth and destroy this relationship, or lie and preserve it.” But perhaps there is a third course: speaking truth patiently, at the right time, without accusation or humiliation. Someone may say, “I must either help this person endlessly or abandon them.” But perhaps help can be offered with boundaries that prevent dependence and resentment.

The mind often presents a false choice when it is tired, threatened, or eager to escape discomfort. Therefore, do not rush to call a hard decision impossible. Pause. Seek facts. Listen to those affected. Consider what has not yet been considered.

Still, not every conflict can be dissolved by ingenuity. There are situations in which every available action carries loss. A judge may have to sentence a person who is guilty and yet deeply repentant. A leader may need to protect a community from violence by using force that no decent person could celebrate. A caregiver may need to choose between treatments, knowing that one life may be prolonged only at the cost of another’s suffering.

When no innocent path is available, the task is not to pretend that all choices are equal. The task is to discern which action most faithfully serves life, truth, justice, and love—and then to bear the remaining sorrow without denial.

propositions.title: The First Duty: See Clearly
propositions.text:
Moral conflict is often worsened by confusion. People make grave choices on the basis of rumor, partial knowledge, inherited prejudice, or the urgency of emotion. Therefore the first duty in a difficult case is attention.

Ask:

- What has actually happened?
- Who is affected, including those whose voices are absent or weak?
- What power is being exercised, and over whom?
- What duties have been undertaken by promise, role, or relationship?
- What harms are immediate, and what harms may unfold over time?
- What facts remain uncertain?
- What desires in me may be distorting my judgment?

Truthful attention is an act of respect. It refuses to use people as symbols in someone else’s argument. It notices the particular child, worker, neighbor, patient, stranger, opponent, and future generation whose life will be touched by the decision.

Facts alone do not tell us what is right. But morality without facts becomes fantasy. A compassionate intention cannot excuse a decision made carelessly. Nor may a person hide behind good intentions while refusing to learn the foreseeable consequences of their actions.

To see clearly also means to see oneself clearly. The human heart is skilled at calling self-interest “necessity,” cowardice “prudence,” domination “order,” and indifference “neutrality.” In moral conflict, ask not only, “What do I want?” but also, “What am I reluctant to admit?”

A conscience that never questions itself is not necessarily strong. It may simply be unexamined.

propositions.title: The Goods That Must Guide Judgment
propositions.claim: The Goods That Must Guide Judgment
propositions.text:
No single rule can settle every conflict. Yet certain moral goods should remain before the conscience as enduring lights.

### The Worth of Every Person

No purpose, however noble, permits treating persons merely as instruments. Human beings are not raw material for another’s ambition, ideology, comfort, or reputation. They possess a dignity that does not depend on usefulness, strength, innocence, wealth, nationality, belief, health, or social approval.

This principle does not mean that every desire must be granted or every choice protected from consequence. It means that even those who must be restrained, opposed, punished, or corrected must not be degraded. Justice may require limits; it must never require contempt.

Whenever a proposed solution depends upon deception, humiliation, abandonment, torture, collective blame, or the deliberate destruction of the innocent, it has crossed a moral boundary. A good end cannot purify a means that denies the humanity of those involved.

### Truthfulness

Truth is not merely accuracy of statement. It is faithfulness to reality. It includes refusing lies, manipulation, concealment for selfish advantage, and speech designed to make another person doubt what they rightly know.

Yet truthfulness is not brutality. To tell the truth well is to consider timing, context, vulnerability, and purpose. A truth spoken to wound is not made virtuous by its factual correctness. There is a difference between candor and cruelty.

Some information should be protected: personal confidences, medical details, the location of those in danger, and knowledge entrusted for legitimate care. Privacy is not the same as deception. But secrecy becomes corrupt when it shields abuse, fraud, violence, or grave injustice from those who have a rightful claim to know.

### Justice

Justice gives each person their due: protection from harm, recognition of rights, accountability for wrong, fair access to common goods, and a meaningful place in the community.

Justice is not identical with punishment. Punishment may sometimes be necessary, particularly when it protects others or acknowledges serious harm. But punishment that serves only revenge deforms both the punished and the punisher. The aim of justice should be truthful accountability, restoration where possible, protection of the vulnerable, and the repair of damaged trust.

When mercy is offered without justice, those harmed may be forgotten. When justice is pursued without mercy, persons may be reduced to their worst act. Moral wisdom holds both truths together: wrong must be named, and no person is only their wrongdoing.

### Compassion

Compassion is not sentimentality. It is the disciplined refusal to remain indifferent to another’s suffering. It asks what pain is present, what burden can be relieved, and what support may help a person recover agency and hope.

Compassion sometimes gives; sometimes it refuses. Giving money to sustain a destructive addiction may feel kind in the moment but may deepen harm. Refusing may be painful, but a refusal joined to practical help, truthful explanation, and continued regard can be more loving than indulgence.

Compassion must extend beyond those who are familiar, agreeable, or useful. Moral concern that stops at the boundary of one’s own tribe is loyalty, not yet love.

### Fidelity

Promises, commitments, and relationships matter. A society in which no one can rely upon a vow, contract, confidence, or shared responsibility becomes unstable and fearful.

Yet fidelity is not obedience to wrongdoing. No promise binds a person to assist abuse, conceal crime, preserve corruption, or remain silent before grave harm. The duty to protect life and dignity can require the breaking of an improper secret or the refusal of an unjust command.

When a commitment must be broken for a higher moral reason, do not do so lightly or secretly for convenience. Name the reason. Accept responsibility. Repair what can be repaired. Fidelity is honored not by blind compliance, but by faithfulness to the good for which commitment exists.

propositions.title: A Way of Discernment
propositions.text:
When duties pull in different directions, proceed with patience.

First, name the conflict without disguising it. Say plainly what goods are at stake. “I wish to protect my friend, but I also have a duty not to conceal harm.” “I want peace, but I must not purchase peace by permitting abuse.” Clear language prevents the conscience from hiding behind vague unease.

Second, identify the non-negotiable limits. Some acts should not be chosen even under pressure: deliberate cruelty, betrayal of the innocent, exploitation, torture, racial or collective hatred, and the intentional use of people as disposable means. A difficult outcome does not justify every method.

Third, consider the least harmful faithful action. When every option carries cost, seek the course that protects dignity most fully, prevents the gravest foreseeable harm, and leaves open the greatest possibility of repair.

Fourth, consult others wisely. Seek counsel from people who are honest, informed, and not invested in flattering your preference. Include, where possible, those who will bear the consequences. A decision about the poor should not exclude the poor; a decision about workers should not ignore workers; a decision about children should not treat children as invisible.

Fifth, examine motive. Would you make the same choice if no one praised you? If your opponent made it, would you still call it just? Are you acting from love, fear, resentment, vanity, or the desire to avoid inconvenience?

Sixth, act with proportion. The greater the harm a decision may cause, the stronger the reason required to justify it. Minor benefits do not excuse major injuries. One may not ruin a person’s livelihood to avoid an awkward conversation, nor endanger many lives merely to preserve institutional reputation.

Seventh, remain accountable after acting. A moral decision is not complete when the choice is made. Ask what consequences followed. Listen to those harmed. Make restitution where possible. Revise future practice. The person of conscience does not say, “My intentions were good; therefore nothing more is required.” They ask, “What has my action done, and what must I now do?”

propositions.title: When Authority and Conscience Collide
propositions.text:
Families, communities, professions, governments, and religious institutions require authority. Shared life cannot endure if every person treats every obligation as optional. But authority exists to serve the good of persons and communities; it does not create goodness simply by issuing commands.

An order may be legal and still unjust. A tradition may be venerable and still require correction. A leader may be sincere and still be wrong. Therefore no human authority should demand the surrender of conscience.

Conscience, however, is not mere preference. It is not the inner voice that says, “I dislike this,” or, “This costs too much.” A mature conscience is formed through truthfulness, self-examination, compassion, knowledge, and willingness to be corrected. It is humble enough to learn and courageous enough to resist.

When conscience requires dissent, dissent should be as truthful and disciplined as possible. Do not imitate the injustice you oppose. Do not spread falsehood to defeat falsehood. Do not dehumanize those whose actions you resist. Speak clearly, protect those in danger, accept appropriate consequences, and seek change rather than humiliation.

There are times when silence is a form of participation. If a colleague is being abused, if public resources are being stolen, if a child is endangered, if a people are being denied their humanity, private disapproval is not enough. Courage may require witness.

propositions.title: The Place of Regret
propositions.text:
A morally serious life includes regret. Not all regret means that one chose wrongly. Sometimes regret is the sorrow that remains after choosing the least harmful course in a tragic situation.

A firefighter who cannot save everyone may carry grief. A physician who respects a patient’s difficult decision may still mourn the outcome. A person who reports a loved one’s violence may feel both relief and heartbreak. These feelings do not prove moral failure. They show that the heart has not become numb.

Do not seek a conscience free from all pain. Seek a conscience free from evasion. There is a difference between remorse, which recognizes wrongdoing and calls us toward repair, and endless self-condemnation, which keeps attention fixed on oneself.

Where wrong has been done, confess it without excuse. Apologize specifically. Restore what can be restored. Accept consequences. Learn. Where grief remains despite a faithful choice, receive it as part of the cost of loving a world that is not yet whole.

propositions.title: Choosing in Hope
propositions.text:
Moral conflict can tempt people toward cynicism. They may conclude that every action is corrupt, every leader hypocritical, every institution beyond repair, and every ideal naïve. This conclusion is understandable, but it is false.

The presence of conflict does not mean that good is unreal. It means that good must be pursued amid limitation. A person cannot always achieve a perfect outcome, but they can refuse needless harm. They can tell the truth more honestly, distribute burdens more fairly, protect someone who would otherwise be abandoned, and repair a portion of what has been broken.

Ethical life is not the search for moral purity at a safe distance from the world. It is the practice of responsible love within the world as it is.

Therefore, when faced with conflict, do not ask only, “How can I remain blameless?” Ask also, “What does love require of me here? Who needs protection? What truth must be spoken? What harm must not be allowed? What repair can begin?”

Then act with courage, humility, and care.

The good is not always easy to see. It is not always possible to accomplish without loss. But it remains worthy of our loyalty.

propositions.title: The Measure of a Life
propositions.text:
A human life cannot be reduced to a single measure. Wealth matters because hunger and insecurity deform the spirit. Health matters because pain and exhaustion narrow the world. Knowledge matters because ignorance leaves people vulnerable to manipulation and harm. Love matters because no person flourishes alone. Justice matters because private happiness built on public misery is a moral fraud.

Yet none of these, held alone, is sufficient.

A wealthy person may be ruled by fear of losing what they own. A healthy person may use strength to dominate the weak. A learned person may become arrogant. A beloved person may refuse the duties of love. A just cause may be pursued with hatred until it resembles the injustice it opposes.

The good life gathers what is worthy into a coherent whole. It asks not only, “What do I have?” but also, “What am I becoming through the way I seek it?”

Therefore, when judging a life, do not ask first whether it appears impressive. Ask:

- Does this life reduce or increase needless suffering?
- Does it make room for truth, even when truth is inconvenient?
- Does it nourish love without demanding possession?
- Does it cultivate courage without worshipping violence?
- Does it enlarge the freedom and dignity of others?
- Does it leave the world, where possible, more habitable than it was found?

These questions do not provide a simple score. Life is more intricate than a ledger. But they turn the heart toward its proper work.

The good life is not a performance for spectators. It can be lived in public office or in obscurity; in a crowded city or a quiet village; in prosperity or under limitation. Its deepest signs are often ordinary: a promise kept, a meal shared, a wrong admitted, a child protected, a stranger treated as fully human, a task done carefully though no one is watching.

propositions.title: To Be Awake in One’s Own Life
propositions.claim: To Be Awake in One’s Own Life
propositions.text:
Many lives are spent half-awake. People inherit ambitions without examining them. They pursue approval from those they do not respect. They fill their hours with noise because silence might reveal their loneliness, grief, or uncertainty. They become busy not because their work is necessary, but because stillness feels dangerous.

To live well requires attention.

Attention is the beginning of ethical life because we cannot care responsibly for what we refuse to see. We must notice the condition of our bodies, the habits of our minds, the needs of our neighbours, the consequences of our purchases, the labour concealed beneath convenience, and the suffering made invisible by distance.

Attention does not mean anxious self-surveillance. It means presence.

Be present to your own life. Know what brings you alive and what leaves you diminished. Notice when anger is warning you of a violated boundary, and when it is merely disguising wounded pride. Notice when pleasure restores you, and when it is being used to avoid grief. Notice which relationships ask you to become more honest, and which demand that you become smaller.

A person who knows nothing of their own motives is easily governed by appetite, flattery, and fear. A person who sees themselves clearly is not freed from weakness, but becomes able to choose differently.

This is why regular reflection is not a luxury. It is a form of inner housekeeping. At the end of a day, ask: Where was I generous? Where was I careless? What did I avoid? Whom did I fail to see? What should I repair tomorrow?

Such questions are not meant to produce shame. Shame says, “You are beyond repair.” Conscience says, “This can be repaired; begin.” The first imprisons. The second restores.

propositions.title: Enough: The Discipline of Sufficiency
propositions.text:
One of the great moral confusions is the belief that more is always better. More money, more possessions, more recognition, more influence, more choices, more speed. But every increase carries a cost. Possessions require attention. Status requires maintenance. Endless choice can weaken commitment. Speed can destroy perception.

The good life requires enough.

Enough food, shelter, safety, health care, rest, education, beauty, companionship, and meaningful opportunity: these are not luxuries. They are conditions of human dignity. A society that withholds them from many while permitting excess for a few has confused wealth with worth.

But beyond sufficiency, accumulation often becomes a burden. The person who cannot say “enough” is not rich, whatever their account may show. They remain governed by lack.

Sufficiency is not denial of enjoyment. It is the ability to receive good things without becoming their servant. Eat with pleasure, but do not make appetite your ruler. Earn honestly, but do not make gain your god. Seek beauty, but do not consume beauty as proof of superiority. Build a home, but remember that a home is made holy by welcome, not by expense.

The practice of enough also has a public meaning. The earth is not an inexhaustible storehouse provided for the appetite of the powerful. Its waters, soils, forests, creatures, and atmosphere are conditions of life shared across generations. To take without restraint is to steal from those not yet born.

Therefore, let your comfort be conscious. Ask what your way of living requires of distant workers, vulnerable communities, animals, and ecosystems. No person can live without impact. The task is not purity, which is impossible, but responsibility: to learn, to reduce harm, to repair where one can, and to support systems that allow all to live with dignity.

propositions.title: Work, Craft, and Service
propositions.text:
Work is part of the good life when it gives shape to ability and contributes to the common good. It need not be glamorous. Much of the work that sustains life is repetitive, hidden, and insufficiently honoured: caring for children, tending the sick, preparing food, cleaning shared spaces, maintaining infrastructure, listening to the distressed, teaching the unformed, repairing what is broken.

No honest labour that serves life is beneath dignity.

Yet work becomes destructive when it consumes the whole person. A society that praises exhaustion as devotion and treats rest as laziness has lost moral balance. Human beings are not machines for output. They require sleep, friendship, play, contemplation, and unproductive time. A life entirely organized around earning cannot fully flourish, even when earnings are necessary.

Seek work that uses your gifts where possible. If circumstances do not permit this, seek dignity within the work available, and do not confuse your occupation with your entire worth. A person is more than their title, wage, productivity, or public usefulness.

Whatever your work, do it with integrity. Learn its consequences. Refuse deception. Do not conceal danger for profit. Do not benefit from another’s ignorance when their safety or livelihood is at stake. Give proper credit. Pay fairly when you hold power. If your work injures people or corrupts the world, do not hide behind the excuse that “everyone does it” or “I was only following orders.”

There are times when conscience requires refusal. Such refusal may carry a cost. But a livelihood gained by destroying one’s moral centre is too expensive.

The good worker is not merely efficient. The good worker is trustworthy.

propositions.title: Love Without Possession
propositions.text:
No account of the good life is complete without love. To love and to be loved are among the deepest human needs. But love is often confused with dependency, control, romance, admiration, obligation, or fear of being alone.

Love is the steady willingness to seek another’s good while honouring their freedom and reality.

To love a person is not to make them an instrument of your happiness. It is not to demand that they heal wounds you refuse to examine. It is not to call jealousy devotion, surveillance protection, or domination care. Love does not require the disappearance of the self, nor does it ask another to disappear.

Good love is truthful. It speaks honestly, listens seriously, apologizes without evasion, and permits disagreement without contempt. It celebrates another’s flourishing even when that flourishing changes the relationship. It gives help without humiliating. It receives help without pretending invulnerability.

Friendship is one of the great schools of this love. A true friend does not merely confirm your preferred image of yourself. They tell you when you have become cruel, foolish, reckless, or vain. They do so not to win power over you, but because your life matters to them.

Family, too, can be a place of profound care, but no bond of blood makes harm acceptable. Where family is loving, cherish it. Where it is wounded, seek repair if repair is possible. Where it is abusive, coercive, or dangerous, distance may be an act of wisdom. No one is commanded to remain available for mistreatment in the name of duty.

The good life includes belonging, but it does not require captivity.

propositions.title: Pleasure, Beauty, and Joy
propositions.text:
A moral life need not be grim.

There is goodness in laughter that does not humiliate, in music that opens the heart, in food prepared with care, in gardens, stories, games, dancing, companionship, and the quiet astonishment of morning light. Beauty does not solve every problem, but it reminds us why solutions matter. It gives the soul a reason to remain faithful to life.

Receive joy without suspicion. Many people have been taught to distrust happiness, as though pleasure were shallow and seriousness were proof of depth. Yet joy can be a form of gratitude. It says: this moment is real; this life, despite its wounds, contains gifts.

But distinguish joy from distraction. Distraction leaves emptiness behind; joy enlarges the capacity to meet life. Distraction numbs; joy awakens. Distraction consumes time; joy makes time feel inhabited.

Cultivate the kinds of pleasure that leave you more generous, more rested, more connected, and more able to face reality.

propositions.title: Justice as a Condition of Personal Flourishing
propositions.claim: Justice as a Condition of Personal Flourishing
propositions.text:
No person can live entirely well inside an unjust order. One may find private comforts, but the suffering of others will remain part of the moral atmosphere. When people are denied food, safety, education, political voice, bodily autonomy, or equal standing before the law, the common life is injured.

Therefore the good life is never merely private.

To seek justice is not to claim moral superiority. It is to recognize that each person’s life has weight. The poor are not failed versions of the wealthy. The disabled are not lesser lives. Foreigners are not less human because they were born elsewhere. Those who differ in race, sex, gender, religion, language, or custom do not require permission to possess dignity. No nation, tradition, or majority is excused from this truth.

Justice requires more than kind feelings. It requires fair institutions, accountable power, honest law, accessible education, decent work, health care, and protection from violence. It requires attention to the ways advantage is inherited and harm is organized.

Do not let the size of these tasks make you passive. Few can change everything; all can refuse indifference. Vote or participate where participation is possible. Learn the conditions under which others live. Support those doing necessary work. Challenge cruelty in ordinary speech. Give time, resources, skill, or protection. Organize when private charity cannot address public wrong.

A good life leaves room for pleasure, but not for complacency.

propositions.title: The Courage to Begin Again
propositions.text:
No one lives well without failure. We speak carelessly. We become defensive. We neglect those we love. We mistake convenience for necessity. We fail to act when action was required. We sometimes cause harm without intending it, and sometimes with motives we would rather not confess.

The question is not whether you will fail. The question is what you will do afterward.

Do not make excuses where apology is due. Do not confuse regret with repair. If you have harmed another, listen to the harm as they name it. Admit what is true. Restore what can be restored. Change the pattern that produced the injury. Accept that forgiveness, though beautiful, cannot be demanded.

Likewise, do not make an identity from your worst act. People are responsible for what they have done, yet human beings are more than the worst thing they have done. Transformation is possible when truth, accountability, and sustained change meet. Communities should protect those at risk, but they should also preserve paths by which the wrongdoer may become trustworthy again.

Mercy without accountability becomes permission. Accountability without mercy becomes despair. The good life requires both.

Each morning offers a beginning, not because the past is erased, but because the future remains open. Let yesterday instruct you, but do not let it imprison you. The work of becoming good is never finished; this is not a cause for discouragement. It is a reason for humility, patience, and hope.

propositions.title: A Rule for the Days We Are Given
propositions.claim: A Rule for the Days We Are Given
propositions.text:
When uncertain how to live, begin simply.

Tell the truth as fully as kindness permits.  
Keep your promises, and repair those you break.  
Care for your body without worshipping it.  
Make time for those whose lives are bound to yours.  
Earn and spend without deception or needless harm.  
Learn continuously.  
Rest without guilt.  
Enjoy beauty.  
Protect the vulnerable.  
Refuse contempt.  
Use power to enlarge the freedom of others.  
When you are wrong, turn around.

And remember that the good life is not elsewhere. It is not waiting beyond a final achievement, a perfect relationship, a larger home, a cleaner reputation, or an imagined future in which difficulty has disappeared.

It is here: in the next honest word, the next act of courage, the next meal shared, the next harm prevented, the next mercy made real.

Live so that your presence becomes, in however small a measure, good news to the world.

propositions.title: Love Is the Measure
propositions.text:
Love is not merely one virtue among many. It is the measure by which every virtue is known.

Courage without love may become domination. Truth without love may become a weapon. Discipline without love may become cruelty dressed in order. Generosity without love may become a bargain for admiration. Even devotion, when emptied of love, may become an escape from the living world.

Love gives the good its direction.

It is not softness in the face of harm. It is not agreement with every desire. It is not the refusal to judge what destroys life. Love can say no. Love can leave. Love can grieve. Love can resist. But even in resistance, love refuses to make another person less than human.

To love is to recognize that no life is disposable—not your own, not the life of a stranger, not the life of one who has failed you, and not the life of one who stands against you.

This recognition does not make all relationships possible. It does not erase consequence. It does not command you to remain where you are wounded, threatened, deceived, or diminished. Love is not the denial of reality. It is the decision to meet reality without surrendering the heart to contempt.

The one who loves well does not ask first, “What may I take?” Nor only, “What must I give?” They ask, “What serves the life between us? What makes truth possible? What protects dignity? What allows each person to become more whole?”

Love begins there.

propositions.title: Love Is Attention
propositions.text:
Most people do not hunger first for praise. They hunger to be seen.

To be seen is not to be watched. It is not to be analyzed, managed, or turned into a story that serves another person’s needs. To be seen is to be received as one truly is: with one’s visible strengths and hidden fears, one’s history and contradictions, one’s hopes not yet spoken aloud.

Attention is one of love’s first forms.
