These faces must be held together. A society that only forbids harm may permit abandonment. A society that only commands care may become intrusive and coercive. Wisdom distinguishes between aid freely offered, aid fairly shared, and aid improperly compelled. But no wise society calls abandonment liberty.

Every later law must answer to the first law. Property law must answer to it. Family law, labor law, criminal law, immigration law, commercial law, and the law of war must answer to it. When any legal order protects privilege while leaving people without bread, shelter, medicine, safety, voice, or recourse, it has mistaken possession for justice.

propositions.title: Law Must Be Knowable
propositions.text:
No person should be punished under a rule that could not reasonably be known.

Laws must be public, understandable, stable enough to guide conduct, and applied consistently. Secret rules are instruments of domination. Vague prohibitions invite selective enforcement. Constantly changing commands turn citizenship into a guessing game in which only the well-connected can be safe.

Those who make law must write plainly. If a rule cannot be explained in the common speech of the people affected by it, its authors may not yet understand it themselves. Technical precision has its place, especially where medicine, engineering, finance, or public safety are concerned; but precision is not the same as obscurity. The people must be able to know what is required of them, what protections they possess, and how they may challenge an abuse.

No penalty should be imposed retroactively. No accusation should become a conviction without evidence. No person should be treated as guilty merely because they are poor, unpopular, foreign, ill, disabled, politically opposed, or associated with someone accused.

The state must not demand perfect obedience from persons while governing by hidden standards of its own. Its records, reasons, expenditures, and procedures should be open wherever openness does not endanger genuine safety or violate the privacy of those entrusted to its care. Power that cannot endure examination is power already inclined toward corruption.

propositions.title: The Equal Worth of Every Person
propositions.claim: The Equal Worth of Every Person
propositions.text:
The law must recognize each person as a bearer of equal worth.

Equal worth does not mean that every person has the same talents, needs, responsibilities, history, or capacities. It means that no person may be counted as naturally lesser: not because of ancestry, skin, sex, gender, religion, lack of religion, language, nationality, caste, disability, wealth, poverty, age, occupation, or opinion.

A law that gives protection only to the admired is not law but favoritism. A court that hears the wealthy more clearly than the poor is not blind; it is trained to look away. A society that criminalizes survival while excusing predation has inverted moral order.

Equality before law requires more than identical words on paper. If one person can hire counsel, understand the system, take time away from work, pay fees, and obtain documents, while another cannot, then formal equality may conceal actual exclusion. Justice requires practical access: interpreters, public defenders, accessible buildings and records, fair notice, affordable procedures, protection for witnesses, and remedies that do not depend upon wealth.

The law must especially guard those who stand at its edges: children, elders, prisoners, migrants, minorities, persons living with disability, persons without secure housing, and all who are likely to be disbelieved or ignored. This is not favoritism. It is the correction of unequal exposure to harm.

The measure is not whether everyone is treated identically. The measure is whether each person can stand before the law as a person rather than as a burden, a threat, or a category.

propositions.title: Authority Is a Trust, Not a Possession
propositions.claim: Authority Is a Trust, Not a Possession
propositions.text:
Those who exercise public authority are custodians, not owners, of power.

A judge does not own the court. A police officer does not own the street. A legislator does not own the law. A minister does not own the public treasury. An administrator does not own the records entrusted to their office. All hold their authority temporarily and answerably, for the sake of the people and the generations not yet born.

Authority becomes dangerous when it forgets its source. The purpose of public power is not to magnify itself, defend its prestige, reward its friends, or silence its critics. Its purpose is to secure the conditions in which people may live freely and responsibly together.

For this reason, power must be divided, limited, reviewed, and renewed. No person, office, party, corporation, religious body, military force, or majority should be beyond law. The greater the power, the greater the obligation to explain its use and submit it to independent scrutiny.

Public servants must not use office to enrich themselves or their households. They must not punish critics through selective enforcement. They must not conceal conflicts of interest. They must not use emergency powers as a permanent door around public consent. They must not invoke security to cover ordinary embarrassment, greed, or political advantage.

When officials break the law, their station must not shield them from accountability. The injury done by an official is often greater than the same injury done by a private person, because it misuses the trust held in common. To excuse abuses of office is to teach the public that law is merely a weapon in the hands of the powerful.

propositions.title: Justice Requires Fair Process
propositions.text:
The path to judgment matters as much as the judgment itself.

A person accused of wrongdoing must be told clearly what is alleged, given sufficient time and means to answer, permitted to examine the evidence, and judged by a body capable of independence. Evidence obtained through torture, coercion, deception that destroys basic fairness, or unlawful intrusion carries the stain of its origin. A system that permits such methods may obtain confessions, but it cannot obtain justice.

No one should be compelled to prove their innocence. The burden rests on those who accuse. Doubt must count in favor of liberty, for the cost of wrongly punishing one person is not confined to that person alone. It wounds families, distorts institutions, hardens communities, and teaches all citizens that they are secure only until power turns toward them.

Judges and decision-makers must give reasons. A bare declaration—*because we say so*—is not sufficient where a person’s liberty, livelihood, home, family, or reputation is at stake. Reasons allow errors to be seen, appealed, corrected, and learned from. They are a discipline against arbitrary power.

Appeal is not an insult to the first judgment. It is an acknowledgment of human fallibility. Every system makes mistakes. The question is whether it has the humility and courage to repair them.

Where a wrong judgment has been made, correction must be real. The innocent must be released, records amended, losses addressed, and responsible institutions required to learn. An apology without repair is only a refined form of dismissal.

propositions.title: Harm, Responsibility, and Repair
propositions.text:
The proper aim of law is not vengeance. It is protection, truth, responsibility, repair, and, where possible, restoration.

Some persons cause great harm. Communities have a duty to protect people from violence, coercion, fraud, abuse, and persistent predation. In certain cases, separation or restraint is necessary. To deny this is not mercy; it is negligence toward those at risk.

But restraint must never become cruelty. A person may lose certain freedoms through just process, yet does not lose their humanity. Food, shelter, medical care, communication, legal counsel, protection from violence, and the possibility of learning and change remain due. Degradation does not heal the injured. Humiliation does not make a community safer. Torture corrupts everyone it touches.

Punishment should be proportionate to harm, necessity, intention, capacity, and likelihood of future danger. It should not be enlarged because a crowd desires spectacle or because an official wishes to appear strong. The law must distinguish between accident and malice, desperation and greed, immaturity and deliberate cruelty, error and corruption.

Whenever possible, justice should ask:

- What harm was done?
- Who has been harmed, including those not immediately visible?
- What does safety now require?
- What truth must be acknowledged?
- What repair is possible?
- What responsibility must the wrongdoer bear?
- What conditions allowed the harm, and how can they be changed?

Restorative processes can be powerful when entered freely, carefully, and safely. They must never pressure victims into forgiveness or contact with those who harmed them. Forgiveness is a gift, not a legal debt. Reconciliation is worthy when it is truthful and voluntary; it is false when it requires the injured to deny their injury.

propositions.title: Property, Work, and the Common Good
propositions.claim: Property, Work, and the Common Good
propositions.text:
The law may protect property, but property is not above life.

A home, a tool, a field, savings earned through honest labor, and the fruits of invention deserve protection. Security in possession allows persons to plan, create, care for families, and participate in society without continual fear of arbitrary seizure.

Yet ownership carries obligations. No one’s claim over land, water, housing, knowledge, or capital permits the destruction of the conditions by which others live. A right to profit does not include a right to poison a river, exploit workers, manipulate the desperate, monopolize necessities, or leave habitable homes empty while people sleep without shelter.

Work must be governed by fairness. Those whose labor creates wealth are entitled to safety, rest, meaningful voice, and compensation sufficient for a dignified life. Children must not be used as instruments of profit. Workers must not be forced to choose between hunger and danger. Care work, often hidden and unevenly assigned, must be recognized as real work upon which every society depends.

Contracts made under severe desperation are not fully free. A person who accepts ruinous terms to avoid hunger, homelessness, deportation, or untreated illness may have signed a document, but a just society does not mistake compulsion for consent.

The law must protect the commons: air, water, soil, forests, oceans, public knowledge, civic trust, and the stable climate that makes civilization possible. These are not inheritances to be consumed by one generation. They are gifts held in trust for all.

propositions.title: Civil Disobedience and the Courage to Refuse
propositions.claim: Civil Disobedience and the Courage to Refuse
propositions.text:
When law commands clear injustice, conscience may require refusal.

This is a grave matter and must not be treated lightly. Personal preference is not enough. Inconvenience is not oppression. A citizen should ordinarily seek change through persuasion, voting, organizing, petition, litigation, public witness, and all peaceful means available.

But when legal systems protect grave wrong—when they command participation in persecution, violence, theft, discrimination, or destruction—obedience may become complicity. Then principled disobedience can serve the law’s deepest purpose by refusing the corruption of its outward form.

Such disobedience should be truthful, disciplined, and directed toward justice rather than humiliation. It should avoid harming uninvolved people wherever possible. It should not delight in chaos. Its aim is not to replace one tyranny with another, but to awaken the conscience of the community and restore the equal dignity that unjust law has denied.

Those who resist unjust authority must also examine themselves. Anger may reveal injury, but anger alone cannot govern. The oppressed are not required to be gentle in order to deserve justice; yet every movement must guard against becoming what it opposes.

propositions.title: The Law Written in Practice
propositions.text:
No society is judged only by its constitution, its courts, or its grand declarations. It is judged by the ordinary encounter: the worker seeking wages, the tenant facing eviction, the child reporting harm, the prisoner needing medicine, the refugee asking for hearing, the debtor receiving notice, the grieving family seeking truth.

In these places, law becomes either a shelter or a threat.

Let every judge remember that a case file contains a human life. Let every officer remember that force, once used, cannot be taken back. Let every legislator remember that words written in chambers enter kitchens, classrooms, clinics, workshops, and cells. Let every citizen remember that law is not an object maintained by others. It is a shared practice of refusing cruelty, telling truth, honoring commitments, and defending the vulnerable.

The highest law is not a sentence carved in stone. It is the living recognition that no one is outside concern.

Make laws that the poor need not fear, that the powerful cannot purchase, that children may inherit without shame, and that strangers may recognize as just. Let law be firm against oppression and gentle toward human frailty. Let it be clear in principle, patient in inquiry, courageous in repair, and humble before the truth.

For where law serves dignity, peace has a foundation. Where law serves power alone, even silence is full of violence.

propositions.title: The Purpose of Public Power
propositions.text:
Government exists because people live together.

Where one person lives alone, there may be need for discipline, memory, shelter, and care; but there is no government. Government begins when lives touch: when roads are shared, when water is drawn from the same source, when children cross the same streets, when illness travels from one home to another, when wealth is gathered through the labor of many, and when the strong might take what the weak cannot protect.

Public power is therefore not an ornament of society, nor a prize to be claimed by the ambitious. It is a trust held on behalf of all.

Its first duty is not to glorify the state, defend the comfort of rulers, preserve ancient arrangements, or make citizens obedient. Its first duty is to secure the conditions in which persons may live with dignity, freedom, safety, and mutual regard.

A government is good not because it is feared, praised, ancient, efficient, or victorious. It is good insofar as it protects the equal worth of persons; restrains violence and domination; administers common goods wisely; corrects preventable injustice; and remains answerable to those whose lives it governs.

No office is sacred in itself. No flag, building, title, uniform, or constitution is beyond moral examination. Institutions deserve loyalty only insofar as they remain faithful to the people and purposes for which they exist.

The people do not exist to serve the government. Government exists to serve the people.

propositions.title: The Equal Standing of Every Person
propositions.claim: The Equal Standing of Every Person
propositions.text:
Every person subject to public power must be regarded as fully human before the law and in the conscience of those who govern.

This includes the poor and prosperous, the native-born and newcomer, the majority and minority, the popular and unpopular, the healthy and disabled, the accused and the injured, the believer and the doubter, the young and old, the settled and displaced. It includes those who can vote, those who cannot vote, and those whose voices are easily ignored.

No person may be treated merely as a tool for the comfort, profit, purity, security, or prestige of another group.

A government betrays its purpose when it divides people into classes of greater and lesser humanity. It does so when it grants dignity only to those of a favored ancestry, religion, language, gender, wealth, party, caste, or manner of life. It does so when it calls cruelty “order,” exclusion “tradition,” exploitation “growth,” or silence “unity.”

The law must not become a polished language for old prejudices.

Equality does not require that every person live the same life, hold the same belief, possess the same talent, or receive the same outcome regardless of circumstance. It requires that each person be entitled to equal concern and respect, equal protection from arbitrary power, and a genuine opportunity to participate in the common life.

Where unequal conditions are inherited, entrenched, or deliberately maintained, merely declaring equality is insufficient. Public institutions must examine whether their rules preserve advantage for some while closing doors to others. Justice is not achieved by impartial words applied to unequal realities without thought.

propositions.title: Authority Must Be Accountable
propositions.text:
Power without accountability decays, even when its first intentions are honorable.

Those entrusted with public authority must be visible in their actions, intelligible in their reasons, and answerable for their decisions. They must explain how public money is spent, how laws are enforced, how contracts are awarded, how emergencies are declared, and how force is used.

Secrecy may sometimes be necessary to protect lives, investigations, or the security of a people. But secrecy is dangerous when it protects embarrassment, corruption, favoritism, or illegality. What is concealed for too long becomes difficult to correct. What cannot be questioned becomes easy to abuse.

Therefore, a healthy society establishes independent courts, free and responsible journalism, public records, inspectors, auditors, civic associations, lawful protest, regular elections, and institutions capable of investigating those in power.

No leader should appoint only those who will praise them. No legislature should surrender its judgment to an executive. No court should become the instrument of a party. No police force should investigate itself alone. No military should become the private possession of a ruler. No wealthy person or corporation should purchase a louder voice than the public itself.

The separation of powers is not an inconvenience to strong leadership. It is a safeguard against the ordinary temptation to become unanswerable.

A government that resents scrutiny has forgotten that public office is not ownership. It is stewardship.

propositions.title: Law and Justice
propositions.text:
Law is necessary, but law is not identical with justice.

Laws provide shared expectations. They define rights, duties, procedures, and remedies. They enable strangers to cooperate and give protection against arbitrary whim. Without law, the vulnerable are often left to the mercy of the powerful.

Yet a law may be clear and still be cruel. It may be consistently applied and still be unjust. It may be old, popular, profitable, or constitutionally valid and still violate the dignity of persons.

History has repeatedly shown that grave wrongs may be performed under legal authority. Enslavement, dispossession, persecution, censorship, and exclusion have often worn the clothing of law. For this reason, obedience to law must never become obedience to injustice.

The just citizen respects lawful order because social life requires it. But the conscientious citizen also recognizes a higher duty: not to cooperate willingly with acts that deny human dignity.

Civil disobedience, when undertaken openly, nonviolently, responsibly, and with willingness to accept legal consequences, may be a necessary appeal from law to justice. It should not be romanticized, for disorder harms real people. Nor should it be condemned automatically, for orderly injustice remains injustice.

The proper response to principled dissent is not reflexive punishment but moral examination. A wise society asks: What harm is being named? Whose voice has gone unheard? What law or practice requires repair?

Justice requires more than punishment. It requires fair procedure, proportion, truth, restoration where possible, and protection from future harm.

Those accused of wrongdoing retain their humanity. They deserve a fair hearing, competent representation, and freedom from torture, humiliation, and prejudgment. The injured deserve to be heard, protected, and supported. Communities deserve safety. None of these needs cancel the others.

A system that is harsh but careless is not strong. A system that is merciful but indifferent to harm is not just. Wisdom joins accountability with the possibility of repair.

propositions.title: The Use of Force
propositions.text:
Government claims powers that private persons do not possess: to collect taxes, regulate conduct, detain offenders, and, in grave circumstances, use force. Because these powers are exceptional, they must be governed by exceptional restraint.

Force may be used only for legitimate public purposes, under lawful authority, with necessity, proportionality, and accountability. It must never be used to humiliate, intimidate, enrich, silence lawful dissent, preserve a leader’s pride, or punish a people for the acts of a few.

The possession of weapons does not create wisdom. The ability to compel does not establish moral right.

Police and security officers should be trained above all in preservation of life, de-escalation, impartiality, and service. Their task is not to dominate the public but to protect it. When officers misuse power, the wrongdoing is not merely individual; it damages the trust upon which public safety depends.

Prisons and detention are sometimes necessary to protect others from serious harm. But no society should become comfortable with cages. Confinement must be lawful, humane, reviewable, and no longer than necessary. Conditions that degrade the mind, body, or spirit of prisoners degrade the society that permits them.

War is a confession that human imagination and diplomacy have failed. Sometimes defense against invasion, mass violence, or imminent attack may be necessary. But war must never be treated as a cleansing force, a spectacle, or an opportunity for conquest. Even in war, the innocent must be protected, prisoners treated humanely, and peace sought without delay.

The lives of strangers are not cheaper because they are distant.

propositions.title: The Common Wealth
propositions.text:
A society is held together not only by laws but by the goods it shares.

Clean water, breathable air, public health, education, safe streets, accessible knowledge, reliable infrastructure, emergency care, fair courts, and a livable natural world are not luxuries for the fortunate. They are foundations of common life.

Government has a duty to preserve and distribute these goods with foresight. It must not consume tomorrow’s safety for today’s applause. It must not sell irreplaceable public resources for private gain without honest consent and enduring public benefit. It must not allow children to inherit poisoned land, broken institutions, and debts created by those who refused responsibility.

Taxation is one means by which a people provides for what no individual can adequately secure alone. Taxes should be collected fairly, used transparently, and directed toward the common good. They should not be designed to burden those who already struggle while excusing those most able to contribute.

Wealth may reward invention, labor, risk, and skill. But wealth also depends upon public order, workers, natural resources, knowledge accumulated across generations, and institutions maintained by everyone. Therefore, no great fortune is wholly private in its origin or consequence.

Economic policy must be measured not only by total production but by whether people can live. Can they eat, rest, learn, obtain care, raise children, age with security, and recover from misfortune without being cast aside? Can workers organize, speak safely, and receive fair compensation? Can small communities endure when distant decisions reshape their lives?

An economy that enlarges wealth while shrinking dignity has lost its measure.

propositions.title: Democracy as a Daily Practice
propositions.text:
Democracy is more than voting, though voting matters greatly.

It is the practice of recognizing that no person or faction possesses all wisdom, and that shared decisions require open contest, patient listening, evidence, compromise, and the peaceful transfer of power.

Elections must be free, fair, accessible, and secure. Votes must be counted honestly. Boundaries must not be manipulated to predetermine outcomes. Citizens must be free to organize, criticize, publish, assemble, and support candidates without fear.

But democracy cannot survive on election day alone. It requires informed citizens, trustworthy information, local participation, ethical disagreement, and the willingness to accept that one’s own side may be mistaken.

Public debate becomes corrupt when lies are treated as ordinary strategy, when fear is manufactured for advantage, or when opponents are described as enemies beyond human regard. To disagree is not to betray. To lose an election is not to be erased. To compromise is not always weakness; at times it is the discipline by which diverse people continue to live together.

Majorities have the right to govern within lawful limits. They do not have the right to strip minorities of fundamental dignity, silence them, or make their safety conditional upon public approval. Democracy is not simply the rule of the many; it is the self-government of a people bound by equal rights.

Citizens must therefore resist the temptation to demand purity from public life. No representative, movement, or policy will satisfy every hope. The question is not whether public action is flawless, but whether it moves toward greater truth, fairness, peace, and shared flourishing.

propositions.title: The Character of Those Who Govern
propositions.claim: The Character of Those Who Govern
propositions.text:
Those who seek office should be judged not only by their promises but by their habits.

Do they tell the truth when truth costs them? Do they admit error? Do they listen to those who cannot reward them? Do they treat rivals with basic respect? Do they profit from division? Do they use fear to avoid explanation? Do they surround themselves with flatterers? Do they confuse personal loyalty with public duty?

Competence matters. Good intentions without skill can cause deep harm. Yet skill without conscience is equally dangerous. The public servant requires both practical judgment and moral seriousness.

A leader should be neither worshipped nor despised as something other than human. Leaders are fallible persons entrusted with consequential work. They should be supported when they act well, criticized when they act poorly, and replaced peacefully when their service ends.

The finest public leaders do not teach people to depend upon them. They strengthen institutions, cultivate capable successors, widen participation, and leave the public more able to govern itself.

propositions.title: The Duty of Citizens
propositions.text:
Government is not only what officials do. It is also what citizens permit, demand, ignore, and build together.

To be a citizen is to care for a shared world beyond one’s household and immediate circle. It is to seek reliable information, to vote when able, to serve where needed, to pay one’s fair share, to defend the rights of others, and to resist contempt.

Citizens need not become experts in every matter. But they must not surrender their judgment entirely to slogans, authorities, or crowds. They should ask who benefits from a claim, what evidence supports it, whose experience is missing, and what consequences may fall upon those with least power.

The duty to oppose injustice does not belong only to its victims. When one group is denied protection, all live under a weakened law. When cruelty is accepted against a disliked minority, the moral defenses of the whole society are lowered.

There will be times when public life disappoints. Institutions will fail. Leaders will deceive. Progress will reverse. In such times, despair may appear more honest than hope. But despair abandons the field to those who profit from indifference.

Hope is not the belief that improvement is guaranteed. It is the decision to work for improvement because people are worth the work.

propositions.title: The Measure of a Nation
propositions.text:
A nation should not measure itself chiefly by territory, military force, monuments, markets, or the magnificence of its leaders.

It should ask instead:

How are the poor treated?  
Are children safe and educated?  
Can the sick obtain care?  
Can the accused receive justice?  
Can minorities live without fear?  
Can workers live by their labor?  
Are elders honored without being abandoned?  
Are the earth, waters, and air preserved for those not yet born?  
Can people speak truth to power?  
Can power be transferred without violence?  

Where these questions are answered well, government has become an instrument of shared human dignity.

Where they are answered poorly, no display of strength can conceal the failure.

Let public power be sober, limited, compassionate, and brave. Let it protect without possessing, lead without dominating, and correct without humiliating. Let citizens remain watchful without becoming cynical, committed without becoming cruel, and hopeful without becoming naïve.

For society is not held together by force alone. It is held together by the continuing decision of people to treat one another as persons whose lives matter equally.

propositions.title: The Equal Voice
propositions.text:
No person is born with a crown upon the soul.

Some are born into comfort and some into hunger; some inherit instruction and some inherit silence; some are praised before they have acted, and some are doubted before they have spoken. These differences are real, and justice must reckon with them. Yet beneath every difference is a common dignity: each person bears a life that cannot be lived by another, a conscience that cannot be wholly surrendered, and a share in the world whose conditions shape them all.

Democracy begins in this recognition.

It is not merely a method for counting hands. It is the public discipline of treating persons as more than instruments of power. It declares that those who must live under laws should have a meaningful part in making, revising, and judging those laws. It refuses the old temptation to suppose that wisdom belongs permanently to a family, a class, a party, a priesthood, a military force, a wealthy house, or a loud majority.

A people may choose badly. A council may be deceived. A vote may be swayed by fear, vanity, resentment, or false promises. Democracy does not make human beings flawless. It gives them a peaceful means to correct error, restrain rulers, replace the incompetent, and learn together without needing to destroy one another.

Its promise is not that the people will always be right.

Its promise is that no ruler is above answer, no office is beyond review, and no generation is condemned to obey an error forever.

propositions.title: Government by Consent and by Law
propositions.claim: Government by Consent and by Law
propositions.text:
Consent is not real when it is extracted by hunger, violence, ignorance, or the threat of exclusion. A citizen who must choose between political obedience and the food of their children is not fully free. A citizen whose vote is purchased, whose speech is punished, whose information is controlled, or whose community is intimidated has not been invited into self-government; they have been managed.

Therefore democracy requires more than elections.

It requires laws that apply to governors as well as governed. It requires independent courts, honest administration, public records, free inquiry, peaceful assembly, and institutions that can investigate wrongdoing even when wrongdoing wears an official seal. It requires regular elections whose outcomes are accepted when fairly conducted, and whose fairness may be tested when doubt is credible.

The law must be strong enough to restrain the powerful and gentle enough to protect the vulnerable. When law becomes merely the weapon of a faction, it loses its moral authority. When law becomes an ornament displayed only for foreign admiration while private influence decides all things, democracy becomes a costume worn by oligarchy.

Let the law be written clearly. Let its reasons be open to examination. Let the poor person understand it without hiring a courtly interpreter. Let the wealthy person find no private door around it. Let public officials explain not only what they have decided, but by what authority and for whose benefit.

A government is not made legitimate by its ability to command. It is made legitimate by its fidelity to the people, the law, and the equal worth of every person.

propositions.title: The Majority and the Person
propositions.text:
The majority has authority, but it does not possess the souls of those who dissent.

A vote can determine many matters: who shall administer public duties, how common resources shall be used, which plans shall be pursued when plans compete, and which representatives shall speak for a time. But a vote must not decide that a minority is less human, less protected, less entitled to speak, worship, learn, love, labor, or belong.

The number of those who approve an injustice does not make it just.

For this reason, democracy must be constitutional: bound by principles that cannot be casually withdrawn from those who are unpopular. The liberty of conscience, equal protection before the law, freedom from torture and arbitrary imprisonment, the right to a fair hearing, and the basic conditions of civic participation must not depend upon whether a frightened public finds them convenient.

A majority that silences all criticism may still call itself democratic. Its name does not change its nature. A state that holds elections while persecuting opponents may preserve the shell and break the living thing within it. Democracy is not the rule of fifty-one against forty-nine. It is the shared rule of a people who understand that tomorrow they may stand among the forty-nine, and that their own freedom depends upon the freedom they protect today.

This is not weakness. It is civic maturity.

The strong person does not need to deny another’s humanity in order to prevail. The confident society does not fear disagreement. It makes room for dissent because dissent may reveal an overlooked truth, an injured neighbor, an unintended consequence, or a better path.

propositions.title: The Duties of Citizens
propositions.text:
A democracy asks much of its citizens.

To vote is important, but voting alone is not citizenship. Citizenship includes paying attention, seeking reliable knowledge, listening beyond one’s familiar circle, serving where service is needed, and refusing to spread what one has not honestly examined. It includes the patient work of schools, unions, associations, neighborhood groups, professional bodies, religious communities, cooperatives, local councils, and every lawful gathering through which people learn to act together.

A free people cannot remain free by outsourcing all judgment to leaders.

Citizens should ask of every public claim:

- What evidence supports this?
- Who benefits if I believe it?
- Whose experience is missing from the discussion?
- What costs are being hidden?
- Does this proposal preserve equal dignity, or does it seek advantage by humiliation?
- Would I accept this power in the hands of my opponents?

These questions do not make public life cold or cynical. They make it less vulnerable to manipulation. Cynicism says that all people are corrupt and that nothing can improve. Civic wisdom says that people are fallible, that power attracts abuse, and that institutions must be built so that abuse can be exposed and corrected.

Do not confuse suspicion with discernment. The citizen who trusts every slogan is easily led; the citizen who trusts nothing cannot cooperate. Democracy needs neither gullibility nor contempt. It needs informed trust, earned through transparency, accountability, and demonstrated care for the common good.

propositions.title: Speech, Truth, and the Public Square
propositions.claim: Speech, Truth, and the Public Square
propositions.text:
Speech is the breath of democratic life. Without the freedom to question, criticize, report, organize, argue, create, and persuade, the people cannot govern themselves. The silencing of a single voice harms not only that voice, but all who might have learned from it.

Yet freedom of speech does not absolve anyone from responsibility for speech.

Words can illuminate, but they can also inflame. Lies deliberately spread to provoke violence, corrupt elections, ruin reputations, or turn neighbor against neighbor injure the common life. The remedy for falsehood must not become a pretext for rulers to suppress inconvenient truth. Such power is easily abused. But neither should a society pretend that coordinated deception is harmless merely because it travels under the banner of expression.

The lasting defense against deception is a culture of truthfulness: independent journalism, careful scholarship, transparent public data, media literacy, correction without humiliation, and institutions that distinguish error from deliberate fraud. It is also the humble habit of saying, “I do not know,” and the honorable courage of saying, “I was wrong.”

A public square becomes poisonous when winning matters more than truth, when ridicule replaces reason, and when every disagreement is treated as evidence of evil. Let arguments be vigorous, for serious matters deserve seriousness. But let opponents remain persons. Denounce cruelty without becoming cruel. Resist falsehood without surrendering honesty. Defend conviction without worshiping victory.

The aim of public speech is not the destruction of the other side. It is the clearer discernment of what serves life.

propositions.title: Representation and Nearness
propositions.text:
In large societies, not every person can deliberate daily over every law. Representation is therefore necessary. The people entrust certain persons with temporary authority to study, negotiate, decide, and administer. But representation is stewardship, not ownership.

Those elected are not masters of the public; they are servants of a public trust.

A representative should hear not only donors, party leaders, and the most powerful voices, but also workers, caregivers, children, elders, disabled persons, migrants, small communities, and those whose injuries are easily overlooked because they have little influence. A representative should report back, explain difficult decisions, disclose conflicts of interest, and accept that public office requires sacrifice.

Likewise, citizens should not demand that representatives become mere echoing instruments of every passing passion. Good representation requires both listening and judgment. A leader may at times need to warn their supporters that a desired action is unjust, unwise, unlawful, or impossible. To do so honestly is not betrayal.

Democracy is healthiest when decisions are made as near as possible to those affected by them, while wider bodies protect rights, coordinate shared goods, and prevent local power from becoming local oppression. A neighborhood may know its streets better than a distant capital. A nation may protect a river that passes through many regions. The human community must address harms that cross all borders: war, climate disruption, disease, exploitation, and the destruction of the living world.

Let authority be close enough to hear suffering, and broad enough to meet shared responsibility.

propositions.title: Wealth and Unequal Power
propositions.text:
Political equality cannot endure where extreme economic inequality gives a few people command over the public voice.

When wealth purchases access, finances misinformation, captures regulation, owns the channels of attention, and turns essential needs into leverage, elections may continue while self-government weakens. The citizen who has one vote but no time, no security, no access to information, and no confidence that anyone listens does not stand on equal ground with the citizen who can fund a campaign, employ lobbyists, and shape the boundaries of public debate.

This does not mean that prosperity is shameful or that enterprise is an enemy of freedom. Honest work, invention, saving, investment, and trade can strengthen communities. But wealth carries obligations. It must not become a private sovereignty standing above the common law.

A democratic society should secure the material foundations of participation: education, healthcare, housing, fair labor conditions, access to information, time for family and civic life, and protection against destitution. These are not luxuries granted after democracy has been achieved. They are among the conditions that make democracy real.

No person should be so poor that their voice can be bought. No person should be so rich that many voices can be drowned.

propositions.title: The Peaceful Transfer of Power
propositions.text:
One of democracy’s holiest disciplines is the peaceful transfer of authority.

To lose an election is painful. To relinquish office can feel like defeat, humiliation, or danger. Yet rulers who cling to power after lawful defeat teach the people that force is more important than consent. They invite retaliation, corruption, and violence. They make every future election a struggle not over policy but over survival.

Accepting a fair result does not require silence about flaws, nor does it require surrendering one’s principles. It requires refusing to destroy the institutions that permit future persuasion and peaceful change. Challenges to elections must be grounded in evidence and resolved through lawful processes. Rumor is not proof. Anger is not proof. Personal disbelief is not proof.

Those who win must show restraint. They should not govern as though half the country has become an enemy population. They should protect the rights of those who opposed them, seek durable agreements where possible, and remember that authority is held in trust and for a limited time.

Those who lose must continue to participate. Opposition is not disloyalty. Loyal opposition is one of democracy’s safeguards: it scrutinizes power, offers alternatives, preserves memory, and prepares the public for choices yet to come.

A society that can change its leaders without bloodshed has achieved something precious. Guard it with vigilance.

propositions.title: Democracy as a Way of Living Together
propositions.claim: Democracy as a Way of Living Together
propositions.text:
Democracy is not completed at the ballot box. It is practiced in homes, classrooms, workplaces, places of worship, streets, and institutions. It is present wherever people affected by a decision are heard with seriousness; wherever authority gives reasons; wherever the small are not mocked; wherever power accepts limits; wherever conflict is addressed without degradation.

Teach children that obedience has a place, but so do questions. Teach them that respect is not the same as silence. Teach them to recognize manipulation, to care for those outside their circle, and to take responsibility for the effects of their choices. Let schools be places not only of instruction but of shared inquiry, where the loud learn to listen and the quiet learn that their voices matter.

Practice democracy in ordinary matters. Share information before decisions are made. Invite those affected to speak. Explain outcomes. Admit mistakes. Rotate authority where possible. Protect the person who brings unwelcome news. These small habits form the character without which democratic institutions become empty machinery.

Democracy will always be unfinished because human beings are always learning how to live more justly together. Its work is slow. It can be disappointing. It asks patience when anger demands immediacy, compromise when pride demands triumph, and courage when fear calls for a strong hand.

Yet its unfinished nature is not a defect. It is an invitation.

Let no one be discarded from the public story. Let no office become sacred beyond question. Let disagreement remain within the bonds of human regard. Let power be answerable, truth be sought, rights be guarded, and the common good be pursued with open eyes.

Then democracy becomes more than a system of rule.

It becomes a daily covenant among equals: that none shall dominate without restraint, none shall be excluded without remedy, and all shall share responsibility for the world they make together.

propositions.title: The City Is a Promise Made Visible
propositions.claim: The City Is a Promise Made Visible
propositions.text:
A city is not merely a concentration of buildings. It is a promise made visible in stone, timber, water, wire, law, and habit.

Every street declares something about who may belong. Every doorway answers, whether generously or cruelly, the question: *May you enter?* Every public bench, school, market, tree, toilet, crossing, clinic, and lamp reveals the measure in which a people understand one another to be worthy of care.

A city gathers strangers into proximity. This is its danger and its gift.

In the countryside, distance may conceal injustice. In the city, lives touch. The wealthy pass the unhoused. The healthy pass the ill. Children cross the paths of laborers, elders, migrants, merchants, teachers, artists, builders, officials, and those whose work is rarely named. No city can truthfully claim not to know that human needs exist, because its streets daily place those needs before every eye.

Therefore let a city be judged not by the height of its towers, nor by the brightness of its commerce, nor by the power of its rulers, but by this: whether a person of little wealth can live there without humiliation; whether a child can grow there in safety and wonder; whether an elder can remain there with dignity; whether the stranger can find welcome; whether the injured can receive help; whether the worker can return home with enough strength for a life beyond labor.

A city is righteous when it makes ordinary goodness easier.

propositions.title: The First Work: Make Room
propositions.text:
No person should be treated as an inconvenience because they require shelter.

To live without a home is not a moral failure. It is an injury inflicted by abandonment, misfortune, violence, illness, exclusion, unaffordable land, or systems that value property more highly than people. Whatever the causes in a particular life, the duty of a city is plain: no one should be left to sleep in danger when dwellings stand empty, when resources are hoarded, or when common effort can provide safety.

Build homes that people can afford without surrendering food, medicine, education, rest, or hope. Build them near transport, work, schools, gardens, markets, and care. Do not exile the poor to distant edges and call this housing. A dwelling without access to community is a form of containment.

Let homes be dry, temperate, accessible, secure, and beautiful enough to affirm the worth of those who live in them. Beauty is not a luxury reserved for the wealthy. A window that admits morning light, a tree beside a path, a shared courtyard, a well-kept stair, a place for children to play, a room in which one may close the door and be at peace: these are portions of human dignity.

Let there be homes of many kinds: homes for one person and for large families; homes for elders who need support and for young people beginning their lives; homes for disabled persons; homes for those escaping violence; homes shared across generations; homes near the places where care is given and received. The city that builds for only one imagined household builds against its own people.

Do not make the homeless invisible by driving them from one district to another. Do not turn park benches into weapons, doorways into cages, and public space into a field of quiet punishment. Such designs do not solve suffering. They make suffering less visible to those with power, while making it more severe for those without it.

The measure of a city is not how effectively it removes poverty from its sight, but how faithfully it removes poverty from human life.

propositions.title: Streets Belong to the Living
propositions.text:
A street is not a machine for moving vehicles as quickly as possible. It is a common room under the open sky.

Children should be able to cross it. Elders should be able to rest beside it. Wheelchairs, walkers, bicycles, carts, buses, and feet should find safe passage upon it. Trees should shade it. Rain should be welcomed and guided rather than treated as an enemy. Shops, homes, libraries, clinics, places of worship, workshops, and parks should meet it with doors and windows, so that public life is watched over not by suspicion but by ordinary human presence.

A city that sacrifices all else to speed becomes hostile to those who move slowly. Yet every person, in time, moves slowly: the child, the pregnant parent, the injured worker, the elder, the exhausted, the grieving, and the person carrying too much. Design first for the vulnerable traveler, and the street will serve everyone.

Let crossings be frequent, visible, and protected. Let public transport be reliable, clean, affordable, and dignified. Let it run often enough that waiting does not become a tax on those who cannot afford private vehicles. Let stations be safe without becoming militarized. Let drivers be trained not only in operation but in patience, for they carry the public trust.

Where journeys can be made by walking, let walking be pleasant. Where journeys can be made by cycling, let cycling be protected. Where people must travel far, let the shared means of travel be excellent. Freedom is not only the ability to own a vehicle; it is the ability to reach work, learning, care, friendship, and beauty without being impoverished by the journey.

Do not confuse noise with vitality. A city may be lively without being unbearable. Let there be places for music, celebration, trade, and assembly, but also places for sleep, birdsong, thought, recovery, and quiet speech. The right to rest is part of the right to belong.

propositions.title: The Commons Must Be Kept
propositions.text:
There are things that must not be left entirely to private ownership, because all depend upon them and no one can flourish without them.

Water must be protected from poison and shared with justice. Air must not be traded away for profit. Parks, libraries, schools, hospitals, sidewalks, public squares, sanitation, emergency services, and honest information belong to the moral foundation of a city. They are not ornaments. They are the means by which strangers become neighbors.

A library says: knowledge is not the inheritance of the wealthy alone.

A public park says: beauty and rest are for everyone.

A school says: the future of one child matters to all.

A clinic says: pain will not be ignored because it is unprofitable.

A public toilet says: bodily dignity is not a privilege.

A safe shelter says: no person will be abandoned to weather and fear.

Guard these institutions from neglect. Their decay is often gradual: shortened hours, broken equipment, exhausted workers, inaccessible entrances, fees too small to trouble the wealthy yet large enough to exclude the poor. Each reduction may be explained as practical. Together they teach people that the city does not consider them worth serving.

The commons require maintenance, and maintenance requires honor. Honor the cleaner, the bus mechanic, the water engineer, the caregiver, the librarian, the street sweeper, the waste collector, the crossing guard, the electrician, the cook, the gardener, the nurse, the clerk, and all whose work prevents public life from falling into disorder. A city rests upon labor that is often unseen. Let its gratitude be expressed in fair wages, safe conditions, rest, representation, and respect.

propositions.title: Let Nature Enter the City
propositions.text:
The city is not outside nature. It is nature rearranged by human intention, and it remains dependent upon soil, water, weather, insects, plants, animals, and seasons.

Where the ground is sealed entirely beneath concrete, rain becomes flood, heat becomes danger, and life withdraws. Where trees are treated as decoration rather than infrastructure, shade vanishes from those who need it most. Where rivers are buried, wetlands drained, and shorelines surrendered to speculation, the city forgets the sources of its own survival.

Plant trees where heat is greatest, not only where wealth is greatest. Create parks within easy reach of every home. Protect riverbanks, coasts, hills, forests, and fertile land from careless extraction. Restore wetlands where possible. Welcome native plants, pollinators, birds, and the small forms of life that make the larger world habitable.

Let gardens be grown on unused land, rooftops, balconies, schoolyards, and shared courtyards. Food grown nearby does not replace the work of farmers, but it teaches citizens that nourishment has a source, a season, and a cost. It creates fellowship across age and language. It gives children a chance to see that a seed becomes food not by command, but by patience.

Prepare for heat, flood, drought, fire, storm, and disease before catastrophe arrives. The climate does not negotiate with denial. Build cooling centers, shaded routes, resilient power systems, clean-air shelters, floodable parks, emergency stores, and networks of mutual aid. The first question in disaster planning must be: *Who will be hardest to reach, and how will we reach them first?*

A resilient city is not one that returns quickly to business as usual. It is one that preserves life, shares resources fairly, and learns enough from grief to prevent its repetition.

propositions.title: Difference Is Not Disorder
propositions.text:
Cities are made of people who do not share one language, history, faith, custom, ability, income, memory, or desire. This is not a defect to be corrected. It is the condition of urban life.

Do not demand that the newcomer become invisible before offering welcome. Do not require the poor to imitate the rich, the young to silence the old, or the old to despise the new. Let people keep names, foods, songs, ceremonies, clothing, stories, and ways of mourning, so long as they do not deny the equal dignity of others.

Difference becomes dangerous when power turns it into hierarchy. Therefore resist every practice that marks some lives as naturally less deserving of safety, authority, beauty, or grief. Resist hatred spoken in the language of race, caste, origin, religion, gender, disability, sexuality, class, neighborhood, or legal status. Such hatred always claims to protect the city while it hollows the city from within.

A people do not become united by becoming identical. They become united by keeping faith with one another amid difference.

Let public institutions speak plainly enough to be understood. Let interpretation and translation be available where needed. Let buildings be accessible. Let civic information be open. Let meetings be held at times when workers and caregivers can attend. Let children, elders, tenants, migrants, disabled people, and those without formal titles be heard before decisions are sealed.

Listening is not a ceremonial act. It is a way of discovering reality.

propositions.title: Power Must Remain Answerable
propositions.text:
Where many people live together, power will arise. It may arise through wealth, land, office, expertise, force, inheritance, or control of information. The question is not whether power exists, but whether it is constrained by justice and answerable to those affected by it.

Let decisions be made as near as possible to the people who bear their consequences, while recognizing that water, air, housing, transport, health, and climate cross neighborhood boundaries. Let local knowledge guide public action, and let wider institutions protect the common good against narrow advantage.

Keep public accounts clear. Explain how money is raised, how it is spent, who benefits, who bears the cost, and what alternatives were considered. A budget is a moral document. It reveals whose safety is urgent, whose time is valued, whose suffering is tolerated, and what future is being purchased.

Do not permit wealth to buy a louder voice than citizenship. When private interests shape public policy in secret, the city ceases to belong to its people. Guard against corruption not only by punishing obvious theft, but by exposing the quieter forms: privileged access, manipulated contracts, speculative vacancy, discriminatory lending, concealed ownership, and rules written to preserve advantage.

Public safety must never become a name for public fear. Those entrusted with enforcement must be trained, supervised, accountable, and restrained. Violence by an authority is not made righteous by its uniform. Prevention, mediation, mental-health care, housing, education, treatment, restorative practice, and trusted community presence often protect life more wisely than force.

Justice seeks safety without cruelty. It protects the vulnerable without creating new victims.

propositions.title: Commerce Must Serve Life
propositions.text:
Markets can nourish a city. They bring provision, invention, craft, exchange, and livelihood. But commerce becomes destructive when it is permitted to consume the conditions that make life possible.

Do not permit every neighborhood to become a product. When rent rises beyond the reach of those who made a place lively, when small businesses disappear beneath chains that send wealth elsewhere, when homes are purchased solely as investments and left vacant, the city loses memory as well as affordability.

Support local enterprise without making it a fetish. A neighborhood shop, market stall, repair workshop, cooperative, family restaurant, and independent artist can root wealth and relationship in a place. Yet every worker, whether employed by a small business or a great corporation, deserves fair pay, predictable hours, safety, leave, and the freedom to organize.

Let there be places to make as well as places to consume. Preserve workshops, studios, kitchens, rehearsal rooms, community halls, and affordable spaces for practical skill. A city that imports everything and produces nothing becomes fragile. A city that values only financial work forgets the intelligence of hands.

Work is necessary, but no person was made only to work. Organize economic life so that people have time for care, friendship, learning, civic participation, worship, play, and rest. Prosperity that destroys time is a poor form of wealth.

propositions.title: Build for Generations Not Yet Seen
propositions.claim: Build for Generations Not Yet Seen
propositions.text:
Those alive today are not the sole owners of the city. We are its temporary stewards.

The foundations we pour, the debt we incur, the soil we poison or restore, the homes we permit or refuse, the institutions we strengthen or weaken—these acts will meet people whose names we do not know. They will inherit not only our structures but our priorities.

Therefore build well. Repair before replacing when repair is possible. Preserve what carries memory and serves present life. Do not preserve every old thing merely because it is old, nor destroy every old thing merely because it stands in the way of profit. Ask instead: What does this place hold? Whom does it serve? What can be renewed? What harm must be ended?

Let every major plan be tested by a child’s future. Will this decision leave cleaner air or dirtier air? More homes or fewer? Greater safety or deeper division? More shade, more learning, more trust, more capacity to endure hardship—or less?

A city cannot love the future in words alone. It must make costly choices in the present.

propositions.title: The Blessing of Nearness
propositions.text:
There will be conflict in every city. People will disagree over land, noise, money, identity, safety, growth, memory, and change. Do not seek a city without disagreement, for such a city would require silence from many. Seek instead a city that can disagree without contempt and repair without forgetting.

Practice the small disciplines of coexistence. Greet those who share your building. Learn the names of the workers whose labor sustains your street. Yield space when another needs it more. Keep public places clean not because someone is beneath you to clean them, but because they belong to all. Attend to the lonely. Notice when a neighbor disappears. Ask before assuming. Apologize without bargaining. Defend the person being mocked. Share what you can.

No policy can replace these acts, though good policy can make them more possible.

The city is made each day by millions of small decisions: whether to look away or to see; whether to exploit scarcity or relieve it; whether to treat another person as an obstacle or as a bearer of a world as real as one’s own.

Let the city be a school of mutual regard.

Let its walls shelter rather than exclude. Let its streets connect rather than divide. Let its institutions serve rather than dominate. Let its wealth circulate rather than harden. Let its diversity become wisdom. Let its public places teach each person, quietly and repeatedly: *You are not alone here. Your life has weight. The common good includes you.*

Then the city will be more than a place where people survive beside one another.

It will become a place where they learn how to live together.

propositions.title: The Many Houses of Humanity
propositions.text:
A nation is a house built in time.

It is made of memory, language, law, labor, grief, celebration, inheritance, and hope. Its foundations may be ancient or recent; its borders may be wide or narrow; its people may speak with one tongue or many. Yet no nation is merely soil marked upon a map. A nation lives wherever its people undertake, again and again, to share a common life.

Therefore honor nations.

Honor the songs by which a people remembers itself. Honor the stories told beside its hearths. Honor the names given to mountains, rivers, streets, ancestors, and children. Honor the crafts, customs, cuisines, prayers, ceremonies, and forms of courtesy through which a people says: *We are here, and we have learned something of how to live.*

Do not mock what you have not taken time to understand.

But do not make an idol of the nation. For the nation is a vessel, not a god; a covenant of people, not a permission to despise other people. It exists to shelter human dignity, cultivate mutual responsibility, and enable a shared life worthy of those who inhabit it. When it serves these ends, it is good. When it demands that conscience kneel before cruelty, it has forgotten its purpose.

No flag is made sacred by its colors alone. No anthem is made true by the force with which it is sung. No border is made just merely because it is guarded.

A nation is honorable insofar as it honors the humanity of those within it and beyond it.

propositions.title: The First Allegiance
propositions.text:
Every person belongs first to the community of human beings.

Before one is citizen, subject, resident, foreigner, refugee, neighbor, or stranger, one is a person: vulnerable to hunger, capable of joy, deserving of safety, answerable for one’s conduct, and endowed with a life that cannot rightly be treated as a tool.

This is the first allegiance.

Love of one’s own country is not opposed to love of humanity, just as love of one’s household need not require contempt for every other household. A person may cherish a native language without silencing another. A people may guard its customs without declaring all unfamiliar customs corrupt. A nation may seek the flourishing of its citizens without building that flourishing upon the injury of others.

Let patriotism be gratitude joined to responsibility.

Be grateful for what your nation has given: the care of teachers, the labor of builders, the wisdom of elders, the protection of laws, the beauty of landscapes, the sacrifices by which public goods were made. Yet gratitude is not flattery. The child who truly loves a parent does not praise a dangerous error; the citizen who truly loves a country does not conceal injustice beneath ceremony.

To love a nation faithfully is to desire its moral repair.

Speak truth concerning its wounds. Remember those whom it excluded, dispossessed, enslaved, neglected, or abandoned. Refuse the lie that national greatness is proved by never admitting fault. A nation that cannot repent is condemned to repeat its harm under new banners and new slogans.

Let remembrance be honest enough to heal.

propositions.title: Borders and Their Burden
propositions.text:
Borders are not inherently evil. They can establish responsibility, make laws administrable, preserve public trust, and protect communities from violence and exploitation. A people cannot govern well if every obligation is vague, every institution powerless, and every decision without an accountable keeper.

Yet a border is a line of responsibility before it is a line of exclusion.

Those who govern a border must remember that persons approach it. The traveler has a name. The worker has a history. The child has fears and dreams. The displaced family did not become less human when it crossed a desert, a river, a checkpoint, or a sea.

Do not let the language of administration erase the face of the vulnerable.

Nations may regulate entry. They may investigate danger. They may maintain orderly processes, protect public health, and resist those who traffic in violence, coercion, and fraud. Wisdom does not require naivety. Compassion without prudence can be exploited, and prudence without compassion becomes brutality.

Therefore govern borders with both discernment and mercy.

Do not imprison children for the convenience of policy. Do not return people knowingly to torture, persecution, famine, or death. Do not treat asylum as a crime when flight is the last refuge of the threatened. Do not profit from the desperation of those whom war, disaster, tyranny, or poverty have driven from home.

Where a nation cannot receive all who seek entry, let it still act with decency: provide clear procedures, humane shelter, fair hearing, and cooperation with other nations. Let powerful countries carry a proportionate share of refuge, for they often possess a proportionate share of the world’s resources and influence.

A border may be firm without being cruel.

propositions.title: The Stranger Among You
propositions.text:
The stranger is not a test of your generosity alone. The stranger is a teacher of your humanity.

In every society there are those who arrive later: migrants, refugees, workers, students, spouses, exiles, and children born between cultures. Some will learn the customs quickly; some will carry an accent all their lives. Some will remain for a season; some will become the ancestors of generations yet unborn.

Receive them neither with romantic fantasy nor with suspicion as a habit.

They are not saviors sent to cure every failure of your society. Neither are they invaders by nature. They are people, and people differ: some are admirable, some difficult, most ordinary, all entitled to justice.

Ask of those who join your common life what you ask of yourselves: respect for the equal dignity of others, obedience to just law, willingness to contribute, and rejection of violence and domination. In return, offer what every decent society owes to those under its authority: due process, protection, education, fair opportunity, and freedom from contempt.

Integration is not erasure.

A shared civic life requires a common commitment to law and mutual regard. It does not require that every family abandon its language, food, memory, or inherited way of celebrating. Let people bring the treasures of their histories into the common square, provided they do not claim a right to wound others in the name of tradition.

A culture is strengthened not by becoming sealed and brittle, but by learning what it can receive without losing its moral center.

propositions.title: Sovereignty as Stewardship
propositions.text:
The authority of a nation is real, but it is not absolute.

No ruler, parliament, court, army, party, or majority is released from moral duty merely because it acts in the name of national sovereignty. A government may possess legal power and still act unjustly. It may command obedience in minor matters while forfeiting trust through corruption, cruelty, or lies.

Sovereignty is stewardship.

Those entrusted with public power are custodians of a people’s safety, liberty, resources, institutions, and future. They are not owners of the nation. They may not spend its youth in reckless war, sell its common wealth to the powerful, poison its land for immediate gain, or turn fear into a permanent instrument of rule.

The state is strong when its laws bind the powerful as well as the poor.

Let courts be independent enough to restrain injustice. Let elections be fair enough to change rulers without bloodshed. Let public records be open enough that citizens may know how they are governed. Let journalism be free enough to expose wrongdoing. Let opposition be protected, for a government that cannot endure criticism has already made itself fragile.

Do not confuse unity with uniformity.

A nation can contain sharp disagreement and remain whole. Indeed, it is healthier when disagreements are brought into lawful speech rather than driven underground, where resentment hardens and conspiracy grows. The duty of public life is not to make every citizen think alike. It is to make it possible for people who differ to remain neighbors.

propositions.title: Wealth, Debt, and the Common Good
propositions.claim: Wealth, Debt, and the Common Good
propositions.text:
Nations are bound to one another by trade, labor, finance, technology, climate, disease, and the movement of goods and ideas. No country feeds, heals, manufactures, learns, or secures itself entirely alone.

Therefore reject the fiction of complete independence.

A nation should develop its capacities, protect essential public systems, and avoid helpless dependence upon distant powers. It is wise to secure food, water, health care, energy, communications, and the institutions necessary for public resilience. But self-reliance is not isolation. No people can flourish by treating every other people as a rival to be weakened.

Trade is good when it serves human well-being. It becomes corrupt when wealth is gained through forced labor, ruined ecosystems, debt traps, stolen resources, or wages too small for a worker to live with dignity.

Let nations ask not only, “What may we gain?” but also, “What conditions do our gains create for others?”

The prosperity of one country should not require the permanent impoverishment of another. Wealthy nations must not lecture poorer nations about responsibility while arranging systems that drain their labor, extract their minerals, evade their taxes, and dictate their choices. Nor should leaders of poorer nations excuse corruption by blaming every failure upon foreign powers.

Justice requires truth in every direction.

Cancel debts that cannot be paid without sacrificing a people’s health, education, food, or basic future. Build agreements that allow developing communities to grow without surrendering their land and dignity. Share knowledge that prevents disease, reduces suffering, and protects life. Reward innovation, but do not make lifesaving medicine a luxury for those whom poverty has already afflicted.

The earth’s abundance was not entrusted to a few nations for the humiliation of the rest.

propositions.title: War and the Discipline of Peace
propositions.claim: War and the Discipline of Peace
propositions.text:
War is a confession of grave failure, even when resistance to aggression becomes necessary.

There are times when people must defend themselves and others against invasion, massacre, enslavement, or violent tyranny. To tell the attacked that they must not resist is not peace; it is abandonment. Those who use force to protect the innocent bear a terrible burden, and they must remain bound by restraint even in danger.

Never make war glorious.

Do not sing of death as though it were a harvest. Do not turn soldiers into decorations for the ambitions of leaders. Do not call civilians expendable, nor treat hunger, terror, rape, torture, and indiscriminate destruction as instruments of victory.

A just defense must distinguish, as far as humanly possible, between those who fight and those who do not. It must use no more force than necessity requires. It must reject cruelty, collective punishment, and vengeance. It must remain open to a peace that is more than the silence imposed by fear.

The purpose of defense is not domination. It is the restoration of safety and just peace.

Before nations take up arms, let them exhaust honest negotiation, mediation, inspection, arbitration, and public accountability. Let those who call for war explain its costs plainly: the dead, the wounded, the displaced, the traumatized, the debt, the bitterness inherited by children. Let no leader send others into danger while hiding from the truth of what violence does.

After conflict, do not build peace upon humiliation. Hold perpetrators accountable, protect victims, repair what can be repaired, and establish conditions in which former enemies need not remain enemies forever.

Peace is not weakness. It is the difficult art of refusing to make tomorrow pay forever for yesterday’s wound.

propositions.title: The Earth Beyond All Borders
propositions.text:
Some gifts and dangers belong to all peoples.

The atmosphere moves without passports. The ocean does not recognize the flags above its shores. Disease travels with breath and trade. Rivers cross boundaries. Forests shape climates far from their roots. The weapons devised in one laboratory may threaten cities continents away.

Therefore nations must cooperate not as a favor, but as a duty.

No country has the right to consume the shared conditions of life while leaving others to bear the flood, drought, heat, contamination, and hunger that follow. Those who have gained most from long use of the earth’s resources carry a greater obligation to lead in repair, adaptation, and support for communities facing the harshest consequences.

Guard the climate as a common inheritance. Protect the seas, the soil, the forests, and the living diversity upon which future generations depend. Share scientific knowledge in times of plague and disaster. Establish agreements strong enough to restrain harms that no single nation can solve.

International institutions will be imperfect because human institutions are imperfect. Reform them where they are weak, biased, secretive, or captive to the powerful. Do not abandon cooperation merely because cooperation is difficult. A flawed table at which nations speak is better than a world in which they speak only through threats.

propositions.title: The Nation Yet to Be
propositions.text:
No nation is finished.

Its identity is not a relic locked in a museum, nor a slogan repeated until it loses meaning. It is a living promise renewed by each generation. Children inherit not only the achievements of their forebears, but also their unfinished work.

Teach them the beauty of their homeland without teaching them to hate another’s. Teach them the courage of those who defended freedom, and the courage of those who exposed injustice. Teach them the language of their people, and also the humility to listen when another language carries a truth they have not yet heard.

Let national memory be broad enough to include both pride and sorrow.

The finest nation is not the one that claims to be chosen above all others. It is the one that becomes trustworthy: trustworthy to its children, to its minorities, to its workers, to its elders, to the stranger at its gate, to the weak beyond its borders, and to the generations who will inherit the consequences of its choices.

Seek not national greatness measured by fear, conquest, spectacle, or wealth alone.

Seek a nation in which no one must be humiliated to belong; in which public power is answerable; in which difference does not become hatred; in which the vulnerable are not abandoned; in which the past is faced honestly; and in which the future is prepared with care.

Then let each people cherish its own house.

Let it keep its door, tend its fire, repair its roof, and welcome the guest with wisdom. Let it stand among the many houses of humanity neither bowed in shame nor raised in arrogance.

For the nations are many, but the human family is one.

propositions.title: The Common Mirror
propositions.text:
Media are the instruments by which a people see beyond the reach of their own eyes, hear beyond the range of their own voices, and remember what would otherwise be lost.

A story told at a table is media. A warning marked upon a wall is media. A song carried across generations is media. So are books, broadcasts, photographs, films, messages, feeds, archives, and the innumerable signals sent each day through machines.

Therefore do not speak of media as though it were merely a collection of devices. Media is the shared mirror of society. It reflects the world, but it also selects, enlarges, diminishes, arranges, and sometimes distorts what it reflects.

What a people attend to becomes weighty among them. What they repeatedly ignore may become invisible, even when it stands at their door.

For this reason, those who make and govern media hold a public trust. They shape not only information but imagination: whom people fear, whom they pity, what they believe possible, and what they learn to call normal.

Let no person say, “I only provided the channel,” when that channel has been designed to reward cruelty, falsehood, humiliation, or despair. A channel is not innocent of the currents it creates.

Yet let no person say, “Media alone has corrupted us,” and thereby excuse their own appetite. Every audience participates in the world it rewards. Attention is a form of payment. Repetition is a form of endorsement. Silence, too, may become a choice.

Use media, then, with wakefulness.

propositions.title: The Dignity of Truth
propositions.text:
Truth is not merely the absence of a lie. Truth requires faithfulness to reality, proportion in judgment, honesty about uncertainty, and willingness to correct what has been wrongly said.

Do not pass along a claim because it confirms your hope, flatters your side, or gives form to your anger. A pleasing falsehood does not become harmless because it comforts the one who repeats it.

Before sharing, ask:

- Is this known, or merely alleged?
- Who is speaking, and what evidence supports the claim?
- What has been omitted?
- Is the account current, complete, and fairly represented?
- Would I speak this in the presence of those affected by it?
- If it is false, what injury might my repetition cause?
