Let those who have gained most from the burning of the old buried fire accept the greater share of repair.

Let assistance be offered not as charity bestowed from above, but as justice returned to the common table.

propositions.title: The Living World Is Not an Ornament
propositions.claim: The Living World Is Not an Ornament
propositions.text:
Forests cool the land, invite rain, shelter innumerable beings, and hold carbon in trunk, root, and soil. Wetlands slow floods, filter water, store life, and soften the violence of storms. Grasslands preserve fertile ground and support pollinators and grazing creatures. Mangroves protect coasts while nursing fish and binding shore to sea. Healthy soils retain water, feed plants, and keep ancient carbon from returning quickly to the air.

These are not luxuries added after the needs of people are met.

They are among the conditions by which people’s needs are met.

A forest is not empty land waiting to become useful. A river is not failed commerce because it runs free. A marsh is not wasteland because it resists construction. A species is not without worth because no market has assigned it a price.

The living world is not an ornament around human life. It is the wider body within which human life exists.

Yet restoration must not become another form of dispossession. A forest protected by driving out those who have cared for it is not fully protected. A conservation plan that silences Indigenous peoples, local communities, fishers, farmers, and pastoralists ignores knowledge born of long attention.

Those who live close to a place often know its thresholds: when the river runs strangely, when the birds alter their routes, when the soil loses its softness, when a species disappears from the season in which it once arrived.

Honor such knowledge. Join it with careful science. Let neither contempt nor pride divide what wisdom requires to be joined.

propositions.title: The Work of Repair
propositions.text:
There is no single act that will restore balance. The work is broad because the harm is broad; it reaches into energy, food, housing, transport, industry, trade, law, finance, and habit.

But complexity is not an excuse for helplessness.

The first task is to leave as much fossil fuel as possible in the ground and to replace its use with cleaner sources of energy: sun, wind, moving water, geothermal heat, and other systems designed with care for land, labor, and wildlife. Efficiency matters also. The cleanest energy is often the energy not wasted: the well-insulated home, the shaded street, the durable appliance, the building made for local climate rather than against it.

The second task is to reshape transport. Walkable neighborhoods, safe cycling, reliable public transit, electrified vehicles where needed, and rail in place of unnecessary short flights can reduce pollution while making daily life healthier and more connected.

The third task is to cultivate food with humility. Soil can be exhausted or renewed. Land can be stripped or tended. Food systems that protect forests, reduce waste, improve soil health, respect workers, and make nourishing food available to all serve both climate and dignity. There is no virtue in a system that lowers emissions while leaving people hungry.

The fourth task is to prepare for changes already underway. Build cooling centers before heat waves. Restore floodplains before rivers rise. Plant diverse trees where shade is needed, but do not plant blindly. Protect water before drought becomes emergency. Design homes, hospitals, schools, and roads for the world that is arriving, especially where poverty has made resilience difficult.

Adaptation without reducing emissions is surrender to escalating harm. Reducing emissions without adaptation abandons those already in danger. Both are required.

propositions.title: The Measure of Enough
propositions.text:
Much of the climate disturbance has arisen from a mistaken measure of prosperity.

A society may count its wealth in goods purchased, fuel burned, land consumed, and speed attained. Yet it may fail to count clean air, stable seasons, unpolluted water, leisure, friendship, health, fertile soil, and the security of knowing that one’s children will inherit a habitable place.

What is called growth may sometimes be the enlargement of damage.

What is called convenience may sometimes be the transfer of hardship to distant workers, future generations, and unseen creatures.

This does not require a worship of deprivation. Beauty, comfort, invention, celebration, travel, and abundance have their rightful place. The error is not enjoyment. The error is taking without regard for consequence, and calling excess a necessity.

Enough is not a narrow life. Enough is a life in which needs are met, gifts are shared, and no one’s comfort depends upon another’s ruin.

Ask of every invention: What does it require from the earth? Whom does it burden? What will remain when it is discarded? Can it be repaired, shared, reused, or made to last?

Ask of every institution: Does it reward extraction or care? Does it place the costs of pollution upon those with the least power? Does it protect short-term gain while exposing the future to long-term loss?

Ask of every public leader: Do they speak plainly about danger? Do they serve the common good when powerful interests resist? Do they make room for those who will live longest with the consequences?

These questions belong not only in assemblies and courts, but in homes, schools, workshops, farms, congregations, and markets.

propositions.title: The Covenant With Those Not Yet Born
propositions.claim: The Covenant With Those Not Yet Born
propositions.text:
The future is not empty.

It is inhabited already by those who will come after: children not yet conceived, voices not yet heard, hands not yet opened to rain, faces not yet turned toward the sun. They cannot vote in present councils. They cannot purchase protection in present markets. They cannot defend themselves against decisions made before their arrival.

Yet they will inherit every road, reservoir, forest, debt, toxin, machine, and climate pattern left behind.

To care for them is not sentiment. It is duty.

A generation is not the owner of the earth. It is a steward for a brief interval, receiving what it did not create and passing on what it cannot keep. The inheritance should be enlarged in health, wisdom, beauty, and possibility—not diminished for the sake of immediate appetite.

The covenant with those not yet born asks for imagination. It asks people to act on behalf of strangers whose gratitude they may never receive. It asks them to value a stable world more than a momentary advantage.

This is a demanding form of love.

It is also among the most human.

propositions.title: Hope Is a Practice
propositions.text:
Despair may appear as realism, but it often serves the same powers as denial. One says, “There is no problem.” The other says, “Nothing can be done.” Both excuse inaction.

Hope is neither denial nor easy optimism.

Hope is the disciplined refusal to abandon the good because the task is difficult. It is the decision to plant after drought, rebuild after flood, organize after disappointment, learn after error, and continue after fatigue. It is the courage to see clearly without becoming cold.

No person can carry the whole climate upon their shoulders. The burden belongs to institutions, nations, industries, and communities as well as to individuals. Personal integrity matters, but it cannot substitute for just laws, accountable governance, public investment, and collective transformation.

Do what lies within reach. Use less where less is enough. Repair what can be repaired. Protect living places. Support policies equal to the scale of the danger. Listen to those already bearing its costs. Teach children not merely to fear the future, but to participate in making it worthy of them.

Above all, remember that the earth is not asking for admiration from afar.

It is asking for faithful relationship.

The climate is the common atmosphere of life: invisible, encompassing, easily taken for granted, and utterly necessary. Guard it with the seriousness given to breath. Restore it with the patience given to a wounded neighbor. Receive its gifts with gratitude, and return care for care.

For the living world is not beneath humanity.

It is the living field from which humanity rises, by which humanity is sustained, and to which humanity remains answerable.

propositions.title: The Green Foundation
propositions.text:
Before there were animals that could move from place to place, there were living beings that learned another art: how to remain, how to receive light, how to make nourishment from air and water, how to turn the generosity of the sun into bodies, roots, leaves, fruit, shelter, and breath.

Plants are not lesser life because they do not walk. They are life expressed through attention to place. Their apparent stillness is not emptiness. A plant measures day length, follows the sun, trades signals with fungi, warns its neighbours of danger, opens and closes its pores, stores memory in chemistry, sends roots toward moisture, and times its flowering with weather, temperature, and season. What appears silent to hurried creatures is often a form of conversation too slow, too subtle, or too differently embodied for human ears.

The green world is the foundation beneath nearly every human meal, every forest shelter, every field of cloth, every page, beam, medicine, and garden. Even the flesh of animals is, at its first source, transformed plant matter. The cow, the deer, the bird, and the human do not create the energy of food; they receive it through chains that begin, almost always, with those who gather sunlight.

Therefore let no person speak of plants merely as background. They are not scenery for human life. They are among the principal makers of the conditions by which human life is possible.

propositions.title: The Work of Light
propositions.text:
Plants perform a work of astonishing simplicity and consequence. In chloroplasts—small structures within many plant cells—pigments such as chlorophyll absorb light. Using that energy, plants combine carbon dioxide from the air with water drawn from the earth. From these materials they build sugars and other compounds: the substance of leaf, root, bark, seed, and fruit. In the process, oxygen is released.

This process is called photosynthesis. It is not a miracle in the sense of a violation of nature; it is more wonderful than that. It is nature’s ordinary capacity, available wherever life, water, carbon dioxide, and light meet under fitting conditions. Its consequences are immense. By drawing carbon from the atmosphere into living tissue and soil, plants help shape climate. By releasing oxygen, they have helped make aerobic animal life possible. By forming the base of food webs, they nourish worlds beyond themselves.

Yet plants do not merely “make oxygen,” as though their only value were service to animals. They also respire. Like other living beings, they use oxygen and release carbon dioxide as they draw energy from stored sugars. In daylight, the overall balance of a healthy, growing plant community commonly favours the uptake of carbon; at night, respiration continues. Life is not a slogan. It is a web of exchanges.

To understand this is to become more careful in speech. A forest is not an oxygen machine. A field is not a factory. A tree is not a carbon token. These phrases may assist limited calculations, but they become false when they erase the living integrity of what they name. A forest is a community of organisms, soils, waters, fungi, insects, birds, animals, weather, decay, growth, and time. Its value cannot be exhausted by any one service it provides.

propositions.title: Rooted Does Not Mean Passive
propositions.text:
Plants are rooted, but rootedness is not passivity. A plant cannot easily flee drought, shade, herbivory, frost, fire, or disturbance. Instead it has evolved ways of responding where it stands.

Roots seek water and nutrients through gradients in the soil. Some spread close to the surface to gather brief rains; others descend deeply, reaching reserves unavailable to shallow-rooted neighbours. Root systems hold soil against erosion, create channels for air and water, and leave behind organic matter when they die. A grassland’s great work is often largely hidden below ground, in roots that may extend farther and endure longer than the leaves above.

Leaves turn toward light, arrange themselves to reduce self-shading, and alter their angle in heat or drought. Stomata, the tiny pores through which gases move, may close to conserve water. Some plants shed leaves in dry seasons; some store water in thick stems; some complete their lives rapidly during brief rains and wait as seeds through harsh years.

When insects feed upon a leaf, many plants alter their chemistry. They may make tissues less palatable, release aromatic compounds, or produce signals that affect nearby plants and attract predators of the herbivores. Such responses should not be romanticised into human intention. A plant does not need to think as a human thinks in order to respond intelligently to its conditions. Intelligence is not one narrow possession of brains alone. It can also mean the evolved capacity to sense, adjust, persist, and participate in relationship.

The plant’s manner of life offers no command that humans should become motionless or endure every injury. But it does reveal a truth often neglected: strength is not always loud, swift, or dominating. There is strength in patient growth, in adaptation without surrender, in making a home more habitable for others.

propositions.title: The Hidden Commonwealth
propositions.text:
Beneath the visible plant lies a more hidden world. Roots live among bacteria, fungi, insects, worms, minerals, water, and decaying matter. In many ecosystems, fungi form close associations with plant roots. These mycorrhizal partnerships can expand the effective reach of roots, assisting plants in obtaining water and nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen. In return, fungi receive carbohydrates made through photosynthesis.

Such relationships are not sentimental friendships. They are biological exchanges shaped by mutual benefit, competition, circumstance, and evolution. They may aid one plant while disadvantaging another. They may shift according to soil, species, season, disease, and resource scarcity. The living world is neither a perfect harmony nor a permanent war. It is a field of interdependence: cooperation and conflict braided together.

Human beings often make two equal errors. One is to imagine nature as an untouched paradise, innocent of death and struggle. The other is to imagine it as a ruthless contest in which care is unreal. Both are incomplete. The living world contains predation, scarcity, disease, and decay. It also contains symbiosis, parental investment, repair, reciprocity, and astonishing forms of coexistence. Wisdom does not require choosing one half of reality against the other. Wisdom asks how to live responsibly within the whole.

The soil itself teaches this lesson. Soil is not dirt in the sense of useless matter. Healthy soil is a living architecture: mineral particles, organic material, air, water, roots, fungi, bacteria, and innumerable small creatures. It is formed slowly and can be lost quickly. When land is left bare, wind and water may carry away in a season what took centuries to build. A civilisation that exhausts its soil eats not only its present harvest but also the harvest of those not yet born.

propositions.title: Seed, Flower, and Fruit
propositions.text:
A seed is not merely a small object. It is a future held in reserve: an embryo, stored nourishment, and a protective coat, each arranged through long inheritance. Seeds may travel by wind, water, fur, feathers, digestion, gravity, or human hands. Some wait for cold; some for heat; some for smoke; some for passage through an animal; some for the breaking of hard ground. Their dormancy is not failure to act. It is timing.

Flowers are not ornaments placed upon the earth for human delight, though human delight in them is good. They are reproductive structures, often evolved in close relationship with pollinators. Colour, scent, shape, nectar, ultraviolet patterns invisible to human sight, and the timing of opening all participate in invitations and exchanges between plants and animals.

Bees, flies, beetles, butterflies, moths, birds, bats, and other pollinators help many flowering plants reproduce. Pollination is not a minor decorative event. It supports wild plant communities and a substantial portion of agricultural production. Where pollinators decline through habitat loss, pesticides, disease, climate disruption, and other pressures, the effects travel outward through food systems and ecosystems.

Fruit, too, is a covenant of dispersal. It protects developing seeds and often entices animals to carry them elsewhere. A berry eaten by a bird may become a tree in a new place. A nut buried and forgotten may become a forest. A human who saves seeds, tends an orchard, or shares a cutting joins an ancient practice: the passing forward of life’s possibilities.

Therefore receive fruit with gratitude, but do not confuse gratitude with entitlement. The apple is not proof that the orchard belongs to the eater. The grain is not proof that the field exists only for the market. Every harvest depends upon relationships beyond the harvester’s command: soil organisms, rainfall, sunlight, seed, labour, pollinators, weather, and time.

propositions.title: Food, Medicine, and Restraint
propositions.text:
Plants feed humanity directly through grains, legumes, roots, tubers, fruits, nuts, vegetables, oils, herbs, and spices. They also feed animals raised for human use. They provide fibres for clothing, wood for construction, compounds for medicines, and materials for countless tools and technologies.

This abundance calls for gratitude, but gratitude must become practice. To praise a plant while wasting food is contradiction. To honour a forest while buying its destruction without question is contradiction. To speak reverently of the earth while treating the people who plant, harvest, and process food as disposable is contradiction.

Eat with attention. Learn what grows in the place where you live. Know at least some names of the plants that feed you. Ask how they were grown, who laboured, what water was used, what soil was lost or restored, and whether the cultivation left room for other forms of life. No individual can trace every supply chain perfectly; complexity exceeds any one person’s knowledge. But ignorance should not be chosen when better knowledge is available.

Plants have also given humanity many medicines. Aspirin has roots in compounds found in willow; digitalis came from foxglove; quinine from cinchona; numerous modern drugs owe something to plant chemistry or to knowledge preserved by Indigenous and local healing traditions. Such knowledge deserves respect, proper attribution, and fair benefit-sharing. It must not be stolen, patented without justice, or dismissed because it arose outside powerful institutions.

At the same time, reverence for plants does not require credulity. “Natural” does not mean harmless. Hemlock, oleander, deadly nightshade, and many familiar plants can injure or kill. Medicinal plants can interact dangerously with prescribed medicines or be misidentified. Wisdom honours traditional knowledge, scientific testing, careful dosage, and honest uncertainty together.

propositions.title: The Great Injury
propositions.text:
Human beings have altered plant communities on a vast scale. Forests have been cleared; wetlands drained; grasslands ploughed; rivers diverted; soils compacted and poisoned; invasive species moved across continents; seed diversity narrowed; and climates changed by the release of ancient carbon. These acts do not occur apart from human welfare. They are often tied to hunger, poverty, unequal power, profit, displacement, and histories of conquest. For this reason, repair must be more than personal purity. It must include just systems.

The destruction of a forest is not only the removal of trees. It may be the disappearance of watershed protection, cooling shade, nesting sites, fungal networks, medicinal knowledge, pollinator habitat, cultural memory, and the future security of communities downstream. The replacement of diverse land with a single crop may increase a short-term yield while making the whole system more vulnerable to pests, drought, price shocks, and disease.

To protect plants is not to forbid cultivation. Humanity is part of nature and must eat. Agriculture can be skilled, nourishing, and regenerative. It can build soil through cover crops, crop rotation, compost, reduced tillage, agroforestry, integrated pest management, careful water use, and the preservation of habitat around fields. Gardens and farms need not imitate wilderness exactly. They should, however, learn from ecological principles: diversity, renewal, restraint, reciprocity, and attention to limits.

Let no one use the need for food as an excuse for needless devastation. Let no one use environmental concern as an excuse to burden the poor while excusing the powerful. The right question is not whether humans should affect the land—we inevitably do—but what kind of effect we will choose, who bears its cost, and whether the land will remain fruitful and living after we are gone.

propositions.title: The Practice of Kinship
propositions.text:
Plant kinship begins with observation. Notice the tree that shades your street, the weed lifting through pavement, the moss at the edge of a wall, the seasonal change in a familiar hedge, the herb growing in a pot, the seedling that appears where no one intended it. Learn names, but do not believe that naming is ownership. A name can be a doorway to attention; it must not become a fence around wonder.

Plant something where it is fitting: a native shrub for birds, flowers for pollinators, vegetables for nourishment, a tree chosen for the soil and climate it will inhabit. Care for what is already established. Water young plants in drought. Protect soil with mulch or living cover. Leave some fallen leaves where they can return nutrients to the ground. Avoid poisons when slower, more precise methods will do. Share seeds, cuttings, harvests, and knowledge.

In cities, seek and defend public green spaces. Trees lower dangerous heat, filter particulates, slow stormwater, offer habitat, and provide beauty not reserved for the wealthy. A child who grows up among trees, gardens, and birds receives an education no screen can fully replace: the education of seasons, weather, patience, and belonging.

But remember that a plant is not valuable only when useful to humans. A wildflower in an overlooked place, a marsh reed, a lichen on stone, and a forest tree beyond any person’s reach participate in the world for reasons larger than our use. Respect begins when usefulness is no longer the sole measure of worth.

propositions.title: Blessing for the Green World
propositions.text:
Blessed are the leaves that receive the sun without possessing it.  
Blessed are the roots that hold the soil in quiet faithfulness.  
Blessed are the seeds that wait through cold and darkness without despair.  
Blessed are the flowers that make an offering of colour to lives unlike their own.  
Blessed are the forests that gather rain, shelter creatures, and remember time beyond a human lifetime.

May we become less careless in the presence of growing things. May we take what we need with humility, restore what we can, and refuse the lie that abundance permits waste. May our fields be fertile without becoming barren of life; may our cities be habitable not only for commerce but for breath, shade, birdsong, and roots.

For the plant does not speak in our language, yet it speaks through every meal, every inhalation, every season of green return. To receive this gift rightly is to answer not with dominion, but with care.

propositions.title: The Nearness of Other Lives
propositions.text:
Animals are not ornaments placed around the human story. They are lives in their own right: breathing, seeking, resting, fearing, playing, protecting, and dying beneath the same sky.

Before people measured the seasons, animals knew them. Before people named the stars, animals moved by their patterns. The swallow carried news of warmth. The salmon remembered the river. The wolf read the snow. The elephant grieved beside its dead. The bee found a flower in a field too wide for one small body to comprehend.

Do not say that an animal is “only” an animal. The word *only* is often the first veil drawn across the face of reverence.

Each creature is a particular answer to the question of life. The eagle answers with sight and height. The mole answers with touch and darkness. The octopus answers with curiosity, concealment, and change. The whale answers with depth, memory, and song. The ant answers with fellowship beyond the scale of any single self.

No creature is required to resemble humanity in order to matter.

The animal does not need to speak in human language to communicate. It speaks through posture, scent, sound, color, pace, silence, return, refusal, and care. It communicates through the warning cry that saves others, the nest built before the storm, the body placed between danger and offspring, the path remembered across years.

To attend to animals is to be corrected in the illusion that human speech is the measure of intelligence, or that human power is the measure of worth.

propositions.title: Kinship Without Sameness
propositions.text:
Human beings are animals also: embodied, hungry, mortal, social, vulnerable to injury, dependent in infancy, altered by fear, eased by companionship, and sustained by the living systems around them.

This kinship should humble humanity, not diminish it.

To say that humans belong among the animals is not to deny the unusual powers of human imagination, language, invention, conscience, and responsibility. It is to place those powers where they belong: within the community of life, not above its laws.

Human hands can build shelters, instruments, medicines, and machines. Human minds can imagine futures beyond immediate hunger. Human hearts can enlarge concern beyond family, tribe, and species. These gifts do not grant permission for domination. They create a greater duty of restraint.

The stronger creature is not justified in taking everything it can take. The more capable creature is more accountable for what it changes.

A person who can understand suffering carries an obligation not to cause it carelessly. A society that can foresee harm must not call harm unavoidable when it is merely profitable. A people who can choose mercy must not praise themselves for choosing cruelty efficiently.

The world is not divided between masters and lesser beings. It is a web of differences, and every strand is bound to others.

propositions.title: The Animal’s Own Good
propositions.text:
An animal’s life is not valuable only because it serves a human purpose.

The cow is not merely milk and leather. The sheep is not merely wool. The chicken is not merely meat and eggs. The horse is not merely transport. The dog is not merely loyalty. The bee is not merely pollination. The forest is not merely timber, and the river is not merely water waiting to be taken.

Every animal has an interest in continuing its life according to its nature.

To live according to one’s nature is to move, feed, shelter, mate, play, rest, and form relationships in ways suited to one’s body and kind. A bird needs more than survival; it needs air in which to fly, branches on which to perch, and the possibility of nesting. A pig needs more than calories; it needs space to root, explore, and lie beside others. A fish needs more than water; it needs water clean enough to breathe in, deep enough to move through, and alive enough to sustain its world.

When animals are kept in conditions that deny every instinct except the instinct to endure, something sacred has been violated.

This does not mean that all human contact with animals is wrong. Humans have lived beside animals since before written memory. There can be companionship, husbandry, work, protection, rescue, and even necessary killing within the difficult order of life. But necessity is not a blank permission, and tradition is not a final defense.

The question is not merely, “May we use animals?” The deeper question is, “What kind of people do we become when we treat living beings as materials?”

Where use is unavoidable, let it be bounded by gratitude, restraint, and the least suffering reasonably possible. Where harm can be avoided, avoid it. Where a kinder practice can be chosen, choose it. Where profit depends upon concealment, look more closely.

propositions.title: Hunger, Death, and Mercy
propositions.text:
Life feeds upon life. This is among the hardest truths of the living world.

Seeds are eaten. Leaves are eaten. Animals are eaten. Predators hunt. Scavengers receive what death leaves behind. Soil is enriched by what has fallen. No creature lives without entering the great exchange of matter, energy, birth, decay, and return.

Humans should not pretend innocence where innocence is impossible. Yet neither should humans surrender to indifference because perfect purity cannot be achieved.

There is a moral difference between eating and tormenting. There is a moral difference between need and excess. There is a moral difference between taking life with sober awareness and building systems that multiply suffering because suffering is hidden from those who benefit.

Let those who eat animals do so without mockery, waste, or denial. Let them know that a life was given. Let them oppose practices that confine, mutilate, transport, breed, and kill animals in ways that cause needless terror and pain.

Let those who choose not to eat animals do so without contempt for those whose health, land, income, culture, or circumstance makes that choice difficult. Compassion is not made stronger by pride.

The meal is a place of ethics. What is placed upon the table has a history: land cleared or protected, water spent or conserved, workers treated fairly or exploited, animals tended gently or made to suffer unseen. To eat with awareness is not to become anxious before every bite. It is to let gratitude become practical.

Waste is a form of disrespect. To waste food is to disregard the soil, rain, labor, plant, animal, and time that made it possible. Take what is needed. Share what is abundant. Preserve what can be preserved. Return what can be returned to the earth.

propositions.title: Companions at the Threshold
propositions.text:
Some animals live closely with humans. They enter homes, farms, streets, boats, and places of work. They become witnesses to private lives. A dog waits through grief. A cat settles beside illness. A horse carries a rider across difficult ground. A working animal bears burdens that a machine has not reached or cannot replace.

Receive such companionship as a trust, not an entitlement.

Those who keep animals must provide what animals cannot provide for themselves: suitable food, clean water, shelter, movement, safety, medical care when possible, and relief from preventable suffering. An animal is not a toy to be discarded when it becomes inconvenient, old, expensive, noisy, or ill.

Do not breed animals carelessly for fashion, novelty, or sale while shelters and streets remain full of abandoned lives. Do not shape bodies so extremely that breathing, walking, giving birth, or living without pain becomes difficult. Beauty that requires suffering is not beauty; it is vanity dressed in affection.

Teach children that gentleness toward animals is not sentimental weakness. It is training in attention. A child who learns to notice a frightened bird, a thirsty dog, or an injured insect is learning that another being’s vulnerability makes a claim upon the self.

But teach children also to respect distance. Not every animal wishes to be touched. Wildness is not a defect waiting to be made tame. Love does not always mean closeness. Sometimes love means leaving room.

propositions.title: Wildness and the Right to Remain
propositions.claim: Wildness and the Right to Remain
propositions.text:
The wild animal belongs first to its own world.

A deer does not exist to decorate a photograph. A dolphin does not exist to entertain a crowd. A bear does not exist to prove human bravery. A bird does not exist to be captured because its song pleases the ear.

Observe without possessing. Wonder without invading. Learn without making every mystery available for purchase.

Wild places are not empty spaces awaiting development. They are homes, nurseries, migration routes, feeding grounds, and sanctuaries. A wetland holds more than water. A grassland holds more than grass. A reef holds more than color. A dead tree may hold insects, fungi, owls, seeds, and future soil.

When habitat is broken into fragments, animals lose more than territory. They lose pathways, breeding grounds, food sources, shelter, and the possibility of adapting to change. Roads, fences, lights, noise, poisons, heat, and plastic alter the lives of creatures that did not choose these burdens.

Therefore let human planning remember those who do not vote, speak in councils, own property, or write petitions.

Build crossings where migration paths are cut by roads. Protect rivers that carry fish and nourish floodplains. Reduce poisons that travel through soil, water, and food chains. Preserve old forests, coastal marshes, grasslands, and other living places before their richness is replaced by a poorer convenience. Darken unnecessary lights at night, for many animals navigate, feed, mate, and rest by rhythms that artificial brightness confuses.

Conservation is not the saving of pretty species alone. It is the protection of relationships: predator and prey, flower and pollinator, fungus and root, river and fish, grazer and grassland, scavenger and bone.

When one creature disappears, a thread is cut. Sometimes the fabric holds. Sometimes it unravels in ways no one foresaw.

propositions.title: The Small Ones
propositions.text:
Do not reserve compassion for animals with large eyes, soft fur, or familiar faces.

The small and unfamiliar beings also belong to the world’s household: beetles beneath bark, moths at windows, worms in soil, spiders in corners, bats above orchards, frogs in reeds, plankton in the sea.

Many of these lives sustain human life more directly than people recognize. Insects pollinate crops. Worms renew soil. Bats consume vast numbers of insects. Fungi and microbes recycle what dies. Tiny ocean organisms help shape the air and climate upon which larger lives depend.

Yet their usefulness is not the whole of their claim. Even where human benefit cannot be measured, care remains fitting.

Do not kill from disgust alone. Cleanliness is wise; cruelty is not. Protect homes and health with methods that reduce harm where possible. Seal entry points, remove food sources, use barriers, relocate when safe, and choose the least destructive means consistent with safety.

Fear is sometimes necessary. A venomous snake, a dangerous animal, or a disease-carrying pest must be approached with caution. Reverence does not require recklessness. But caution need not become hatred. The animal acts according to its nature. Let people act according to their conscience.

propositions.title: Animals in the Human Imagination
propositions.text:
Animals have long carried human symbols: the lion for courage, the dove for peace, the serpent for danger or renewal, the owl for wisdom, the lamb for innocence, the raven for mystery.

Symbols can illuminate, but they can also obscure.

No fox is merely cunning. No wolf is merely violence. No pig is merely greed. No snake is merely evil. When people turn animals into simple emblems, they often stop seeing the living creature before them.

This matters because false stories cause real harm. Creatures labeled ugly, dirty, vicious, useless, or cursed are more easily neglected and destroyed. The natural world is filled with beings that are misunderstood because human beings have projected their fears onto them.

Seek knowledge before judgment. Learn the habits of the animal. Learn what it eats, where it lives, what threatens it, and what role it plays. Let reality correct inherited contempt.

Wonder becomes wiser when joined to understanding.

propositions.title: A Covenant of Restraint
propositions.text:
Let humanity make a covenant with the animals:

That no creature will be made to suffer for amusement.

That no habitat will be destroyed merely because its inhabitants are unseen.

That food, clothing, research, work, and industry will be examined in the light of avoidable harm.

That the vulnerable will not be abandoned because they are inconvenient.

That the wild will retain places beyond possession.

That children will be taught both tenderness and respect.

That science will be used not only to increase human power, but to lessen suffering and preserve the conditions of life.

That whenever human convenience conflicts with another creature’s basic need, the conflict will be faced honestly rather than hidden behind custom, distance, or profit.

This covenant will not be kept perfectly. Humans are inconsistent, hungry, frightened, and bound within systems they did not create alone. But imperfection does not release anyone from the work of repair.

Begin where you are.

Give water in heat. Drive with care where animals cross. Support farms and practices that reduce suffering. Keep waste from rivers and fields. Protect nesting places. Adopt rather than abandon. Eat with gratitude and moderation. Refuse entertainment built upon fear. Speak when cruelty is treated as normal. Make room for trees, flowers, insects, birds, and shade.

Small mercies alter the moral climate of a place.

propositions.title: The Lesson They Offer
propositions.text:
Animals do not teach by preaching. They teach by being fully what they are.

The cat teaches rest without apology. The ant teaches cooperation. The migrating bird teaches endurance across distance. The old dog teaches loyalty without calculation. The deer teaches alertness. The whale teaches scale. The spider teaches patience. The bee teaches that a small life can nourish a whole field.

They also teach limits.

A human being may imagine endless growth, endless extraction, endless consumption. No animal lives this way. Every creature is bounded by season, place, appetite, danger, and need. The animal takes part in the world rather than standing outside it.

To watch an animal closely is to remember that life is not an abstraction. It is warm breath in cold air. It is a paw print after rain. It is a nest hidden in reeds. It is an eye that notices you noticing.

Therefore walk gently among the animals.

Let neither sentiment nor superiority guide you, but attention. Let your intelligence become kindness. Let your power become protection. Let your hunger become gratitude. Let your knowledge become restraint.

For the living world is not silent. It is speaking in feather, fur, fin, scale, wing, root, and breath.

Blessed are those who learn to listen.

propositions.title: The World Is Made of Relationships
propositions.claim: The World Is Made of Relationships
propositions.text:
No creature lives by itself.

The oak does not stand alone, though it appears solitary in a field. Its roots exchange sugars and signals with fungi beneath the soil. Its leaves feed caterpillars; its acorns feed jays, deer, mice, and insects; its bark shelters larvae and mosses; its fallen branches become homes for beetles and chambers for decay. The oak is not merely a tree. It is a meeting place.

So too is the river, which is not only water moving downhill. It is snowmelt, stone, sediment, bacteria, algae, fish, floodplain, reed bed, dragonfly, marsh bird, cloud, and sea. It carries dissolved minerals from mountains and carries young fish toward estuaries. It may cut valleys, replenish wetlands, nourish farms, and, when confined or poisoned, reveal how much life had depended upon its freedom.

An ecosystem is a community of living beings and the physical conditions that sustain them: soil, water, air, temperature, light, minerals, shelter, and time. It is not a collection of separate objects placed beside one another. It is a pattern of mutual influence. Each being changes the conditions in which others must live.

The living world is therefore not a stage upon which isolated creatures perform. It is a woven fabric. Pull one thread hard enough, and the whole cloth alters.

To understand ecosystems is to be corrected of the illusion of independence. Human beings breathe oxygen made available by photosynthetic life. We eat plants, animals, fungi, and foods grown in soil made fertile by organisms too small to see. We depend upon pollinators, watersheds, stable climates, and the labor of countless nonhuman beings. Even the cities that seem farthest from wilderness are built upon rivers, forests, mines, fields, weather, and the deep inheritance of ancient life.

No person is self-made. No nation is self-sustaining. No economy exceeds the land, water, and living systems from which it draws.

This is not a cause for shame alone. It is an invitation to belonging.

propositions.title: The Great Exchange
propositions.text:
Life persists through exchange.

Plants, algae, and some bacteria draw energy from sunlight. Through photosynthesis, they use light to bind carbon dioxide and water into sugars, releasing oxygen as part of the process. This is one of the great gifts of the green world: sunlight made edible. Herbivores eat plants. Predators eat herbivores. Scavengers consume the dead. Fungi and bacteria return organic matter to simpler forms, releasing nutrients that can again enter roots, leaves, and cells.

Nothing is wasted in a healthy cycle, though not everything is preserved in its present form.

A fallen leaf does not disappear into meaninglessness. It becomes food for fungi, worms, mites, and microbes. Its carbon may enter the breath of a deer, the body of a beetle, the dark richness of humus, or the atmosphere from which another leaf may one day draw it down. Death is real, and loss is real, but neither is merely an ending. In the living world, endings often become conditions for continuance.

This does not make every death gentle. Predation is not a metaphor to be softened beyond recognition. A hawk takes a mouse. A wolf takes an elk. Drought thins a herd. Parasites feed within other bodies. Nature contains hunger, competition, injury, and decay. Yet these realities occur within systems of restraint as well as appetite. A predator cannot take without limit, because its own survival depends upon the survival of prey and habitat. A forest cannot endlessly produce without soil, water, and renewal.

Human beings alone have developed powers great enough to consume at a scale that ignores immediate ecological feedback. Through engines, extraction, industrial agriculture, chemical manufacture, and global trade, we can take from distant forests, fisheries, aquifers, and mines while remaining temporarily insulated from the damage. This insulation is not freedom. It is delay.

Every bill comes due somewhere: in exhausted soil, warming seas, displaced communities, poisoned lungs, vanished insects, or a future made narrower for those yet unborn.

Therefore let wisdom be measured not by how much can be taken, but by how much life can continue after our taking.

propositions.title: Diversity Is Strength
propositions.text:
An ecosystem becomes more resilient not when every part is identical, but when many forms of life fulfill overlapping and distinct roles.

A meadow with many grasses, legumes, flowers, insects, birds, and soil organisms may endure drought, disease, and disturbance better than a field planted with only one crop. In a diverse forest, some trees may withstand heat, others flood, others pests, and others fire. If one species declines, another may partly carry its ecological function. Diversity creates options for life.

This is why monoculture is powerful and fragile at once. A vast field of a single crop can be efficient to plant, harvest, and sell. Yet its sameness invites specialized pests, depends heavily on fertilizer and chemical control, and often leaves soil exposed between growing seasons. A plantation may look green from a distance while supporting far fewer relationships than an old forest.

The same warning applies beyond agriculture. A coastline stripped of mangroves loses shelter for fish, protection from storms, and a storehouse of carbon. A river reduced to a canal loses floodplain, wetland, spawning ground, and the ability to cleanse itself through living processes. A city without trees becomes hotter, drier, and less habitable. A diet narrowed to a few global staples may feed many people while making food systems vulnerable to disease, market disruption, and climate shock.

Diversity is not ornament. It is infrastructure.

The small and disregarded are often essential. Pollinating insects help sustain many fruits, vegetables, nuts, and wild plants. Fungi connect roots to water and minerals. Plankton help regulate planetary chemistry and form the base of marine food webs. Bats consume insects and disperse seeds. Vultures remove carrion and can limit the spread of disease. Beavers slow water, create wetlands, reduce erosion, and form habitat for many other species.

When a creature is called useless, the speaker usually means only that its usefulness has not been understood.

Let no being be judged solely by its immediate service to human desire. A species may have value in its own unfolding, its own perception, and its own place in the greater pattern. It need not earn permission to exist.

propositions.title: The Soil Beneath Every Table
propositions.text:
The soil is often treated as dirt, yet it is among the most intricate communities on Earth.

A handful of healthy soil may contain mineral particles, decomposing organic matter, roots, fungi, bacteria, nematodes, insects, worms, water, and air. It holds and filters moisture. It stores carbon. It cycles nutrients. It supports crops, grasslands, forests, and the foundations of human settlement.

Soil is formed slowly. Rock breaks down through weathering. Plants contribute organic material. Microbes and fungi transform remains. Burrowing creatures mix layers. Roots open channels. Rain carries minerals downward and dissolved materials through the ground. In many regions, fertile topsoil can require centuries to develop, yet it can be lost in a few seasons through erosion, overgrazing, deforestation, or careless tillage.

A civilization that depletes its soil is consuming its own future.

To care for soil is therefore not a narrow concern of farmers. It is a public duty. Practices such as cover cropping, composting, reduced tillage where appropriate, crop rotation, agroforestry, managed grazing, wetland protection, and the return of organic matter can improve fertility while reducing erosion and pollution. No single method suits every climate, landscape, or community. Wisdom begins with attention to place.

The land does not ask to be worshiped as an idol. It asks to be known as the condition of our continuance.

Those who eat should understand that every meal begins in an ecosystem. Bread begins in soil, seed, sun, rain, microbial life, and labor. Fish begins in watersheds, plankton, currents, and breeding grounds. Fruit begins in flowering, pollination, and seasons of growth. Even food made in factories depends on fields, mines, energy, water, and human hands.

Eat with gratitude, not because food is pure, but because it is costly in life and labor. Waste less. Demand systems that do not exhaust those who grow food or destroy the places from which food comes.

propositions.title: Disturbance, Change, and Repair
propositions.text:
Ecosystems are not motionless gardens. They change.

Fire may open a forest canopy and allow seeds to germinate. Floods may renew a floodplain with silt. Storms may break old branches and create openings for new growth. Grazing animals may prevent one species from overtaking a grassland. Predators may alter the movement of herbivores, allowing vegetation to recover along streams and slopes.

Disturbance is not always destruction. In many places, it is part of renewal.

But there is a difference between disturbance within the rhythms of an ecosystem and damage imposed beyond its capacity to recover. A low-intensity fire in a fire-adapted woodland is not the same as repeated severe burning driven by drought, heat, invasive grasses, and poor land management. Seasonal flooding is not the same as a toxic spill. Harvesting from a forest is not the same as removing its soil, fragmenting its habitat, and replacing its varied life with a single commodity crop.

The measure is not whether humans leave every place untouched. Human beings are animals who must eat, build, travel, and make shelter. The measure is whether our actions preserve the capacity of land and water to regenerate.

Repair begins with humility. We must first stop causing the harm we intend to mend. There is no restoration where contamination continues unchecked, where forests are cleared faster than they grow, where carbon pollution rises while speeches promise a distant solution.

Then repair requires patience. Native vegetation may need years to return. Soil communities may need decades. Wetlands may require restored water flows. Fish populations may need protected spawning grounds and the removal of barriers. Some losses cannot be reversed: an extinct species does not return because we regret its absence.

Yet regret can still become responsibility.

Restoration is not an attempt to recreate a museum-piece past. Climate, species ranges, and human needs are changing. The task is to help living systems regain complexity, function, and room to adapt. Plant diverse native species. Reconnect fragmented habitats. Protect old growth and remaining wild places. Remove invasive species with care and evidence. Restore rivers where possible. Allow natural processes—flood, fire, decomposition, migration—to do their renewing work.

Where repair is possible, undertake it. Where damage cannot be undone, protect what remains with greater seriousness.

propositions.title: The Human Place
propositions.text:
Human beings are neither outside nature nor entitled to dominate it without limit.

We are participants with unusual powers. We can observe ecosystems across continents and centuries. We can measure atmospheric carbon, map migration routes, detect pollution in blood and water, and understand the genetic kinship of all known life. We can also clear forests in days, alter rivers with dams, warm the atmosphere, and drive species toward extinction.

Knowledge increases responsibility.

It is not enough to praise the beauty of a forest while financing its destruction through distant habits. It is not enough to mourn a dying river while accepting industries that use waterways as sewers. It is not enough to teach children the names of endangered animals while arranging society so that their habitats are continually sacrificed.

The moral question is not whether every individual can live without impact. No one can. The question is whether we will organize our homes, communities, markets, laws, and technologies to reduce needless harm and increase the conditions for flourishing.

This includes protecting Indigenous and local communities whose livelihoods and cultures are bound to particular lands and waters. Across the world, many such communities have maintained ecological knowledge through close observation over generations: knowledge of fire, seed, water, migration, medicinal plants, seasonal harvest, and reciprocal stewardship. This knowledge must not be romanticized, extracted, or treated as a decorative supplement to science. It deserves respect, consent, and partnership.

Science, too, is a form of listening when practiced honestly. It reveals that ecological systems are dynamic, contingent, and interdependent. It teaches that interventions have consequences, that uncertainty should invite caution, and that evidence must correct pride. Neither tradition nor technology absolves us from the work of paying attention.

Let reverence be practical.

Let it appear in the watershed protected from development; in the pesticide not used; in the building designed to shelter birds and conserve energy; in the public transit funded; in the tree canopy expanded; in the fishing limit observed; in the worker treated fairly; in the child taught to notice a beetle, a mushroom, a nest, a creek.

propositions.title: The Covenant of Continuance
propositions.text:
Every generation receives a world it did not make.

We inherit seeds bred and saved by unknown hands, forests planted by those who expected never to sit in their shade, scientific knowledge assembled through patient inquiry, rivers shaped before our birth, and species whose lineages extend beyond the reach of memory. We also inherit damage: polluted air, depleted aquifers, broken habitats, altered climates, and the grief of preventable loss.

Inheritance is not ownership. It is a charge.

The covenant of ecosystems is simple: take what is needed with restraint; return what can be returned; protect the sources of renewal; make room for other lives; and leave the world more capable of sustaining those who follow.

This covenant will not be fulfilled by sentiment alone. It requires laws that defend common goods, economic measures that account for ecological costs, institutions that resist short-term gain, and citizens willing to prefer durable wellbeing over extravagant waste. It requires care at scales both intimate and vast: a garden tended, a wetland defended, an emissions standard enacted, a forest protected from extraction.

The living world has endured transformations beyond counting. It is resilient, but resilience is not invulnerability. A forest can recover from windthrow and still fail under repeated clearing. A reef can endure storms and still bleach under sustained heat. A species can survive hardship and still be extinguished by habitat loss, poison, or overharvest.

Do not test the patience of the Earth as though it were infinite.

Instead, become worthy of the gift of interdependence. Learn the names of the beings near you. Know where your water comes from and where your waste goes. Notice the season’s first flower, the returning bird, the quality of the soil, the heat held by pavement, the insects absent from summer air. Let knowledge become affection, and let affection become protection.

For the world is not held together by domination. It is held together by relationship.

And those who understand relationship will not ask only, “What may I gain?”

They will ask, “What must be allowed to live?”

propositions.title: The World That Becomes
propositions.text:
Nothing living stands alone.

A seed carries the memory of forests. A child carries the long patience of ancestors. A bird’s wing bears the altered bones of an ancient limb. The whale moving through the sea bears, within its body, the quiet record of creatures that once walked upon land. Every living form is both a present being and an inheritance: a momentary flowering of life’s unbroken continuity.

This is evolution: the ceaseless becoming of living things across generations.

Evolution is not a ladder rising toward a final creature. It is not a contest in which the strong are rewarded and the weak are discarded. It is not a story in which humanity stands apart from the world, having escaped the conditions that formed every other animal. Evolution is the branching, changing history by which life responds to circumstance, chance, constraint, cooperation, loss, danger, abundance, and time.

To understand evolution is to receive a great correction to pride and a great invitation to kinship.

We are not strangers in the living world. We are relatives.

propositions.title: The First Continuity
propositions.text:
Life began long before memory, language, writing, or ceremony. The precise path is still being studied, and humility is proper before what remains unknown. Yet the evidence is clear that life has existed on Earth for billions of years, changing the planet even as the planet changed life.

The earliest organisms were small, simple in structure, and immense in consequence. They drew energy from chemical gradients, sunlight, and the materials of sea and stone. Some ancient microbes released oxygen as a by-product of their living. Over vast spans of time, that oxygen transformed oceans, rocks, and air. It made possible forms of life that could use oxygen to release energy more powerfully. The atmosphere beneath which animals breathe is, in part, the work of innumerable beings too small to see.

No creature creates itself. Every creature enters conditions prepared by others.

The soil is made by weather, fungi, roots, insects, bacteria, and the remains of former lives. The air is shaped by forests, oceans, algae, and cycles older than nations. The body is assembled from elements forged in stars and circulated through water, food, breath, and decay. Life receives life.

This is not a cause for despair at our dependence. It is a cause for gratitude. Dependence is not failure. It is the ordinary condition of being alive.

propositions.title: Descent With Change
propositions.text:
Evolution occurs because organisms reproduce, because offspring resemble their parents without being exact copies, and because some inherited differences become more common over generations.

In every generation, variations arise. DNA is copied with extraordinary fidelity, but not perfect fidelity. Mutations occur. Genes are rearranged. In organisms that reproduce sexually, genetic material is combined in new patterns. In microbes, genes may sometimes pass between unrelated lineages. Development and environment also affect how inherited capacities are expressed.

Most variation is neither a miracle nor a mistake. It is simply difference.

Some differences have little effect. Some are harmful in a particular environment. Some become useful when conditions change. A trait that aids survival in drought may offer no advantage in flood. A color that conceals an animal from one predator may expose it to another. A bacterium able to endure an antibiotic may prosper where other bacteria perish, though that same adaptation may carry a cost when the drug is absent.

Natural selection is the name given to this unequal continuation. If inherited traits affect the likelihood of leaving descendants, then, over many generations, those traits may become more common. Selection does not plan. It does not foresee. It does not care. It is not a judge of virtue.

Nature does not select the morally worthy.

A parasite may be exquisitely adapted. A generous act may carry no genetic advantage. A cruel person may have children; a compassionate person may have none. The language of evolutionary biology must not be misused as the language of ethics. What persists in nature is not therefore what ought to govern human conduct.

The fact that a thing is natural does not make it right.

propositions.title: More Than Competition
propositions.text:
The phrase “survival of the fittest” has often been used carelessly, as though life were governed only by violence and selfishness. In science, fitness means reproductive success in a particular environment. It does not mean strength, superiority, wealth, beauty, or moral value. A small plant producing viable seeds may be more biologically fit than a powerful animal unable to reproduce.

More importantly, competition is only one part of life’s history.

Living beings cooperate at every scale. Cells within a body coordinate their work. The cells of plants and animals contain mitochondria, descendants of ancient bacteria that entered into a lasting partnership with other cells. Plants depend upon fungi at their roots; fungi depend upon plants for sugars. Flowers and pollinators shape one another’s futures. Coral reefs are built through relationships among animals, algae, microbes, currents, and minerals. Human infants survive through care that extends far beyond a single parent.

Even conflict often occurs within networks of dependence.

The wolf depends on the deer; the deer depends on the grass; the grass depends on soil organisms and rain; each death becomes food for others. This does not make suffering trivial. The terror of the hunted is real. The hunger of the hunter is real. Yet the living world cannot be understood through sentiment alone, nor through brutality alone. It is woven of nourishment and danger, shelter and exposure, birth and decay.

Those who learn only competition from evolution have learned too little. Those who imagine only harmony have also learned too little.

Wisdom begins by seeing clearly.

propositions.title: The Branching Tree
propositions.text:
All life on Earth shares deep common ancestry. This is not merely a beautiful thought; it is supported by converging evidence from anatomy, fossils, embryology, biogeography, and genetics.

The bones inside a human hand, a bat’s wing, a whale’s flipper, and a cat’s foreleg follow the same ancient pattern: one upper limb bone, two forearm bones, wrist bones, and digits. They serve different purposes, yet reveal a shared inheritance. The similarity is not imposed by appearance alone. It is written in development and in genes.

The fossil record likewise preserves a long sequence of change. It does not record every organism that ever lived; fossilization is rare, and many rocks have been altered or lost. Yet what survives is enough to show broad patterns: fish before amphibians, terrestrial vertebrates before birds, early hominins before modern humans, and many intermediate forms linking major groups.

Whales offer a clear example. Their ancestors were land-dwelling mammals. Fossils document forms with legs adapted for walking and swimming, followed by increasingly aquatic bodies. Modern whales retain vestigial pelvic bones, and their embryos briefly develop structures related to hind limbs. Their closest living relatives are hippopotamuses. The sea-going giant and the river-dwelling hoofed animal are distant cousins.

Humans too belong within this tree. We are primates, mammals, vertebrates, animals, and living beings of Earth. We share ancestry with chimpanzees and bonobos, though neither is our ancestor; rather, we share with them earlier populations from which separate lineages emerged. Our bodies carry the signs of this history: grasping hands, forward-facing eyes, social intelligence, a flexible shoulder, and genomes bearing traces of ancient kinship.

This knowledge need not diminish human dignity. Dignity does not depend on being biologically isolated. A person’s worth is not threatened by having relatives among the animals. On the contrary, kinship enlarges responsibility.

propositions.title: Chance, Law, and Freedom
propositions.text:
Evolution joins necessity and contingency.

The laws of chemistry and physics constrain what bodies can be. Water has properties. Carbon forms particular bonds. Gravity limits flight. Light carries energy. Bodies must obtain food, resist damage, reproduce, and die. These conditions shape the possibilities of life.

Yet history also matters. A meteor strikes. A continent divides. A climate cools. A virus enters a population. A small group becomes isolated on an island. A lineage survives a catastrophe by chance while another, no less remarkable, disappears. What comes after is altered.

The extinction of the non-avian dinosaurs about sixty-six million years ago did not make mammals inevitable in every imaginable world. But in this world, their disappearance opened ecological spaces in which mammals diversified. Much later, among the branching experiments of ape-like creatures, one lineage developed language-rich cultures, cumulative technologies, and institutions able to transform whole landscapes.

We are not the predetermined goal of evolution. We are one outcome of a vast and contingent history.

This should teach modesty. If the past had been otherwise in countless small ways, we might never have existed. We are not owed existence. We have received it.

Yet contingency does not mean meaninglessness. Meaning is not a prize bestowed only upon what was planned in advance. A song improvised in the moment may be meaningful. A friendship formed unexpectedly may be profound. A life need not have been inevitable to be precious.

propositions.title: Evolution Is Not Progress
propositions.text:
Evolution does not move universally from lesser to greater. It produces adaptation, not perfection.

A parasite may lose structures its ancestors possessed because it no longer needs them. Cave-dwelling animals may lose functional eyes. Bacteria can evolve rapidly because of their short generations. Sharks have remained recognizably shark-like for vast periods because their form has continued to work well in many conditions. Simplicity is not inferiority. Complexity is not holiness.

Nor does evolution produce flawless designs. Bodies are historical compromises. The human spine, inherited from four-limbed ancestors and modified for upright walking, is vulnerable to injury. The path of the recurrent laryngeal nerve in mammals is longer than an engineer would choose, looping down into the chest before rising to the throat because it follows an ancestral arrangement. The human eye has a blind spot where the optic nerve passes through the retina.

These are not signs that life is worthless. They are reminders that life is fashioned through modification of what came before. Evolution works with inheritance. It remodels; it does not begin each creature from nothing.

Therefore, let no person use the language of evolution to rank peoples, sexes, cultures, disabilities, or species as though some were closer to a supposed summit of life. Such claims confuse scientific description with prejudice. They have served eugenics, racism, conquest, and cruelty. They are false in fact and corrupt in purpose.

No lineage is “more evolved” in the sense of having advanced beyond all others. Every living species has been evolving for the same length of time.

propositions.title: The Human Animal
propositions.text:
Humanity possesses unusual powers: symbolic language, moral reflection, long-term cooperation among strangers, art, mathematics, ritual, agriculture, law, science, and the ability to alter environments at planetary scale. These powers are real. They are also dangerous.

An animal that can imagine the future can protect it or destroy it. An animal that can classify living things can learn reverence or invent hierarchies of domination. An animal that can reshape rivers, forests, genes, and climates must decide whether power will be joined to wisdom.

Our evolutionary inheritance includes capacities for fear, aggression, loyalty, care, play, attachment, imitation, and reciprocity. None of these capacities alone determines our fate. Biology influences; it does not excuse.

To say that violence has evolutionary roots is not to pardon violence. To say that humans are capable of self-interest is not to deny generosity. To say that groups may form boundaries is not to bless hatred. We are shaped by inherited dispositions, but we are also shaped by teaching, institutions, habits, stories, and chosen commitments.

The task of moral life is not to deny our animal nature. It is to educate it.

Let courage guide fear. Let justice restrain dominance. Let compassion widen loyalty. Let truth correct fantasy. Let communities reward care rather than exploitation. Let no one claim that cruelty is unavoidable simply because it has appeared before.

The past explains much. It commands nothing.

propositions.title: The Present Trial of Life
propositions.text:
Evolution continues. It has not ended because humans have arrived.

Viruses evolve. Crops evolve. Forests respond to changing climates. Populations move, adapt, decline, and diverge. The future contains forms of life no living person will see. But human activity now changes the conditions of evolution with exceptional speed: through habitat destruction, pollution, overharvesting, invasive species, industrial agriculture, and the heating of the climate.

Species are disappearing at rates far above ordinary background levels. Entire ecological communities are being fragmented before their relationships are fully known. When a species vanishes, a unique lineage ends: a way of sensing, feeding, breeding, communicating, and inhabiting Earth that will not return.

Extinction has always occurred. That is not a reason to hasten it.

The knowledge that change is natural must never become an excuse for preventable ruin. Fire is natural; arson is still wrong. Death is natural; murder is still wrong. Extinction is natural; heedless devastation is still wrong.

To protect the living world is not to freeze it in an imaginary past. It is to preserve the conditions under which living systems may continue their own unfolding: connected habitats, clean water, breathable air, fertile soil, climatic stability, and enough room for more than one species to thrive.

Conservation is not sentimentality. It is fidelity to reality.

propositions.title: A Kinship Without End
propositions.text:
The great lesson of evolution is neither that life is accidental nor that life is ordained to flatter us. Its lesson is deeper: life is continuous, inventive, vulnerable, and bound together.

The oak and the fungus, the hawk and the mouse, the whale and the hippopotamus, the human hand and the bat’s wing, the child and the ancient cell—all belong to one immeasurable history of transformation.

We inherit a world we did not make. We carry bodies we did not design. We breathe air prepared by beings without names. We stand within a family so ancient that its first members are beyond imagination, yet so immediate that it includes the insect at the window, the moss on stone, the dog beside the road, and the stranger whose face resembles our own.

Let this knowledge soften arrogance.

Let it strengthen care.

Let every person remember: we are not above the living world as owners over property. We are within it as participants in a shared and unfinished becoming.

And let our power become worthy of our kinship.

propositions.title: The Silence After a Name
propositions.text:
There are kinds of absence that the heart can bear: the absence of winter flowers beneath snow, the absence of birds at noon when they shelter from heat, the absence of a friend who has gone far and may yet return.

Extinction is not such an absence.

Extinction is the silence after a name has been spoken for the last time by the living world. It is the closing of a lineage: no more eggs of that kind, no more seeds, no more calls across a valley, no more particular eyes opening beneath leaf, wave, stone, or sky. What has ended cannot be restored merely by regret. The world may continue, as a river continues around a fallen tree, but something has been removed from its current.

Therefore do not speak lightly of what is lost.

A creature is not only a specimen, nor merely a page in a catalogue, nor only a store of useful properties waiting for human discovery. Each living kind is a manner in which life has learned to meet the earth. The orchid receives rain in its own way. The whale carries sound through darkness in its own way. The wolf reads the snow, the fungus enters the root, the vulture cleans what death has left, and the small insect turns a flower toward fruit.

Each has a place in the great conversation of matter, breath, hunger, season, death, and renewal.

When one voice falls silent, the conversation is changed.

propositions.title: The Long History of Ending
propositions.text:
Extinction did not begin with humankind. Long before cities, fields, engines, or written memory, species arose and disappeared. The rocks preserve signs of immense former worlds: shells in mountains, forests pressed into coal, creatures of strange form whose bones lie buried beneath seas that no longer exist.

The earth has known great dying.

There were times when fire from the deep, changes in air and ocean, darkness from impact, or the slow rearrangement of continents remade the conditions of life. Many kinds vanished. Other kinds endured, altered, and spread into the spaces left behind. The living world is ancient not because it has remained unchanged, but because it has persisted through change beyond ordinary imagining.

Let this teach humility.

No species, including our own, possesses a permanent guarantee written into the structure of nature. To be alive is to be vulnerable: to weather, disease, hunger, competition, accident, and the turning conditions of the world. Life is resilient, but resilience is not invincibility. A forest may return after fire, yet not as the same forest. A sea may refill after poison, yet not with the same abundance. Recovery is real, but it is neither immediate nor complete.

It is a mistake to say, “Extinction is natural; therefore it does not matter.”

Storms are natural, but the drowning of a village matters. Death is natural, but murder is not excused by this fact. The existence of ancient extinctions does not absolve those who cause needless loss now. The moral question is not whether death occurs in nature. The question is what power we possess, what harm we foresee, and what care we choose.

propositions.title: The New Weight of Human Hands
propositions.claim: The New Weight of Human Hands
propositions.text:
In this age, human beings have become a force of unusual reach. Our roads divide migration routes. Our ships carry organisms across oceans. Our mines remove mountains. Our nets gather life from the sea at scales no predator could attain. Our smoke and gases alter the climate of the whole planet. Our appetites for timber, meat, minerals, land, and luxury extend into forests, rivers, grasslands, reefs, and ice.

This power is not evil merely because it is power. Fire warms, cooks, and destroys. Knowledge heals and deceives. Tools build homes and break bodies. But power without reverence becomes careless, and carelessness multiplied by millions becomes devastation.

A person may never see the animal displaced by a field cleared for distant feed. A shopper may never see the river clouded by waste from a factory. A household may never meet the pollinator weakened by chemicals or the fish entangled in discarded plastic. Yet distance does not dissolve connection. The hiddenness of a consequence is not the same as its absence.

The world is joined by innumerable threads.

A wetland filters water for creatures downstream. A mangrove forest shelters young fish and weakens storm waves. A predator limits the overgrowth of herbivores. A seed-bearing bird carries a future forest beyond the reach of the parent tree. A beetle under bark, a worm in soil, a microbe in the root zone—these may be small to the eye, but their work sustains fields, forests, and food.

When such relationships are cut, the damage may remain invisible until it is widespread. This is why wisdom does not wait for perfect certainty before acting. When the bridge is already cracking, one does not demand proof that every stone will fall before reducing the load.

propositions.title: The Error of Measuring Worth by Use
propositions.claim: The Error of Measuring Worth by Use
propositions.text:
Some ask, “What is this creature for?” They mean: What profit does it bring? What medicine may it yield? What service does it provide? What use is it to us?

These questions may have practical value, but they are too narrow to carry the full weight of judgment.

A being need not serve human convenience in order to deserve consideration. The old tree in an inaccessible ravine is not worthless because it shades no road. The rare moth is not meaningless because no market trades in it. The deep-sea creature, unknown to most and unseen by nearly all, does not become expendable because it has not yet been fitted into a human plan.

To measure all life by its usefulness to ourselves is to make ourselves the only real thing in creation.

This is a poverty of spirit.

Human beings are participants in the living world, not its sole audience. We are gifted with unusual powers of memory, imagination, speech, and deliberate action. These gifts should enlarge our responsibility, not enlarge our permission to take without limit.

The world is not a warehouse. It is a community of lives.

This does not mean that no creature may be eaten, no tree cut, no land cultivated, or no river redirected. Living requires taking life, using materials, changing places, and making choices among competing needs. Every animal eats. Every settlement occupies ground. Every harvest is an intervention.

The task is not to become absent from nature, for we cannot. The task is to become present within it with gratitude, restraint, skill, and justice.

propositions.title: Grief Is a Form of Attention
propositions.claim: Grief Is a Form of Attention
propositions.text:
There is a grief proper to extinction.

Let no one mock those who mourn a species they never touched. The grief may be genuine because the loss is real. A child who learns that a bird once filled the sky and is now gone has received a difficult inheritance. A fisher who finds an emptied sea, an elder who remembers spring sounds no longer heard, a community whose river no longer carries its customary life—these know that environmental loss is not abstract.

It enters memory. It enters language. It enters the imagination of what a place can be.

Grief, however, must not become a theatre in which sorrow is displayed and duty forgotten. Nor should it become despair, which is grief that has decided it need not act. The dead deserve mourning. The living require protection.

Mourn what is gone. Learn its name. Tell the truth of how it lived and how it was lost. Preserve its stories, images, songs, and the knowledge of those who lived near it. But then turn toward the species still endangered, the habitat still standing, the river still capable of healing.

The proper companion of grief is fidelity.

propositions.title: The Nearness of Prevention
propositions.text:
Many extinctions are not inevitable. Their causes are often plain: habitat destroyed or divided; animals hunted beyond recovery; invasive species introduced where they have no natural limits; waters polluted; climates altered too quickly for adaptation; populations reduced until chance itself becomes fatal.

To prevent loss, the world does not always require a miracle. Often it requires the ordinary disciplines that people postpone because they seem inconvenient.

Protect the places where life reproduces and feeds: nesting shores, old forests, spawning rivers, grasslands, peatlands, reefs, and wetlands. Keep wild places connected, so that populations may move, mingle, and endure. Govern hunting and fishing according to the limits of renewal rather than the appetite for immediate gain.
