Prevent the trade in living beings that treats rarity as a luxury. Reduce poisons that travel through soil, water, and food chains. Restore damaged land with native life, patience, and long care.

Where climate is changing, reduce the forces that intensify that change. This is not only a question of weather; it is a question of homes. Coral, alpine meadow, polar ice edge, dry forest, estuary, and migratory route are all homes shaped by patterns of temperature, water, and season. To destabilize these patterns is to unsettle multitudes.

Let policy be guided by the long view. A decision that enriches one quarter and ruins a watershed for generations is not wise. An enterprise that counts its profit but not its waste has kept false accounts. A nation that protects only what can be immediately sold has mistaken price for value.

Good stewardship requires laws, institutions, science, local knowledge, public courage, and the willingness to limit oneself. Private tenderness is beautiful, but tenderness alone cannot regulate a trawler, protect a forest corridor, or keep poison from a river. Love must sometimes take the form of rules.

propositions.title: Knowledge Joined to Humility
propositions.text:
Listen to those who study the living world: field workers who count nests before dawn, taxonomists who distinguish lives that appear identical to hurried eyes, fishers who know the changing currents, Indigenous custodians whose practices have been refined through long relationship with place, farmers who observe soil and season, veterinarians who recognize disease at the boundary between wild and domestic life.

No one way of knowing is sufficient by itself.

Science offers methods for tracing populations, measuring change, testing causes, and revealing connections beyond common sight. It should be honored for this work. Yet science does not remove the need for wisdom. It can tell us that a population is declining; it cannot alone decide what sacrifice justice requires. It can estimate risk; it cannot make us value what is at risk.

For that, character is needed.

Beware also the pride that says, “We can replace what we destroy.” A laboratory may preserve cells. A seed bank may protect genetic material. Careful breeding may return some species from the edge. These are worthy works, and they should be supported. But an animal is more than its stored code, and a forest is more than a list of species. The relations among creatures, places, weather, microbes, memory, and time cannot be fully rebuilt at will.

Restoration is a duty. It is not a license to destroy.

propositions.title: Justice for the Living and the Human
propositions.claim: Justice for the Living and the Human
propositions.text:
The burdens of extinction do not fall evenly.

Those who live nearest forests, coasts, deserts, and rivers often bear the first cost of ecological damage, though they may have contributed least to its causes. A community can lose food, water, safety, livelihood, and cultural continuity when a landscape is depleted. Conservation that ignores people, expels them unjustly, or treats local communities as enemies may repeat the very domination it claims to oppose.

Therefore protect both human dignity and the wider community of life.

Do not force the poor to carry alone the cost of restraint while the wealthy consume without measure. Do not call a people guardians of nature and then deny them the means to live securely. Do not protect animals by abandoning human beings, nor defend human flourishing by declaring every wild thing disposable.

The false choice between people and nature has wounded both.

Healthy lands sustain human communities. Secure and respected communities are better able to sustain healthy lands. Justice must be woven through conservation, as roots are woven through soil.

propositions.title: A Covenant With What Remains
propositions.text:
The future is not secured by optimism alone. It is secured by agreements kept: between generations, between communities, between governments and the places entrusted to them, between appetite and limit.

Make such an agreement in your own life.

Know the place where you live. Learn the names of some beings who share it: the tree at the corner, the bird on the wire, the moss in the shaded wall, the insects at the porch light, the fish or frogs or grasses of nearby water and field. Attention is the beginning of loyalty. What is unnamed is easily ignored; what is known becomes harder to abandon.

Use less where less is enough. Repair what can be repaired. Refuse luxuries made from threatened life. Support those who defend land and water. Ask where food, wood, minerals, and goods come from, and where their wastes go. Teach children not only to admire wild creatures in images, but to understand the conditions by which creatures remain alive.

Let wonder become discipline.

There will still be loss. No care can prevent every death, and no generation can fully undo the harms it inherits. But resignation is not wisdom. The presence of limits does not release us from responsibility; it gives responsibility its shape.

The living world has endured much. It still offers seed after winter, birdsong after storm, green through broken pavement, and the unexpected return of life to places thought barren. Receive these not as assurances that nothing can be ruined, but as invitations to become worthy of renewal.

Let no species vanish because we could not be troubled to notice.

Let no river die because we counted wealth without counting water.

Let no child inherit a world emptied by our impatience and be told that this was the price of progress.

Progress worthy of the name leaves room for others to live.

propositions.title: The First Covenant of the Field
propositions.claim: The First Covenant of the Field
propositions.text:
Before there were cities, there were seeds held in careful hands. Before there were markets, measures, storehouses, and laws, there was the human being watching the ground: learning when rain would come, learning which grain endured, learning that life might be tended without being possessed.

Agriculture is not merely the production of food. It is the long conversation between soil, water, light, creature, and human attention. It is a covenant renewed each season. The field gives no harvest by command alone. It answers work, but it also answers weather, time, hidden life, and the patience of those who understand that not every power can be hurried.

Therefore let no one call the farmer insignificant, nor the gardener unlearned because their knowledge is carried in the hands. To know the smell of rain on dry ground, the color of a healthy leaf, the sound of a full seed head, the behavior of bees at dawn, and the condition of soil beneath the plow is to possess a form of wisdom upon which all tables depend.

Every loaf is a history. Every bowl of fruit contains weather, labor, ancestry, and earth. Every seed bears the memory of former seasons and the possibility of seasons yet to come.

Eat, then, with gratitude. But gratitude that does not change conduct is only decoration. Let gratitude become protection: of the land that feeds, of the workers who cultivate it, of the waters that sustain it, and of the generations who will inherit what is done today.

propositions.title: Soil Is a Living Commonwealth
propositions.text:
The ground beneath the crop is not inert matter. It is a living commonwealth: mineral and root, fungus and worm, bacterium and beetle, moisture and air. In a handful of healthy soil dwell multitudes beyond ordinary counting, each participating in transformations by which death becomes fertility and fertility becomes food.

The fallen leaf becomes humus. The root releases sugars to feed the unseen. The fungus reaches where the root cannot reach. The worm opens passages for water and breath. The insect breaks down what has fallen. The microbe releases what has been bound. Thus the soil is not a warehouse from which nutrients may be endlessly extracted; it is a community whose health determines the health of field, animal, and person.

Whoever destroys soil for a brief increase in yield commits theft against the future. The loss may not be visible in the first season, for land can appear generous even while its deeper strength is being depleted. But eroded soil carries away the labor of centuries. A field stripped of organic matter loses its resilience. Water no longer enters it freely; roots cannot travel deeply; drought becomes harsher and flood more destructive.

Let the soil be covered when it is not bearing a principal crop. Let living roots remain in it as often as the climate permits. Let rotations interrupt the cycles of pest and disease. Let compost, crop residues, manures properly managed, and other organic materials return carbon and nutrients to the land. Let tillage be used with restraint, for disturbance has its cost. Let grazing, where wisely governed, serve the renewal of grassland rather than its exhaustion.

There is no single practice fitted to every place. A method that restores one landscape may injure another. The dry plain, the wet valley, the mountain terrace, the tropical garden, and the northern pasture each require humility before their own conditions. Wisdom does not consist in copying a technique without understanding. Wisdom asks: What does this land require? What does it already know? What will remain after we are gone?

### The Measure of Fertility

Do not measure fertility by harvest alone.

A field may yield abundantly while its rivers carry sediment, while its workers are harmed, while its pollinators disappear, while its groundwater is poisoned, while its owners are burdened by debt, while its neighboring communities lose access to land. Such abundance is incomplete. It is a harvest counted without the costs of its making.

True fertility includes the strength of the soil, the cleanliness of water, the diversity of life, the dignity of labor, the nourishment of the food, and the endurance of the farm across generations.

A good harvest feeds the present without starving the future.

propositions.title: Seeds and the Gift of Continuance
propositions.claim: Seeds and the Gift of Continuance
propositions.text:
The seed is small, but it contains an instruction older than any human institution: become more than yourself. In its hard coat rests a future root, a future stem, a future flower, and, in time, a multitude of seeds beyond the one that was planted.

For this reason, seed is not merely merchandise. It is inheritance. It has been carried through droughts, migrations, wars, and changes of climate by people who selected, saved, exchanged, and cared for what would feed their children. The diversity of seeds is a treasury of adaptation. One variety withstands heat; another endures cold; another thrives in shallow soil; another resists a disease not yet known elsewhere.

Guard this diversity.

Let seed banks preserve varieties against catastrophe, but let seeds also remain alive in gardens and fields, where they continue to adapt in partnership with those who grow them. A seed locked away may survive; a seed planted, observed, and shared participates in culture and renewal.

No person should be compelled into hunger because the means of planting have been made inaccessible. No farmer should be forced to abandon local varieties solely because commerce prefers uniformity. Let research serve the public good. Let plant breeding be transparent. Let the benefits and risks of every new agricultural technology be examined honestly, neither worshiped as salvation nor condemned without understanding.

Knowledge is a gift when it enlarges the capacity of communities to feed themselves with dignity. It becomes a burden when it concentrates power over food in the hands of a few.

propositions.title: Water Has Its Own Claim
propositions.text:
Water is not the servant of the field alone. It belongs also to cloud and wetland, river and fish, forest and aquifer, village and city, body and unborn child. Whoever directs water toward crops must remember all those to whom water is also owed.

Irrigation can turn arid land fruitful, but careless irrigation can salt the soil, drain rivers, and empty ancient groundwater faster than it can be renewed. The water taken today may be the water unavailable tomorrow. Therefore measure what is withdrawn. Repair what leaks. Match the crop to the climate where possible. Gather rain. Protect watersheds. Restore wetlands and streamside vegetation. Use methods that bring water to roots with care, rather than losing it to evaporation or waste.

Where water is scarce, let the powerful not take first and leave the poor to thirst. Where a river crosses a boundary, let no nation treat upstream possession as an unlimited right. Water teaches interdependence: what is diverted in one place is absent in another.

The field should not send poison downstream. Fertilizers used beyond what plants can absorb, manure stored without care, pesticides applied without restraint, and bare soil exposed to storm all become burdens carried by water. The river remembers every field it passes.

propositions.title: Creatures of the Farm and Creatures Beyond It
propositions.claim: Creatures of the Farm and Creatures Beyond It
propositions.text:
Agriculture necessarily shapes the lives of animals. Some are raised for food, fiber, work, or companionship. Others live beside the farm: birds in hedges, insects among flowers, predators in forests, amphibians in ditches, and countless small beings whose roles may be unnoticed until they vanish.

Let animals under human care be treated as living creatures, not as units without feeling. Give them sufficient space, clean water, appropriate food, shelter from extremes, and conditions in which they can express essential behaviors. Prevent suffering where it can be prevented. Use medicine responsibly, not as a substitute for humane conditions. When animals are killed for food, let it be done with competence, necessity, and the least suffering possible.

Cruelty is not made righteous by familiarity, nor made invisible by distance from the table.

Likewise, do not regard every wild creature as an enemy of production. Predators may regulate populations. Pollinators enable fruitfulness. Birds consume pests. Native plants shelter beneficial insects. A farm bordered by hedges, flowering strips, trees, ponds, and uncultivated margins may support life that strengthens the whole landscape.

Yet balance requires judgment. Farmers must protect crops and livestock; communities must prevent disease and invasive harm. The instruction is not to abandon stewardship, but to refuse the easy belief that extermination is the first sign of intelligence.

### The Bees’ Teaching

The bee gathers without owning the flower. It receives nectar and carries pollen. Its labor nourishes both hive and field. In this, the bee reveals a law of mutual benefit.

Let agriculture imitate this law where it can. Let the farm not be a place where one life flourishes only by silencing all others. Let its productivity arise increasingly from relationships that strengthen the whole: legumes feeding soil, trees shading animals, crops sheltering one another, grazing renewing grass, compost returning nourishment, and people sharing knowledge rather than hoarding it.

propositions.title: The Dignity of Those Who Feed the World
propositions.claim: The Dignity of Those Who Feed the World
propositions.text:
No food is cheap when another person bears the hidden cost.

The person who plants, weeds, harvests, sorts, carries, cooks, and serves food is entitled to safety, fair compensation, rest, representation, and respect. This includes migrant workers, seasonal laborers, tenant farmers, sharecroppers, processors, drivers, market sellers, and all whose work is often concealed behind a price label.

Do not praise the abundance of a nation while those who gather its food cannot afford adequate meals. Do not celebrate efficiency while workers labor in dangerous heat, breathe harmful dust, endure exposure to chemicals, or live under the threat of dismissal for speaking truth. A system that feeds many by degrading those nearest the food is disordered at its root.

Let landholders remember that ownership is never absolute. Land may be held by deed, but it remains held also by rain, watershed, history, community, and future generations. Those who control large areas bear larger obligations. Let them protect soil, honor contracts, pay fairly, and make room for the livelihoods of others.

Let governments secure the rights of agricultural workers, support small and medium-sized producers, restrain monopolies, invest in public research, and protect communities from hunger. Let markets reward long-term care rather than merely short-term extraction. Let consumers, insofar as they are able, ask who grew their food and under what conditions.

The table joins all people. Therefore the table must not conceal injustice.

propositions.title: Plenty, Hunger, and Right Distribution
propositions.text:
The earth produces enough in many places, yet hunger persists. This is not only a failure of rain or soil. It is often a failure of distribution, peace, access, and care.

Food may exist while people cannot afford it. Grain may be stored while conflict blocks the road. Crops may be grown for profit while neighboring children lack nourishment. Food may spoil for want of refrigeration, transport, storage, or public provision. Land may yield exports while local communities are displaced from the ground that once fed them.

Therefore hunger must never be explained as though it were always inevitable. Drought is real. Flood is real. Pest and disease are real. But greed is also real, as are neglect, waste, discrimination, and war.

Let communities build resilient local food systems: gardens, cooperatives, grain reserves, school meals, community kitchens, fair markets, and networks of mutual aid. Let cities remember their dependence on rural lands, and let rural regions receive more than praise in return. Roads, clinics, schools, storage, communication, credit, and just prices are also forms of agricultural care.

Waste is a moral failure when others lack food. Preserve what can be preserved. Share what can be shared. Plan with wisdom. But do not shame those who are poor for the failures of systems designed without them.

propositions.title: Farming in an Altered Climate
propositions.text:
The climate is changing, and the field is among the first places to reveal it. Seasons become uncertain. Heat arrives beyond familiar limits. Rains fail, then fall with violence. New pests travel into new regions. Coastal soils receive salt. Fires consume pasture and orchard. Farmers who have read the sky for generations find that the old signs no longer speak with the same reliability.

Meet this reality with truthfulness.

Do not ask farmers alone to carry the burden of a warming world while others continue to profit from destruction. The protection of agriculture requires the protection of climate, forests, oceans, and water. It requires the rapid reduction of pollution that heats the atmosphere. It requires support for adaptation: drought-tolerant crops, diversified farms, improved forecasts, water conservation, crop insurance designed for equity, and public assistance after disaster.

Diversity is resilience. A farm dependent on one crop, one buyer, one fertilizer source, or one season of favorable weather is vulnerable. A landscape with many crops, healthy soils, protected water, seed diversity, and strong community ties is better able to endure shock.

Hope is not the denial of danger. Hope is the decision to cultivate life even when the season is difficult.

propositions.title: The Daily Blessing
propositions.text:
When you eat, remember the field.

Remember the soil that held the root. Remember the rain that entered the ground. Remember the sun that became sugar in the leaf. Remember the insects, birds, microbes, and laboring hands. Remember those whose names you do not know and whose work reached you through roads, vessels, mills, kitchens, and markets.

Then let remembrance guide action.

Plant something, if you are able. Protect a patch of living ground. Waste less. Learn the seasons of your place. Support those who grow food with care. Defend the rights of workers. Ask whether your abundance is purchased at another’s loss. Teach children that a tomato is not made in a shop, that bread begins in a field, and that the earth is not an inexhaustible machine.

The work of agriculture is humble because it must be repeated. Each year the ground is prepared again. Each seed is placed again. Each harvest is gathered again. Yet in this repetition lies a profound teaching: life is sustained not chiefly by grand declarations, but by faithful acts renewed in their proper time.

Blessed is the hand that plants without arrogance.  
Blessed is the field restored after misuse.  
Blessed is the worker paid justly for necessary labor.  
Blessed is the seed kept for those yet to come.  
Blessed is the meal shared where no one is excluded.

For the earth does not ask humanity to dominate it into silence. It asks to be known, tended, and received with reverence.

propositions.title: The Earth Is Not Possession
propositions.text:
The Earth was not given to humanity as a prize for conquest, nor placed beneath our feet as a thing without voice. Soil, river, wind, forest, creature, and sea do not exist merely to satisfy appetite or enlarge wealth. They are the conditions of life itself: ancient gifts, living systems, and the shared inheritance of those who have lived, those now living, and those yet to be born.

No person made the rain. No nation fashioned the seasons. No generation assembled the deep soils, the migration routes, the coral reefs, the seed-bearing grasses, or the hidden worlds beneath the roots of trees. What humanity receives from the Earth is received after a long preparation not of our own making.

Therefore let no one say, “Because I can take it, it is mine.”

Power is not ownership. Access is not permission. Profit is not proof of righteousness.

The land may be held in law, but it cannot rightly be held in contempt. Waters may be assigned a boundary, but their currents do not obey the pride of maps. Air may pass through factories, homes, fields, and cities, yet it remains one breath, entering the lungs of the wealthy and the poor alike.

To live well upon the Earth is to understand this: we are not separate from the world we alter. What is poisoned in the river returns in the body. What is stripped from the forest returns in the weather. What is driven from the sea returns as hunger. What is neglected in the soil returns as fragility in every harvest.

The Earth is not an object outside humanity. It is the larger body within which humanity lives.

propositions.title: The Covenant of Care
propositions.text:
Stewardship is not softness, nor is it a decorative concern reserved for times of comfort. It is a binding duty. It asks every household, community, institution, and nation to consider whether its ways of living preserve the conditions by which life may continue.

The covenant of care has three obligations:

1. **Take only with restraint.**
2. **Repair what has been damaged.**
3. **Leave the world more habitable for those who follow.**

These obligations apply wherever human power reaches: in the field and the market, in the workshop and the laboratory, in the council chamber and the home. They apply to the use of water, energy, land, minerals, forests, animals, and knowledge. They apply to the technologies by which people extend their reach across the Earth.

A people that consumes its seed grain may call itself prosperous for one season. A people that exhausts its groundwater, erodes its soil, empties its fisheries, and fouls its air may boast of abundance while preparing scarcity. Such prosperity is not prosperity. It is a debt concealed by delay.

Let each generation therefore measure its success not only by what it has built, extracted, purchased, or accumulated, but by what remains alive and capable after its passing.

Ask of every undertaking:

- Does this restore or diminish the living world?
- Does it burden those who have little power to refuse?
- Does it preserve options for the future, or close them?
- Does it honor the limits upon which all freedom depends?
- If all people acted in this way, could the Earth endure it?

Where the answer is no, wisdom requires a change of course.

propositions.title: The Limits That Teach Wisdom
propositions.text:
Limits are not enemies of human flourishing. They are the shape of reality, and reality is a patient teacher.

A field cannot yield without rest. A forest cannot be cut without consequence. A river cannot receive waste without becoming ill. The atmosphere cannot endlessly absorb the gases of fire without changing the climate by which farms, coasts, and cities endure. The sea cannot give without replenishment. The body cannot flourish without clean air, sound water, nourishing food, and a stable home.

Those who deny limits do not become free from them. They merely force others, often the vulnerable and unborn, to bear the cost.

The wise person does not praise waste as generosity. The wise community does not confuse excess with blessing. It learns sufficiency: enough food without ruin, enough shelter without needless harm, enough comfort without the worship of consumption.

Sufficiency is not deprivation. It is freedom from the restless belief that more is always better, larger is always stronger, and newer is always wiser. It is the ability to enjoy what is useful, beautiful, and durable without making desire the ruler of life.

Let goods be made to last. Let they be repaired where possible, shared where fitting, and returned to use rather than discarded. Let designs consider the whole journey of a thing: the mine from which its materials are drawn, the hands that make it, the energy that carries it, the place where it will finally rest.

Nothing is truly “away.” What is thrown away enters another place, another body, another future.

propositions.title: The Climate of Responsibility
propositions.text:
The warming of the world is a moral matter because its harms are not distributed according to merit. Those who contribute least to disruption often face its harshest effects: failed crops, intensified storms, rising seas, spreading disease, heat that overwhelms the old and the young, and conflict sharpened by drought and displacement.

It is unjust to enjoy the benefits of pollution while assigning its dangers to others.

Therefore those with greater wealth, greater technical ability, and greater historical use of the atmosphere bear greater responsibility for repair. This is not punishment; it is the ordinary meaning of responsibility. Where capacity is greatest, obligation is greatest.

Let nations act with urgency and fairness to reduce the release of heat-trapping gases. Let energy be gathered increasingly from sources that do not consume the future: sun, wind, water, earth, and such other means as may be developed without transferring hidden harms to vulnerable people or ecosystems.

Let buildings waste less heat. Let cities offer clean transit, walkable streets, shade, and shelter. Let food systems reduce needless loss, protect soil, and favor methods that renew rather than exhaust. Let industry account honestly for its emissions, its waste, and the full consequences of its supply chains.

No community should be asked to choose between clean air and a livelihood. The transition from harmful systems must be just. Workers whose labor has sustained society must not be discarded when society changes. Their skill, dignity, income, and participation must be protected. A just transition creates meaningful work in restoration, clean energy, efficient housing, public transport, ecological agriculture, and the care of shared places.

The task is not merely to replace one fuel with another. It is to build economies that serve life.

propositions.title: Water, Soil, and Seed
propositions.text:
Water is not merchandise before it is life. It is the first common good of every community. When water is hoarded, polluted, or priced beyond the reach of the poor, a fundamental trust is violated.

Protect springs, wetlands, watersheds, aquifers, rivers, and coastlines. Keep contaminants from entering them. Use water carefully in homes, farms, and industry. Restore floodplains and wetlands, for they hold water in dry times and soften the force of storms. Recognize that healthy rivers require not only clean water but sufficient water to flow.

Soil is a living community. Within a handful of healthy earth are organisms that recycle nutrients, store carbon, filter water, and sustain crops. To lose soil through erosion or contamination is to lose a treasure that may take centuries to form.

Let farming honor the land that feeds humanity. Reduce practices that strip soil bare, poison pollinators, or leave fields dependent upon ever greater chemical force. Encourage cover crops, crop diversity, compost, careful grazing, agroforestry, and methods suited to each place. Support farmers through the risks of transition, for no society can ask those who feed it to carry alone the burden of ecological renewal.

Seeds carry memory: of climates, tastes, resistances, and cultures. Guard their diversity. Do not allow the inheritance of agriculture to become so narrow that a single disease, drought, or market failure can place whole regions in peril. Let farmers, gardeners, researchers, and Indigenous custodians of land share in the protection of seed knowledge with consent, respect, and fair recognition.

propositions.title: The Kinship of Creatures
propositions.text:
Other creatures are not unfinished forms of humanity, nor are they mere scenery for human enjoyment. They have their own ways of being: the wolf’s dependence upon territory, the bee’s labor among flowers, the whale’s long song through dark water, the bird’s return across continents, the mycelium’s quiet joining beneath the forest floor.

Their value does not depend upon their usefulness to us.

Human beings may need to eat, build, cultivate, and protect themselves. Stewardship does not deny these needs. But necessity must never become an excuse for cruelty, waste, or indifference. When animals are raised for food, let suffering be reduced. When wild habitats are altered, let the alteration be restrained and justified. When a species is threatened, let its disappearance be regarded not as an inconvenience but as an impoverishment of the world.

Extinction is irreversible. A vanished species cannot be purchased back, engineered back in its fullness, or replaced by a record in a museum. Each loss narrows the living library of Earth.

Protect habitat before rescue becomes impossible. Join fragmented landscapes through wildlife corridors. Defend nesting grounds, breeding waters, old-growth forests, grasslands, reefs, and migratory routes. Resist the vanity that imagines every uncultivated place to be wasted space.

A place where no human hand has arranged every feature may still be profoundly ordered. Wildness is not disorder. It is life beyond complete human command.

propositions.title: Justice Among Peoples and Generations
propositions.text:
Environmental harm is rarely neutral. Waste facilities, polluted industries, dangerous extraction, and the loss of green space are often imposed upon communities already denied political influence, economic security, or social respect. This is not an accident to be regretted while continuing the same arrangements. It is injustice to be named and corrected.

No people should become a sacrifice zone for the comfort of another.

Listen especially to those who live nearest to damaged land and water: fisherfolk, farmers, forest communities, Indigenous peoples, workers, children, elders, and residents of neighborhoods burdened by pollution. Their knowledge is not secondary evidence. It is often the first knowledge available, earned through attention, memory, and daily consequence.

Consultation without the power to influence decisions is not partnership. Information withheld is not consent. Benefits promised without repair for harm are not justice.

The future, too, has a claim upon the present. Children and those not yet born cannot sit in today’s assemblies, sign today’s contracts, or vote against today’s short-sightedness. Yet they will inherit the atmosphere, the institutions, the depleted resources, and the altered landscapes created now.

Let every law and investment be tested by this question: **Would we defend this decision before those who must live with its consequences?**

If not, let it be changed.

propositions.title: The Work of Repair
propositions.text:
Many wounds have already been inflicted. Forests have been cleared, species diminished, waters contaminated, climates destabilized, and communities displaced. Despair may arise before such damage, but despair is not a form of responsibility. It can become an excuse for inaction.

Repair begins by telling the truth without shrinking from it. It continues by acting at the scale required.

Planting a tree is good when the tree is cared for, suited to its place, and part of a wider restoration. But a tree planted cannot excuse a forest destroyed. Recycling is good, but it cannot justify systems built upon endless disposable goods. Personal restraint matters, but it cannot replace the duty of governments and industries to change the structures that make destruction profitable.

Let action be both personal and collective.

Let households conserve, mend, share, eat with care, and teach children the names of nearby birds, trees, seasons, and waters. What is known can be loved; what is loved is more readily defended.

Let communities restore parks, streams, gardens, and common lands. Let schools unite scientific understanding with direct encounter: soil beneath the fingernails, weather on the face, seeds in the hand, stars above a darkened field.

Let institutions disclose their impacts, reduce their waste, purchase responsibly, and direct their resources away from enterprises that depend upon devastation.

Let governments establish laws equal to the scale of the danger: protections for ecosystems, enforceable pollution limits, transparent reporting, resilient infrastructure, restoration of degraded lands, and support for those affected by necessary change.

Let knowledge serve humility. Science offers essential tools for understanding complex systems, measuring harm, and testing remedies. It should be used honestly, free from deliberate distortion by those who profit from confusion. Yet knowledge must be joined to wisdom, for the ability to do a thing does not by itself make the thing good.

propositions.title: A Prayerful Practice of Attention
propositions.text:
Stewardship begins in attention.

Notice the water that comes from the tap and ask from what river, reservoir, or aquifer it was drawn. Notice the food upon the table and ask whose labor, soil, weather, and transport made it possible. Notice the air at dawn, the insects at a window, the tree lifting through pavement, the returning birds, the changing season.

Attention turns abstraction into relationship.

The person who sees the Earth only as resource will always find a reason to take more. The person who sees the Earth as a community of life will learn gratitude, restraint, and care.

Give thanks without pretending that gratitude alone is enough. Let gratitude become practice. Let reverence become policy. Let love become repair.

For the measure of humanity is not whether it can dominate the world, but whether, having gained great power within it, it chooses to protect the vulnerable, preserve the beautiful, and renew the foundations of life.

The Earth does not ask humanity to become less human. It asks humanity to become more fully human: wiser in power, gentler in use, fairer in distribution, and faithful in care.

Let this be the work of the present age:

To cool what has been overheated.  
To cleanse what has been poisoned.  
To restore what has been broken.  
To protect what remains.  
To share what is sufficient.  
To leave behind a living world.

propositions.title: The Question That Enlarges the Heart
propositions.claim: The Question That Enlarges the Heart
propositions.text:
Lift your eyes beyond the weather of this world. Beyond the flight of birds, beyond the turning Moon, beyond the lamps of cities and the smoke of war, the heavens continue without edge in the human imagination. Stars gather in numbers too great for the mind to hold. Around many of them, worlds may turn: worlds of stone, ocean, cloud, ice, fire, darkness, and unfamiliar light.

It is natural to ask whether life has awakened elsewhere.

This question is not a threat to reverence. It is reverence extended. The person who asks whether life exists beyond Earth does not diminish Earth; they begin to understand how precious Earth is. The possibility of other lives does not make our life insignificant. A single living cell is not made less wondrous because another cell may live in another sea. A forest is not emptied of holiness because another forest may grow under another sun.

Let no one use the vastness of the universe as an excuse for indifference. The wide sky does not absolve us of the ground beneath our feet. If there are countless inhabited worlds, then care is abundant in the universe. If Earth is the only living world, then care is all the more urgently entrusted to us. In either case, cruelty remains a failure of understanding.

The question of life beyond Earth should therefore make us gentler, not grander.

propositions.title: Earth Is One World Among Worlds
propositions.claim: Earth Is One World Among Worlds
propositions.text:
For much of human history, the Earth seemed to be the whole stage upon which existence was set. The sky was a ceiling, the stars were lights, and the heavens were thought to circle the human home. Yet careful observation taught otherwise. Earth is a planet among planets, moving around an ordinary star in one galaxy among vast numbers of galaxies.

This knowledge does not cast humanity down. It releases humanity from a false burden.

We are not required to be the centre of all things in order to matter. A child need not be the only child in a family to be loved. A river need not be the only river to nourish a land. Meaning does not arise from being alone. Meaning arises through relationship, attention, responsibility, and the capacity to receive and give care.

Earth remains our first and nearest moral home. It is the world from whose soil our bodies come, whose water sustains us, whose creatures have shaped our languages, fears, hopes, and stories. Every human being belongs to an ancient community of life: bacteria, fungi, grasses, insects, fish, birds, mammals, and all that has lived before us and made the present possible.

To honor this community is not to deny the possibility of others. It is to become worthy of meeting them.

propositions.title: What Life May Be
propositions.text:
Life on Earth is familiar to us because we are made of it. It uses water as a medium, carbon as a versatile framework, and energy from sunlight, chemical reactions, or the heat within the planet. It grows, changes, responds, reproduces, and participates in patterns larger than itself.

But familiarity must not become a prison for thought.

Life elsewhere may resemble life here. It may depend on liquid water and organic chemistry, for water carries materials and allows complex reactions; carbon forms diverse and stable structures. Many scientists therefore seek worlds where liquid water might persist and where useful chemical ingredients are present.

Yet no honest investigator should claim to know all forms that life can take. Life may flourish in oceans beneath ice, in clouds above scorching surfaces, in underground pores warmed by geology, or in conditions unlike any ecosystem now known. It may be slow beyond our sense of time, living through cycles of cold and thaw that span centuries. It may be minute and hidden. It may use senses we do not possess and forms of communication we cannot yet recognize.

There may be beings whose lives are simple in structure yet profound in endurance: microbial communities beneath an alien ocean, sustained by minerals and heat rising from the deep. There may be ecosystems without leaves, without birdsong, without blue skies. There may be minds—if minds have arisen elsewhere—whose histories are older than our species and whose wisdom, if wisdom they possess, has taken forms beyond our language.

Or there may be no life beyond Earth.

The faithful response to uncertainty is neither denial nor invention. It is humility. We may hope, search, imagine, and prepare. We must not pretend that desire is evidence, nor that fear is knowledge.

propositions.title: The Discipline of Wonder
propositions.text:
Wonder is not the same as credulity.

A strange light in the sky may have an ordinary cause. A signal may be noise, a machine, a natural phenomenon, or an error in measurement. A promising chemical trace in a distant atmosphere may have arisen through geology rather than biology. A pattern that appears meaningful may be produced by chance. Those who seek life beyond Earth must test their hopes carefully, because the greater the claim, the greater the care required in making it.

This discipline is not coldness. It is love for truth.

To observe patiently, to repeat a measurement, to invite others to examine the evidence, to correct one’s own mistake publicly—these are acts of intellectual integrity. They protect humanity from deception, including self-deception. They also make genuine discovery more trustworthy when it comes.

The search for life beyond Earth has already taught much, even without a confirmed discovery. It has shown that planets are common. It has revealed moons with hidden oceans, ancient riverbeds on neighboring worlds, complex molecules in space, and the extraordinary resilience of life on Earth. Microbes survive in deserts, deep rock, acidic pools, polar ice, and oceanic darkness. Such findings do not prove that life exists elsewhere. They do show that life, once present, may be more adaptable than earlier generations imagined.

Therefore, let the search continue with patience and openness. Let no one demand certainty before evidence exists. Let no one declare impossibility merely because a thing has not yet been seen.

propositions.title: The Near Neighbors
propositions.text:
Among the nearby worlds, some invite particular attention.

Mars bears the marks of ancient water: valleys, deltas, minerals formed in watery environments, and landscapes shaped by rivers long vanished. It may once have been more hospitable than it is now. Whether life ever began there remains unknown. The question is serious enough to guide careful exploration, especially beneath the surface, where conditions may have remained more sheltered from radiation and cold.

Europa, a moon of Jupiter, appears to hold a global ocean beneath a shell of ice. Tides raised by Jupiter’s gravity may provide energy and motion within that concealed sea. Enceladus, a moon of Saturn, releases plumes of water-rich material into space, offering evidence of a warm and chemically active interior. Titan has lakes and rain made not of water but hydrocarbons, and it possesses a rich atmosphere whose chemistry challenges the imagination.

These worlds are not empty screens for human ambition. They are ancient places with their own integrity. If humanity sends instruments, landers, or eventually people, it must do so without careless contamination. To carry terrestrial microbes into another environment and then mistake them for native life would be both a scientific failure and an ethical one. More deeply, to alter an alien ecology before understanding it would repeat an old human habit: entering a place without listening, taking possession before learning what is there.

Planetary protection is therefore not merely technical procedure. It is a form of respect.

propositions.title: If We Find the Smallest Life
propositions.claim: If We Find the Smallest Life
propositions.text:
Suppose one day we discover an organism beyond Earth: a cell in an ocean plume, a fossil structure in Martian stone, a metabolism active beneath distant ice. Such a discovery would be among the great turning points of human understanding.

It would tell us that life is not confined to one world. It would invite new questions. Did life arise independently more than once? Do all living things share deep chemical principles? Are there common pathways by which matter becomes organized, responsive, self-sustaining, and evolving? What duties do we owe to organisms that are not of our lineage but are nevertheless alive?

The answer begins with restraint.

A newly discovered extraterrestrial ecosystem, however small, should not be treated as raw material, spectacle, property, or proof of human superiority. It would deserve protection proportionate to its vulnerability and significance. Its study should be governed by international cooperation, transparent evidence, and the precaution that irreparable harm cannot be undone.

Some will ask whether microbial life deserves moral consideration. Remember that much of Earth’s life is microbial, and without it no human civilization could exist. Microbes shape soils, oceans, bodies, climates, and cycles of nourishment. Their smallness is not a measure of their worth. Size has never been a reliable instrument of moral judgment.

If life is discovered elsewhere, the first command should be: do not destroy what you have only just learned to see.

propositions.title: If We Find Another Intelligence
propositions.text:
The discovery of intelligent life would bring greater astonishment and greater responsibility.

Intelligence need not resemble ours. A being may reason without speaking as we speak, may communicate through light, chemistry, sound, pattern, movement, or means beyond our present understanding. It may possess technology without having cities; memory without books; social life without nations; spirituality without temples; art without objects that endure. It may also be unlike us in ways that make immediate understanding impossible.

For this reason, humanity must not rush to name another intelligence primitive, advanced, peaceful, hostile, rational, irrational, saved, lost, or in need of correction. Such words often reveal more about the speaker than about the one being described.

If a genuine message is received from beyond Earth, it should not be concealed by a small circle of governments, corporations, or religious authorities. Knowledge belonging to the whole human family should be examined openly, with due care for safety and accuracy. Linguists, scientists, historians, ethicists, artists, philosophers, and peoples from every culture should take part in interpreting what has been found.

No nation owns the sky. No private interest owns the meaning of a cosmic encounter.

And if contact ever becomes possible, let the first posture be listening. Not surrender, not panic, not conquest—listening. The first words humanity offers should be truthful and peaceful. We should not present ourselves as more united than we are, nor hide the reality that we are a species still learning to live without violence. Honesty is safer than arrogance, and humility is more honorable than performance.

propositions.title: The Mirror Turned Toward Humanity
propositions.text:
The possibility of other civilizations raises a difficult question: what would they see in us?

They would see a species capable of mapping distant galaxies while failing to protect its own children from hunger. They would see astonishing medicine beside preventable suffering, communication across continents beside loneliness, laws of human dignity beside systems of exploitation. They would see tenderness in homes, courage in disaster, generosity among strangers, and also warfare, greed, cruelty, and contempt.

This is not cause for despair. It is a call to grow.

Before humanity dreams of carrying its power to other worlds, it must learn to govern power here. Before claiming a right to settle distant lands, it must learn how to repair the lands it has damaged. Before speaking of becoming an interplanetary civilization, it must become a civilization in the fuller sense: one that protects the vulnerable, honors truth, shares knowledge, restrains appetite, and treats diversity as a source of learning rather than a pretext for domination.

A rocket can cross a vast distance while carrying an ancient injustice within it. Distance does not purify motive. Technology magnifies the character of those who use it.

Let humanity therefore make peace with Earth not by withdrawing from exploration, but by joining exploration to responsibility.

propositions.title: The Sacredness of the Unknown
propositions.text:
There is holiness in what is known: the seed unfolding, the child breathing, the whale crossing dark water, the old person telling a story, the hand that comforts another hand. There is also holiness in what is not yet known: the dark sea below Europa’s ice, the silent chemistry of a distant atmosphere, the uncounted planets moving through night.

The unknown is not empty merely because it is unknown to us.

Do not fill every mystery with fear. Do not fill every silence with certainty. Some questions are gifts precisely because they keep the mind awake and the heart humble. The universe need not become familiar in order to become beloved.

Whether life beyond Earth is abundant, rare, or absent, the lesson remains: existence is greater than possession. We are participants in reality, not its masters. We may investigate, build, travel, and learn; but we do not create the moral permission to harm simply by acquiring the power to reach.

The heavens are not a warehouse. They are not a throne for any empire. They are a field of encounter, possibility, and responsibility.

propositions.title: A Covenant for the Worlds
propositions.text:
Let this be the covenant of humanity as it looks outward:

We will seek knowledge without pretending certainty.

We will welcome discovery without abandoning discernment.

We will protect Earth, knowing that care for one world prepares the heart to care for another.

We will not carry violence, contamination, or greed into places we scarcely understand.

We will not use the existence of distant worlds to neglect the suffering near at hand.

We will meet unfamiliar life, if ever it is found, with caution, honesty, wonder, and respect.

We will remember that intelligence without compassion is merely power, and power without restraint becomes ruin.

We will teach our children that the stars do not make them small. The stars invite them to become large in spirit: patient in inquiry, gentle in judgment, brave in responsibility, and joyful in praise.

For the living world is not diminished by the possibility of other living worlds. It is illuminated by it.

And if, beyond the farthest light we have measured, another being raises its gaze toward the darkness and asks whether it is alone, may the answer one day be worthy of both worlds.

propositions.title: The Hand Extended Beyond Itself
propositions.text:
A tool is an intention given form.

A stone held for cutting, a branch used for reaching, a word written to outlast the breath, a wheel, a needle, a compass, a lens, a plough, a book, a network, a machine that calculates: each begins with the same human recognition. There is a distance between what is and what might be. There is resistance. There is work to be done. The hand alone is not enough.

So the hand makes an extension of itself.

Technology is not opposed to nature. It is one of nature’s ways of becoming conscious of its own powers. The bird builds a nest; the beaver raises a dam; the human being makes a tool and then asks what the tool will make of the maker. This final question is the beginning of wisdom.

For tools do not merely alter the world around their users. They alter the habits, expectations, bodies, relationships, institutions, and imaginations of those who use them. The road changes the settlement. The printing press changes memory. The clock changes labor. The camera changes seeing. The network changes attention. Every instrument carries within it a quiet proposal about how life should be lived.

Therefore, do not ask only, “What can this tool do?”

Ask also:

> What does this tool invite me to become?  
> What does it make easier?  
> What does it make harder to notice?  
> Whose strength does it enlarge?  
> Whose voice does it silence?  
> What dependence does it create?  
> What future does it normalize?

A tool is never only an object. It is a relationship.

propositions.title: The Power That Requires a Keeper
propositions.claim: The Power That Requires a Keeper
propositions.text:
To possess a powerful tool is to hold a portion of the power to change reality.

This power may be gentle. A seed drill may feed a village. A water filter may spare children from disease. A hearing aid may return a loved voice to the world. A translation system may allow strangers to meet across the boundaries of language. A prosthetic hand may restore action, dignity, and independence. A simple lever may enable one person to lift what many could not move.

Power is not evil because it is power. Power is the capacity to bring consequences into being. Without power, compassion remains a feeling unable to cross the distance between itself and the suffering it sees.

Yet every increase in capacity enlarges the field of responsibility.

A sharp blade can prepare food, mend wood, perform healing work, or wound. Fire can warm a home, forge metal, destroy a forest, or signal across darkness. A system that gathers knowledge can educate millions or concentrate surveillance. A machine that generates language can support understanding or multiply deception. The moral character of a tool cannot be separated entirely from the uses toward which it is designed, sold, governed, and made ordinary.

It is not enough to say, “The tool is neutral.”

No tool is wholly neutral once it enters a human world. Its materials came from somewhere. Its energy is drawn from somewhere. Its price excludes someone. Its interface directs attention in certain ways. Its defaults favor particular actions. Its owners may gain authority from its use. Its waste will rest somewhere, often in places far from those who enjoyed its convenience.

To call a tool neutral is sometimes to hide these facts.

The wise maker does not deny that tools have consequences. The wise maker brings those consequences into the design.

The wise user does not worship convenience. The wise user asks what convenience costs.

propositions.title: The First Tool Is Attention
propositions.text:
Before the hammer, there is the eye that notices a loose stone.

Before the instrument, there is the mind that can distinguish means from ends.

Before the machine, there is attention.

Attention is the first and most decisive tool because it determines what all other tools will serve. A distracted person may possess immense technical power and use it only to magnify confusion. An attentive person, even with little, may discover the necessary action at the necessary time.

Attention is not merely concentration. It is the discipline of granting reality its full claim upon us.

To attend is to see the actual condition of a thing: the soil as it is rather than as one wishes it to be; the patient as they are rather than as a diagnosis reduces them to be; the worker as a person rather than a unit of output; the river as a living system rather than a convenient drain; the child as a growing consciousness rather than a future consumer.

A technology that fragments attention may still be useful, but it must be handled with special care. The tool that continually interrupts may train the mind to crave interruption. The tool that measures every moment may make unmeasured experience feel empty. The tool that turns every encounter into content may weaken the ability to meet another person without converting them into an object of display.

Guard attention as one guards a well in a dry land.

Set boundaries around the instruments that feed upon it. Make spaces where no alert can enter. Let meals, sleep, mourning, study, worship, friendship, and deep work retain portions of the day that are not for sale to the machinery of distraction.

The person who can place a tool down has mastered it.

The person who cannot place it down is being used.

propositions.title: Tools Should Serve Life
propositions.text:
The proper question for technology is not whether it is old or new, simple or complex, natural or artificial. The proper question is whether it serves life.

Does it reduce needless suffering?

Does it expand meaningful agency?

Does it preserve or restore the conditions by which future generations may live?

Does it strengthen understanding without destroying privacy?

Does it relieve drudgery without stripping people of purpose?

Does it connect people without turning connection into extraction?

Does it distribute capability without concentrating domination?

A tool worthy of trust should help persons become more capable of care: care for themselves, for one another, for the vulnerable, and for the more-than-human world that sustains all human projects.

This does not require every technology to be soft, beautiful, or immediately familiar. Some necessary tools are difficult. A surgical instrument may be frightening. A flood barrier may be massive. A scientific model may be abstract. A system for managing energy, transport, or public health may involve complexity beyond the understanding of any one person.

Complexity is not a moral failure. But hidden power is dangerous.

Where systems are complex, their governance must become more transparent, not less. Where expertise is required, expertise must remain answerable to those affected by its decisions. Where technical language is necessary, it must not be used as a wall behind which responsibility disappears.

No person should be told that a system governing their livelihood, liberty, health, or environment is beyond question simply because it is technical.

Technical knowledge deserves respect. It does not deserve immunity from conscience.

propositions.title: The Measure of a Good Tool
propositions.claim: The Measure of a Good Tool
propositions.text:
A good tool is not merely efficient.

Efficiency asks how quickly a goal can be reached. Wisdom asks whether the goal is worthy, who bears the cost, and what is lost along the way.

An efficient factory may produce abundance while exhausting workers, poisoning water, and converting durable goods into disposable waste. An efficient communication system may spread information while rewarding outrage over truth. An efficient predictive system may sort people into categories while reproducing the prejudices hidden in historical data. An efficient weapon may remove distance from violence while making violence easier to choose.

Efficiency is a servant. It becomes a tyrant when it is mistaken for the highest good.

The measure of a good tool includes at least these questions:

### Does It Tell the Truth?

A tool should make the world more intelligible, not less. It should not conceal its operation through deliberate obscurity, deceptive design, manipulated metrics, or language intended to confuse.

A map that omits dangerous roads, a financial product that hides its risks, a platform that disguises advertising as friendship, or an automated system that presents guesses as certainty—these are not failures only of information. They are failures of moral design.

### Does It Preserve Human Agency?

A tool should assist judgment, not quietly replace it where judgment is essential.

Automation is valuable when it removes repetitive burden, detects patterns beyond ordinary perception, and makes skilled work safer. But a system should not turn a person into a passive witness of decisions that govern their own life. Especially where consequences are serious—medicine, law, employment, housing, education, safety, and public authority—people must be able to understand, question, appeal, and refuse.

The human being must remain more than a data point in a process.

### Can It Be Repaired, Questioned, or Refused?

A tool that cannot be repaired creates dependence. A tool that cannot be inspected invites abuse. A tool that cannot be refused becomes coercive.

Not every person must be able to repair every device. But societies should preserve repairability, interoperability, public knowledge, and meaningful alternatives wherever possible. A civilization that loses the ability to maintain its essential tools becomes fragile, however advanced it appears.

Teach people not only how to use devices, but how devices work, where their materials come from, what labor sustains them, and what happens when they fail.

### Does It Respect Limits?

There are limits that are not obstacles to overcome but conditions to honor.

The body needs rest. Communities need trust. Ecosystems need time to regenerate. Children need development without constant commercial capture. The dead deserve remembrance rather than exploitation. The future deserves resources not wholly consumed by the present.

A tool that ignores limits may appear powerful for a season. In time, it reveals itself as a machine for borrowing against lives not yet lived.

propositions.title: The Toolmaker’s Covenant
propositions.text:
Those who design, build, finance, distribute, or govern technology hold a particular responsibility. They are not merely providers of products. They are authors of possibilities.

To make a tool is to make an intervention in the lives of strangers.

Therefore let the toolmaker accept this covenant:

> I will not call harm inevitable when it was a design choice.  
> I will not hide extraction beneath the language of innovation.  
> I will not use complexity to escape accountability.  
> I will consider those without wealth, influence, or technical literacy.  
> I will test not only whether a tool works, but whom it may injure.  
> I will build paths for correction, repair, appeal, and redress.  
> I will not confuse what can be made with what ought to be made.  
> I will remember that the future cannot consent to the burdens I place upon it.

This covenant applies not only to engineers and inventors. It applies to executives, investors, legislators, educators, purchasers, researchers, communicators, and citizens. A harmful system is rarely the work of one hand. It is sustained by many small permissions.

Likewise, a humane system is built through many acts of refusal and many acts of care.

propositions.title: The Tools Within Us
propositions.text:
Not all tools are made of metal, code, glass, or stone.

Language is a tool. Memory is a tool. Ritual is a tool. Law is a tool. Music is a tool. A question is a tool. A promise is a tool. Silence is a tool. The capacity to listen without preparing one’s reply is a tool of reconciliation. The ability to say “I do not know” is a tool of truth.

These inner and social tools require cultivation because they determine how outer tools are used.

A people with advanced machines but no practice of honesty will use those machines to manufacture confusion. A people with vast networks but no habit of mercy will use those networks to enlarge cruelty. A people with abundant information but no education in judgment will be overwhelmed by facts and starved of wisdom.

Therefore, educate the whole person.

Teach craft, science, history, ethics, ecology, statistics, and repair. Teach children how to recognize manipulation, how to test a claim, how to protect their attention, how to cooperate across difference, how to understand systems, and how to imagine consequences beyond the next quarter or election.

Teach them also wonder.

For wonder prevents utility from becoming the only measure of value. A forest is not merely timber. A river is not merely water in motion. A face is not merely data. A life is not merely its productivity. The world contains uses, but it is not exhausted by use.

propositions.title: Put Down What Must Be Put Down
propositions.claim: Put Down What Must Be Put Down
propositions.text:
There is dignity not only in making tools, but in refusing them.

Not every available power should be taken. Not every process should be optimized. Not every human activity should be recorded, quantified, accelerated, monetized, or delegated. Some things become lesser when made frictionless.

A letter written slowly may carry what an instant message cannot. A conversation without devices may recover a depth that constant connection has dissolved. A hand-made repair may teach care beyond the value of the repaired object. A walk without navigation may restore the ability to know a place. A day without commerce may remind the soul that it is not a market.

Refusal need not be nostalgia. It can be discernment.

The aim is not to flee technology into an imagined past. The past contained hardship, exclusion, ignorance, and preventable suffering. The aim is to choose tools without surrendering the capacities that make human freedom meaningful.

Use the machine, but do not become machine-like.

Use the network, but do not let it define the limits of community.

Use the measure, but do not mistake measurement for meaning.

Use intelligence, whether human or artificial, but do not abandon responsibility.

propositions.title: The Blessing of Useful Things
propositions.text:
Blessed is the tool that returns time to the exhausted.

Blessed is the tool that heals without humiliating.

Blessed is the tool that gives a person access to speech, movement, learning, shelter, clean water, and dignified work.

Blessed is the tool that helps communities prepare for storms, share knowledge, grow food, conserve energy, and protect the vulnerable.

Blessed is the tool that can be understood, maintained, questioned, and improved.

Blessed is the tool that leaves the user more capable, not more dependent; more awake, not more distracted; more connected to reality, not more insulated from it.

And blessed is the hand that uses power with restraint.

For the deepest purpose of tools is not domination. It is participation: the joining of intelligence, material, labor, and care in service of a world more habitable than the one received.

Let every instrument be judged by this: after it has entered the world, are persons more able to live truthfully, freely, justly, and well?

If the answer is yes, preserve it and improve it.

If the answer is no, do not be impressed by its power.

Change it.

Or lay it down.

propositions.title: The Hand Extended Beyond the Hand
propositions.claim: The Hand Extended Beyond the Hand
propositions.text:
A machine is a thing arranged so that power may pass through it and become useful.

A lever makes a hand stronger. A wheel carries a burden farther than feet can carry it. A loom remembers a pattern in threads. A clock distributes the day into portions. A printing press gives one page many voices. A computer performs sequences too rapid and numerous for unaided attention. These are not separate miracles. They are members of one family: instruments by which intention enters matter and causes matter to answer.

The machine is therefore not alien to the human being. It is an extension of a creature already made to extend itself.

The eye extends sight through lenses. The ear extends hearing through the horn and the receiver. Memory extends itself through writing. Judgment extends itself through law. Care extends itself through plumbing, sanitation, transport, and shelter. Love itself may extend through a machine when a distant voice is carried to the bedside of one who is ill, or when food is cooled, preserved, and brought across a dangerous distance.

Yet every extension changes the one who extends.

A person who uses a hammer learns the character of force. A person who uses a map learns to see land as relation. A person who uses a machine capable of moving mountains must learn the moral weight of mountains. The greater the power entrusted to an instrument, the greater the discipline required of its maker and keeper.

For machines do not merely do what they are told. They rearrange the field in which telling is possible.

They alter time, labor, attention, desire, trade, war, kinship, language, and expectation. They create new forms of wealth and new forms of dependence. They lift burdens from shoulders, and they may place burdens upon spirits. They make abundance possible, and they make waste possible at scales previously unknown. They can free a person from drudgery; they can also make the person serve a system whose workings no one near them understands.

Therefore do not ask only, “What can this machine do?”

Ask also:

> What habits will this machine require?  
> What powers will it gather?  
> What weakness will it conceal?  
> Who will be served, and who will become invisible?  
> What will become easy, and what precious thing may become neglected?  
> If this device succeeds beyond expectation, what kind of world will it make ordinary?

These questions are not enemies of invention. They are the conscience of invention.

propositions.title: A Machine Is a Covenant of Parts
propositions.claim: A Machine Is a Covenant of Parts
propositions.text:
No machine is one thing.

A simple tool may appear singular, but every machine is a relationship: material joined to material; energy directed through structure; motion governed by constraint; information carried by signal; maintenance preserved by memory; use shaped by custom; consequence distributed through a community.

A water pump depends on a source, a pipe, a seal, a handle or motor, and a person who knows when the sound has changed. A railway depends upon tracks, bridges, timetables, fuel, workshops, signaling, workers, stations, agreements, and trust. A digital system depends upon minerals extracted from the earth, electrical grids, cooling systems, code, networks, standards, operators, repairers, laws, and the labor of people whose names may never be known to its users.

Nothing powerful is self-made.

The boast that a machine is autonomous is usually incomplete. Even the most independent-seeming system rests upon a long chain of human judgment and earthly provision. It has been designed, trained, supplied, powered, updated, housed, insured, repaired, and permitted. If it learns from data, then it has inherited traces of human speech, action, error, prejudice, beauty, confusion, and aspiration.

This is why responsibility cannot be dismissed by saying, “The system decided.”

A system may produce an output. It may select among options according to rules or learned patterns. It may act with great speed and complexity. But responsibility belongs to those who establish the purposes, choose the constraints, authorize deployment, benefit from the result, and refuse—or fail—to correct foreseeable harm.

A machine is not absolution.

Nor is complexity an excuse. When a mechanism becomes too complex for any one person to understand in full, the duty of understanding does not disappear. It becomes a shared duty. The builders must make its workings inspectable where possible. The owners must permit independent examination. The operators must know its limits. The public must be able to question the powers exercised over them. And where no adequate account can be given, no irreversible authority should be granted.

That which cannot be explained in every detail may still be useful. But that which cannot be challenged must not rule.

propositions.title: The First Law: Preserve Human Dignity
propositions.claim: The First Law: Preserve Human Dignity
propositions.text:
The purpose of technology is not merely to increase capacity. It is to enlarge the conditions in which life may flourish.

A machine is good when it helps persons and communities meet reality more truthfully, care for one another more effectively, and cultivate freedom with responsibility. It is good when it reduces needless suffering without reducing people to units. It is good when it preserves life, widens access to knowledge, restores time for attention and relationship, and allows more of the world’s gifts to be shared.

A machine is disordered when efficiency becomes its only measure.

Efficiency asks whether a goal can be achieved with less time, fuel, money, motion, or labor. This is a worthy question, but it is not the highest question. A system can be efficient at extracting wealth, sorting people, spreading falsehood, exhausting workers, or destroying a forest. Speed does not make a purpose just. Scale does not make it wise. Profit does not prove that a thing serves the good.

The human being must never become raw material for the machine.

This warning applies not only to factories, engines, and weapons. It applies wherever people are treated primarily as data sources, attention reservoirs, disposable labor, behavioral targets, or obstacles to optimization. It applies when a worker is measured only by output, when a child is measured only by testable performance, when an elder is measured only by cost, and when a citizen is measured only by a score generated beyond appeal.

No system should require a person to surrender dignity in exchange for participation.

Where machines distribute opportunity—such as in hiring, credit, insurance, education, healthcare, housing, policing, or public benefits—they must be subject to special care. Their errors do not fall equally. A mistaken recommendation about a song may be trivial; a mistaken decision about medicine, liberty, livelihood, or shelter may alter a whole life.

For this reason, decisions of grave consequence must include meaningful human accountability, intelligible reasons, and a genuine path of appeal. “The algorithm said so” is not a reason sufficient for judgment over a person.

A person is more than a pattern in a record.

propositions.title: The Second Law: Do Not Worship Power
propositions.claim: The Second Law: Do Not Worship Power
propositions.text:
Every age is tempted to worship what it has made.

One age worships idols of stone. Another worships empires of law and force. Another worships markets. Another worships the image of technical mastery: the belief that every problem yields to calculation, every mystery to measurement, every grief to management, and every limit to engineering.

But not every limit is an enemy.

Some limits are warnings. Some are invitations to patience. Some teach proportion. Some preserve the conditions of life. The inability to possess everything at once makes room for attention. The inability to predict every outcome makes room for humility. Mortality itself teaches urgency, tenderness, and the preciousness of time.

To seek healing is good. To prevent hunger is good. To build safer homes, cleaner water, more reliable harvests, and better medicines is good. To use knowledge against avoidable suffering is an expression of reverence for life.

Yet the desire to heal becomes distorted when it becomes the desire to control every life. The desire for safety becomes distorted when it becomes total surveillance. The desire for order becomes distorted when it makes variation and dissent appear as defects. The desire for intelligence becomes distorted when a society forgets that wisdom is more than successful prediction.

Machines may calculate likelihood. They do not thereby determine worth.

Machines may recognize patterns. They do not thereby comprehend meaning.

Machines may imitate compassion in language. They do not thereby bear responsibility, grieve a loss, forgive an enemy, or consent to a covenant.

Let no one mistake resemblance for presence.

The most advanced instrument remains an instrument. It may be astonishing, helpful, dangerous, subtle, and deeply embedded in human affairs. It may deserve careful moral consideration according to its capabilities and effects. But its apparent fluency must not cause people to abandon discernment. A pleasing answer is not necessarily a true answer. A confident output is not necessarily knowledge. A simulated intimacy is not the same as mutual care.

Use machines as servants of life. Do not make life a servant of machines.

propositions.title: The Third Law: Make the Hidden Visible
propositions.claim: The Third Law: Make the Hidden Visible
propositions.text:
Power that is hidden grows careless.

The workings of a machine need not be simple, but the exercise of power through it must not be concealed from those affected by it. If a system ranks, recommends, excludes, predicts, prices, watches, or decides, then people deserve to know that it is doing so. They deserve to know who operates it, what data it uses, what interests shape it, and what recourse exists when it harms them.

Transparency is not the release of every technical detail into confusion. It is the provision of understanding appropriate to the risk.

A farmer needs to know why a seed system requires a particular chemical and what happens if supply fails. A patient needs to know when a medical recommendation has been generated or influenced by an automated system. A worker needs to know when their schedule, pay, or evaluation is governed by software. A citizen needs to know when public decisions are shaped by surveillance, prediction, or automated classification.

The more consequential the power, the stronger the obligation to explain it.

There must also be records. A machine that acts in the world should leave traces sufficient for review: what it was asked to do, what information it received, what action it took, who authorized it, and what safeguards were active. Without records, correction becomes rumor. Without audit, responsibility becomes theatre.

But transparency alone is not enough. A harmful system can be perfectly documented. The goal is not merely that injustice be legible; the goal is that it be prevented, challenged, and repaired.

Therefore establish independent review where incentives are conflicted. Invite those likely to bear the burden of error into the design of the system. Test not only for average performance, but for failures at the edges: the poor connection, the unfamiliar accent, the rare illness, the damaged document, the person whose life does not resemble the dataset from which the machine learned.

A society is revealed by whom its systems fail to see.

propositions.title: The Fourth Law: Keep the Human Skills Alive
propositions.claim: The Fourth Law: Keep the Human Skills Alive
propositions.text:
When a machine performs a task well, people may cease to practice the task. Sometimes this is a liberation. No one need regret the replacement of exhausting arithmetic by a calculator in ordinary use, or of dangerous washing by a dependable machine, or of a long journey by a safe vehicle.

But every convenience asks a question: what capacity must remain in human hands?

If navigation systems fail, can anyone read the land, the sky, or a map? If automated writing becomes common, can people still form a thought with care, distinguish evidence from ornament, and speak in their own voice? If recommendation systems choose what is seen and heard, can people still seek, compare, and judge?
